original_information.commit_message:
tun: call dev_get_valid_name() before register_netdevice()

register_netdevice() could fail early when we have an invalid
dev name, in which case ->ndo_uninit() is not called. For tun
device, this is a problem because a timer etc. are already
initialized and it expects ->ndo_uninit() to clean them up.

We could move these initializations into a ->ndo_init() so
that register_netdevice() knows better, however this is still
complicated due to the logic in tun_detach().

Therefore, I choose to just call dev_get_valid_name() before
register_netdevice(), which is quicker and much easier to audit.
And for this specific case, it is already enough.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

original_information.commit_message:
net: ip_expire() must revalidate route

Commit 4a94445c9a5c (net: Use ip_route_input_noref() in input path)
added a bug in IP defragmentation handling, in case timeout is fired.

When a frame is defragmented, we use last skb dst field when building
final skb. Its dst is valid, since we are in rcu read section.

But if a timeout occurs, we take first queued fragment to build one ICMP
TIME EXCEEDED message. Problem is all queued skb have weak dst pointers,
since we escaped RCU critical section after their queueing. icmp_send()
might dereference a now freed (and possibly reused) part of memory.

Calling skb_dst_drop() and ip_route_input_noref() to revalidate route is
the only possible choice.

   The function `apply_xml_diff` takes three parameters:  
   - `old`: the original XML document (as an `xmlNode*`)  
   - `diff`: an XML document describing what to remove and what to add  
   - `new`: address of an `xmlNode*` where the resulting document will be stored  

   Internally it does the following steps:

   A. Initialization  
   - Declares and initializes local variables:  
     • `result` flag (starts as TRUE)  
     • `root_nodes_seen` counter (starts at 0)  
     • A static pointer `digest_cs` for optional tracing  
     • Retrieves the expected digest (`XML_ATTR_DIGEST`) and CRM version from the `diff` element.  

   - Looks for two child elements of `diff`:  
     • `<diff-removed>`: nodes to subtract  
     • `<diff-added>`: nodes to add  

   - Verifies the `new` pointer is not NULL.  

   B. Subtraction Phase  
   - Logs “Substraction Phase.”  
   - Iterates over each direct child of `<diff-removed>`:  
     • Ensures only one top-level change set by checking `root_nodes_seen==0`.  
     • On the first child, calls `subtract_xml_object(NULL, old, child_diff, FALSE, ...)` to remove matching portions from `old`, storing the result in `*new`.  
     • Increments `root_nodes_seen`.  
   - After the loop:  
     • If no removal nodes were seen (`root_nodes_seen==0`), simply does `*new = copy_xml(old)`.  
     • If more than one removal group was seen, logs an error and marks `result = FALSE`.  

   C. Addition Phase  
   - Resets `root_nodes_seen` to 0 and logs “Addition Phase.”  
   - If subtraction succeeded (`result` still TRUE):  
     • Iterates over each direct child of `<diff-added>`:  
        – Again requires only one top-level change by checking `root_nodes_seen==0`.  
        – On the first child, calls `add_xml_object(NULL, *new, child_diff, TRUE)` to apply additions.  
        – Increments `root_nodes_seen`.  
   - After the loop:  
     • If more than one addition group was seen, logs an error and sets `result = FALSE`.  

   D. Digest Verification and Cleanup  
   - If everything so far succeeded and an expected digest was provided:  
     • Calls `purge_diff_markers(*new)` to remove any diff-related metadata.  
     • Calculates a new digest of `*new` via `calculate_xml_versioned_digest`.  
     • Compares the calculated digest to the expected one:  
        – On mismatch, logs the discrepancy, sets `result = FALSE`, and (if tracing is enabled) saves the old, diff, and new XML to files for debugging.  
        – On match, logs a trace.  
     • Frees the locally allocated digest string.  
   - If there was no expected digest but result is still TRUE, it still calls `purge_diff_markers(*new)` to finalize the XML.  

   Finally, it returns the boolean `result`, indicating whether the diff application (and optional digest check) succeeded.

   • NULL-pointer safety  
     – The code checks that `new` is non-NULL.  
     – It assumes `old` and `diff` are valid pointers to parsed XML nodes (caller responsibility).  

   • Buffer overflows / integer overflows  
     – The only counter is `root_nodes_seen`, incremented at most once per child node. Typical XML sizes won’t overflow a 32-bit int.  

   • XML-specific attacks (e.g., XXE)  
     – This routine operates on in-memory `xmlNode*` trees that presumably come from elsewhere. Any XXE prevention must be handled at parsing time, not here.  

   • Resource exhaustion / DoS  
     – Large XML trees could consume memory, but this function does not introduce unbounded loops beyond the number of children.  

   • Digest handling  
     – Uses `calculate_xml_versioned_digest` and a safe string comparison (`safe_str_neq`).  
     – Frees the computed digest.  
     – No string-format vulnerabilities in logging calls (the format strings are constant).  

   • Race conditions / TOCTOU  
     – Not applicable: single-threaded in-memory operations.  

   Overall, the code applies high-level XML diffs safely and validates them with a digest. No obvious buffer overflow, format-string, or pointer misuse is present. Diff markers are explicitly purged, and only one change set is allowed in each phase to prevent ambiguous modifications.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly bounds loop iterations, validates pointers, and checks its digest.

IB/security: Restrict use of the write() interface

The drivers/infiniband stack uses write() as a replacement for
bi-directional ioctl().  This is not safe. There are ways to
trigger write calls that result in the return structure that
is normally written to user space being shunted off to user
specified kernel memory instead.

For the immediate repair, detect and deny suspicious accesses to
the write API.

For long term, update the user space libraries and the kernel API
to something that doesn't present the same security vulnerabilities
(likely a structured ioctl() interface).

The impacted uAPI interfaces are generally only available if
hardware from drivers/infiniband is installed in the system.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function nsec_to_cycles(u64 nsec) converts a time interval in nanoseconds to CPU cycles.
- WARN_ON(preemptible())  
  - Emits a kernel warning if the caller is preemptible, since the conversion relies on a per-CPU TSC rate and must not be interrupted.
- if (kvm_tsc_changes_freq()) printk_once(…)  
  - If running under KVM with an adjustable-rate TSC, it prints a one-time warning that the cycle conversion may be unreliable.
- ret = nsec * __get_cpu_var(cpu_tsc_khz);  
  - Reads the per-CPU TSC frequency in kHz and multiplies it by the nanoseconds value.
- do_div(ret, USEC_PER_SEC);  
  - Divides the 64-bit product by USEC_PER_SEC (1,000,000), effectively computing  
    ret = (nsec * tsc_khz) / 1,000,000  
  to yield the number of CPU cycles in that interval.
- return ret;  
  - Returns the computed cycle count.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer overflow  
  - The multiplication nsec * cpu_tsc_khz can overflow a 64-bit value if nsec is very large. There is no explicit check or use of 128-bit arithmetic before division. In pathological cases (e.g. nsec > ~2^64/tsc_khz) this will wrap modulo 2^64, leading to an incorrect (wrapped) cycle count.
- Division-by-zero  
  - USEC_PER_SEC is a compile‐time constant (1,000,000), so do_div(ret, USEC_PER_SEC) cannot divide by zero.
- Preemption/race safety  
  - The WARN_ON(preemptible()) check ensures the caller is non-preemptible; otherwise the per-CPU TSC rate could change mid‑calculation. No race appears if the check succeeds.
- Security impact  
  - The only notable weakness is a potential arithmetic overflow, but it simply yields a wrong cycle count rather than corrupting memory or enabling code execution. No buffer overflows or memory corruption are present.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a security vulnerability. The only theoretical issue is a 64‑bit arithmetic overflow in the multiplication, which can cause incorrect results but not a security breach.

- The function is annotated with __acquires(rose_node_list_lock), indicating it will take the rose_node_list_lock.
- It declares a pointer `rose_node` and an iteration index `i` initialized to 1.
- It acquires the lock via `spin_lock_bh(&rose_node_list_lock)`.
- If the caller’s position counter `*pos` is zero, it returns the special token `SEQ_START_TOKEN`.
- Otherwise it walks the global linked list `rose_node_list`, advancing `rose_node = rose_node->next` and incrementing `i` until either the end of the list or until `i == *pos`.

- Locking Discipline: The lock is acquired here and (by convention in the seq_file pattern) released in the corresponding stop callback. There is no obvious lock imbalance in this snippet alone.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any practical vulnerabilities. It correctly locks and bounds its list traversal and follows the seq_file locking conventions.

  - `find_hdr_value_end(char *s, const char *e)` takes two pointers:  
    • `s` points to the start of the header‐value substring to scan  
    • `e` points just past the last valid character  
  - It returns a pointer to the first comma (`,`) that lies outside any quoted segment, or `e` if none is found.

- Local state  
  - `quoted` tracks whether the parser is currently inside a double‐quoted (`"… "`) span.  
  - `qdpair` tracks whether the immediately preceding character was a backslash (`\`), so that an escaped quote (`\"`) is not treated as closing the quoted span.

- Word‐at‐a‐time “speedup” loop (only on certain x86 or ARM‐7 builds)  
  - It treats the memory as a sequence of 32‐bit words and tries to detect any byte equal to `','` (0x2C) or `'"'` (0x22) in one go.  
  - It does this by XORing each 32‐bit word with a repeated‐byte constant, using a standard zero‐detection trick to break out as soon as one of those two bytes appears in the next few bytes.

- Byte‐by‐byte remainder scan  
  - Once the fast loop either finds a candidate word or runs out of room, it falls back to a simple `for (; s < e; s++)` loop.  
  - If currently in an escape pair (`qdpair`), it simply clears `qdpair` and moves on.  
  - Else if inside quotes (`quoted`):  
    • if it sees `\`, it sets `qdpair = 1` to skip the next character  
    • else if it sees `"`, it ends the quoted segment (`quoted = 0`)  
  - Else (outside any quoted span):  
    • if it sees `"`, it begins a quoted span (`quoted = 1`)  
    • if it sees `,`, it returns that pointer (the end of the current header‐value token)  
  - If no comma is found before `e`, it returns `e`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory‐safety / bounds  
  - The code only ever reads in the range `[s, e)` and carefully stops the word‐loop when `s > e - sizeof(int)` and the byte‐loop when `s == e`. There is no buffer overflow or read past `e`.  
- Quoted‐string logic  
  - Handles escaped quotes (`\"`) correctly and does not treat a comma inside a quoted span as a delimiter.  
- Strict‐aliasing / alignment  
  - The word‐at‐a‐time path casts `char *` to `int *` and dereferences it.  
    • On architectures with strict alignment requirements (some ARM variants), this can trigger a hardware fault if `s` is not 4‐byte aligned.  
    • From a C‐standard standpoint, reading arbitrary bytes as `int` may also violate strict‐aliasing rules, though many compilers tolerate it with `-fno-strict-aliasing`.  
  - That said, this only affects the “speedup” path; the fallback byte‐by‐byte loop is always safe.  
- No other exploitable conditions  
  - There is no dynamic memory allocation, no buffer writes, no format‐string or integer‐overflow risks.  
  - An attacker cannot use a crafted header string to make the function write out of bounds or return an arbitrary pointer outside `[s, e]`.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities in normal use. The only caveat is that on strict‐alignment platforms, the unaligned 32‐bit reads may fault; it is otherwise memory‐safe and correctly handles quoted commas.

1. Functional Analysis

  The function ext4_block_truncate_page() is called when a file is being truncated or when writes leave a “tail” of a page that must be zeroed. Briefly, it does the following:

  a. Compute the page index and byte-offset within that page corresponding to the file offset ‘from’.  
  b. Look up (or allocate) the page in the page cache and lock it.  
  c. Calculate blocksize and determine how many bytes at the end of the block need zeroing.  
  d. Calculate the logical block number (iblock) within the file corresponding to that offset.  
  e. If the “nobh” (no buffer-heads) mount option is in effect and the page is already up-to-date, zero the user portion directly in the page, mark it dirty, and skip buffer-head I/O.  
  f. Otherwise, ensure the page has buffer_head structures for each filesystem block.  
  g. Walk the buffers to find the one covering the truncate offset.  
  h. If that buffer has been freed (a hole), or is unmapped, or is already up-to-date, skip any read. Otherwise, submit a read to bring it in.  
  i. If the filesystem is journaling file-data, acquire write access to that buffer in the journal.  
  j. Zero the user-visible bytes in the page from the truncate offset to the end of the block.  
  k. Mark the buffer and/or inode appropriately—either buffer-dirty under the journal or mark the inode for write-ordering.  
  l. Unlock and release the page, returning 0 or an error code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  • Integer arithmetic:  
    – ‘offset = from & (PAGE_CACHE_SIZE-1)’ confines offset to one page.  
    – ‘length = blocksize - (offset & (blocksize-1))’ confines length to at most one block.  
    – Block number computation ‘iblock = index << (PAGE_CACHE_SHIFT - sb->s_blocksize_bits)’ matches ext4’s internal limits. ext4 enforces a maximum file size so that iblock never overflows the 32-bit block number.  
  • Bounds checks:  
    – Offsets and lengths are masked to page-size and block-size boundaries.  
    – Buffer traversal stops when offset < pos, so no out-of-bounds access to page buffers.  
  • Concurrency and races:  
    – The page is locked (via find_or_create_page) until zeroing and buffer manipulation complete.  
    – ext4_get_block, buffer state checks, and journal write-access calls are all done under proper synchronization.  
  • I/O failures:

ext4: use ext4_get_block_write in buffer write

convert the extent to initialized after io completes.

initialized after it has been written with new data so

Remove the Simple Default Stylesheet, it's just a foot-gun.

We've been bitten by the Simple Default Stylesheet being out
of sync with the real html.css twice this week.

The Simple Default Stylesheet was invented years ago for Mac:
http://trac.webkit.org/changeset/36135
It nicely handles the case where you just want to create
a single WebView and parse some simple HTML either without
styling said HTML, or only to display a small string, etc.

Note that this optimization/complexity *only* helps for the
very first document, since the default stylesheets are
all static (process-global) variables.  Since any real page
on the internet uses a tag not covered by the simple default
stylesheet, not real load benefits from this optimization.
Only uses of WebView which were just rendering small bits
of text might have benefited from this.  about:blank would
also have used this sheet.

This was a common application for some uses of WebView back
in those days.  These days, even with WebView on Android,
there are likely much larger overheads than parsing the
html.css stylesheet, so making it required seems like the
right tradeoff of code-simplicity for this case.

net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

This prevents numerous uninitialized memory leaks we had in the
recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

Optimize for the case recvfrom is called with NULL as address. We don't
need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Also document these changes in include/linux/net.h as suggested by David
Miller.

non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "

".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

comments to netdev style.

seems sane, as these packets are going to be dropped anyway.

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix hash overflow handling

The handling for directory crc hash overflows was fairly obscure,
split_leaf returns EOVERFLOW when we try to extend the item and that is
supposed to bubble up to userland.  For a while it did so, but along the
way we added better handling of errors and forced the FS readonly if we
hit IO errors during the directory insertion.

Along the way, we started testing only for EEXIST and the EOVERFLOW case
was dropped.  The end result is that we may force the FS readonly if we
catch a directory hash bucket overflow.

This fixes a few problem spots.  First I add tests for EOVERFLOW in the
places where we can safely just return the error up the chain.

btrfs_rename is harder though, because it tries to insert the new
directory item only after it has already unlinked anything the rename
was going to overwrite.  Rather than adding very complex logic, I added
a helper to test for the hash overflow case early while it is still safe
to bail out.

Snapshot and subvolume creation had a similar problem, so they are using
the new helper now too.

Signed-off-by: Chris Mason <chris.mason@fusionio.com>
Reported-by: Pascal Junod <pascal@junod.info>

1. Functional Analysis

- The function nested_vmx_exit_handled_io checks whether an I/O instruction VM‐exit in a nested VM should be handled by the L1 hypervisor (returns true) or injected back into the L2 guest (returns false).
- It first tests if the VMCS12 control field CPU_BASED_USE_IO_BITMAPS is set.  
  - If not, it falls back to CPU_BASED_UNCOND_IO_EXITING.  
- It reads the EXIT_QUALIFICATION field, from which it extracts:  
  - `port` (bits 16–31) – the I/O port number.  
  - `size` (bits 0–2 + 1) – the transfer size (1–8 bytes).  
- It then iterates over each byte of the transfer:  
  - Chooses IO_BITMAP_A if port < 0x8000, IO_BITMAP_B if port < 0x10000, or unconditionally returns true if port ≥ 0x10000.  
  - Computes the byte‐offset within the bitmap (`(port & 0x7fff)/8`) and reads one byte from the guest’s bitmap page via kvm_vcpu_read_guest (unless it’s the same page as the previous iteration).  
  - Tests the bit corresponding to the port within that byte; if the bit is set or the read fails, it returns true (meaning “exit is handled by L1”).  
  - Otherwise it increments port, decrements size, and continues.  
- If all ports in the range are clear in the bitmaps, it returns false (inject the I/O back to L2).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Port and size are derived from a fixed-width VMCS field and bounded to 1–8 bytes, so the loop iteration count is limited.
- The code branches correctly between the two 32K‐bit bitmaps and rejects ports ≥ 0x10000.
- Address arithmetic (`bitmap + offset`) uses a 4K‐byte maximum offset (0x7fff/8 ≤ 4095), so it cannot overflow the host’s address space.
- kvm_vcpu_read_guest safely handles faults or invalid GPAs by returning an error, which causes the function to return true (a conservative safe path that triggers a VM exit rather than cause host memory corruption).
- Temporary storage for the byte read is a single u8; there is no buffer overflow or uninitialized memory use (b is set before use or triggers the safe-exit path).

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities; it correctly bounds and validates all indices, handles read errors safely, and enforces the VMX I/O bitmap semantics.

fbdev: Fixing arbitrary kernel leak in case FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC in sbusfb_ioctl_helper().

Fixing arbitrary kernel leak in case FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC in
sbusfb_ioctl_helper().

'index' is defined as an int in sbusfb_ioctl_helper().
We retrieve this from the user:
if (get_user(index, &c->index) ||
    __get_user(count, &c->count) ||
    __get_user(ured, &c->red) ||
    __get_user(ugreen, &c->green) ||

green = cmap->green[index + i] >> 8;
blue = cmap->blue[index + i] >> 8;

This is a classic information leak vulnerability. 'index' should be
an unsigned int, given its usage above.

This patch is straight-forward; it changes 'index' to unsigned int
in two switch-cases: FBIOGETCMAP_SPARC && FBIOPUTCMAP_SPARC.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

- The function `ebt_size_mwt` walks through a sequence of “compat” match descriptors (`compat_ebt_entry_mwt`) in a user‐supplied buffer, computing how much additional space (the “growth”) will be needed when each descriptor is transformed into its native (kernel) representation.
- It takes as inputs:  
  • `match32` – pointer to the first compat header  
  • `size_left` – remaining bytes in the input buffer  
  • `type` – whether we’re in match or target mode  
  • `state` – holds the kernel‐side output buffer and current offset  
  • `base` – a pointer used by the compat‐to‐native converter  
- If `size_left` is zero, it immediately returns zero growth.  
- Otherwise it loops while there’s at least enough input left for one header:  
  a. It appends the 32-bit header to the kernel buffer (`ebt_buf_add`).  
  b. It pads the kernel buffer as required for alignment.  
  c. It checks that the `match_size` field in the header does not exceed the remaining input; if it does, it returns –EINVAL.  
  d. It calls `compat_mtw_from_user`, which copies and converts exactly `match_size` bytes of match‐specific data into the kernel buffer, returning `ret` = actual bytes written.  
  e. A `BUG_ON(ret < match_size)` asserts that the converter did not shrink the data.  
  f. It increments the total `growth` by `(ret – match_size) + padsize`.  
  g. It adjusts the input pointer and `size_left` by the header size and original `match_size`, then repeats.  
- At the end it returns the accumulated `growth`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer‐overread / out‐of‐bounds: Each time before reading a header or the variable‐length payload, the code checks `size_left` against the header size and `match_size`, so it cannot read past the user buffer.  
- Integer overflows: `size_left` is monotonically decreased by known positive amounts; no wrap-around is possible. The only arithmetic on `growth` adds small nonnegative differences—overflow into a negative return is extremely improbable in practice.  
- Kernel buffer overflow: All calls that write into the kernel buffer (`ebt_buf_add`, `ebt_buf_add_pad`, and whatever internal calls `compat_mtw_from_user` makes) are assumed to check remaining kernel‐buffer capacity and return an error if there is insufficient space.  
- Infinite loop: Even if `match_size` were zero, `size_left` is decreased by at least the header size each iteration, guaranteeing progress.  
- Unchecked WARN or BUG: The `BUG_ON` and `WARN_ON` are sanity checks but do not open an exploitable path under normal operation.

3. Decision

No, the code correctly bounds and validates its reads and writes, so no exploitable vulnerability is present.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function __ctr_crypt implements CTR-mode encryption (or decryption, symmetric for CTR) over a 3DES-EDE cipher context.
- It retrieves:
  • ctx            – the 3DES-EDE key schedule  
  • bsize          – block size (8 bytes)  
  • nbytes         – total bytes to process  
  • src, dst       – pointers to input/output buffers as 64-bit BE words  
  • ctrblk         – current counter value (taken from the IV, big-endian)
- It processes the bulk of the data in batches of three blocks (24 bytes) to leverage the 3-way parallel block encryption routine des3_ede_enc_blk_3way:
  • It builds an array ctrblocks[0..2] with three successive counter values, converting each to big-endian.  
  • It encrypts these three counters in parallel.  
  • It XORs each encrypted counter block with the corresponding plaintext block to produce ciphertext (or vice versa).  
  • It advances src, dst and increments ctrblk appropriately, looping until fewer than 3 blocks remain.
- If any full blocks remain (< 3 but ≥ 1), it handles them one by one:
  • Encrypt a single counter block with des3_ede_enc_blk  
  • XOR with one input block  
  • Increment src, dst, counter, repeat until < 1 block remains.
- Finally, it stores the updated counter back into walk->iv for the next call and returns the leftover byte count (< block size).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Correctness of CTR transformation:  
  • Uses a monotonically incremented counter, unique per block.  
  • Converts counter to big-endian when encrypting, matches DES block ordering.  
  • XORs encrypted counter with plaintext in place.
- Parallelization:  
  • The 3-way routine is used only when at least 3 blocks remain; leftovers fall back to the single-block routine.  
  • No overrun: loops guard on nbytes and bsize.
- State management:  
  • The IV (counter) is consistently updated and stored back.  
  • No reuse of the same counter value for two different blocks in one invocation.
- Memory safety:  
  • src and dst pointers are advanced only by whole blocks.  
  • Reads/writes are in 8-byte increments matching block size; alignment is implied by the walking infrastructure.
- No direct mitigation or enforcement of:
  • Replay protection or authentication (CTR mode provides confidentiality but not integrity).  
  • Proper IV uniqueness across distinct encryption operations (caller responsibility).
- Side-channels:  
  • The code does not include any key-dependent branches inside the encryption routines; assuming the lower-level DES library is constant-time, this wrapper preserves that behavior.
- Conclusion: The code correctly implements CTR-mode 3DES block processing without introducing buffer overflows, counter reuse within one call, or obvious side channels at this layer.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities in its block-processing logic—it correctly implements CTR mode for 3DES.

original_information.Summary: The try_to_unmap_cluster function in mm/rmap.c in the Linux kernel before 3.14.3 does not properly consider which pages must be locked, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (system crash) by triggering a memory-usage pattern that requires removal of page-table mappings.
original_information.commit_message:
mm: try_to_unmap_cluster() should lock_page() before mlocking

A BUG_ON(!PageLocked) was triggered in mlock_vma_page() by Sasha Levin
fuzzing with trinity.  The call site try_to_unmap_cluster() does not lock
the pages other than its check_page parameter (which is already locked).

The BUG_ON in mlock_vma_page() is not documented and its purpose is
somewhat unclear, but apparently it serializes against page migration,
which could otherwise fail to transfer the PG_mlocked flag.  This would
not be fatal, as the page would be eventually encountered again, but
NR_MLOCK accounting would become distorted nevertheless.  This patch adds
a comment to the BUG_ON in mlock_vma_page() and munlock_vma_page() to that
effect.

The call site try_to_unmap_cluster() is fixed so that for page !=
check_page, trylock_page() is attempted (to avoid possible deadlocks as we
already have check_page locked) and mlock_vma_page() is performed only
upon success.  If the page lock cannot be obtained, the page is left
without PG_mlocked, which is again not a problem in the whole unevictable
memory design.

1.1 Initialization and Quick-Path Detection  
- The function takes two pixel cache descriptors (`cache_info` and `clone_info`) and an exception structure.  
- If the source cache is a “ping” cache (metadata only), it immediately returns success.  
- It compares dimensions (columns, rows), channel counts, channel maps, and metacontent extent.  

1.2 Direct Memory or Disk Copy for Identical Layouts  
- If both caches have identical geometry and both are in-memory or memory-mapped, it does a single `memcpy` of the pixel buffer (and metacontent buffer if present), then returns.  
- If both are disk-based caches with identical layout, it delegates to `ClonePixelCacheOnDisk`.

1.3 General-Purpose Clone via Nexus Buffers  
- Allocates per-thread “nexus” buffers for source and destination.  
- Determines whether a channel‐order “optimize” path can be taken (same number of channels and same channel_map).  
- Computes a safe copy length as the minimum of source and destination row sizes.

1.4 Parallel Row-by-Row Copy  
- Uses OpenMP (if enabled) to iterate over each source row `y`.  
- For each row:  
   • Reads one row of source pixels into the source nexus.  
   • Sets up a write buffer in the destination nexus.  
   • If layouts match, does a single `memcpy` of row data; otherwise iterates through columns and channels mapping and copying individual channel values.  
   • Writes the filled row into the destination cache.  

1.5 Metacontent Copy  
- If per-pixel metadata (metacontent) is present, repeats a similar parallel loop to read each row’s metacontent from source and write it into destination, using `memcpy` with the minimum metacontent extent.

1.6 Cleanup and Logging  
- Frees the nexus buffers.  
- Optionally logs the cache-type transition if debugging is enabled.  
- Returns overall success/failure status.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

2.1 Buffer Overflows  
- All `memcpy` calls use size computations constrained by the minimum of source and destination dimensions or extents.  
- In the channel-­reordering path, loops check column bounds and break when reaching `clone_info->columns`.  
- No unbounded writes or overruns appear possible given these bound checks.

2.2 Null and Error Checks  
- Allocation failures for nexus buffers trigger a fatal exception.  
- Every call that returns a pointer is checked for NULL before use.  
- Read/write operations check and propagate a boolean status.

2.3 Integer and Loop Bounds  
- Loop indices (`x`, `y`) are compared to both source and destination bounds before indexing.  
- Calculations use `size_t` for sizes and cast only for signed loop counters, always guarded by comparisons.

2.4 Concurrency and Data Races  
- The `status` flag is shared among threads under OpenMP without explicit synchronization.  
- Concurrent writes to `status` constitute a data race, but they only flip the flag from true to false. The worst outcome is extra work or missed early exit, not memory corruption.

2.5 Other Attack Vectors  
- No user‐controlled pointers or offsets are dereferenced without bounds checks.  
- All low‐level memory operations guard against overflow.

Conclusion: There are no paths leading to buffer overflow, uncontrolled memory access, or pointer misuse. The only minor concern is a benign data race on the `status` flag under parallel execution.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain security vulnerabilities. It correctly bounds all memory operations and handles errors, with only a harmless race condition on the shared success flag.

   - The function cirrus_mem_writeb_mode4and5_16bpp writes a byte’s worth of graphics data into 16‑bpp VGA VRAM in either mode 4 or mode 5.

     • s: the VGA state (which holds pointers, register shadows, masks, etc.).  
     • mode: the current graphics mode (4 or 5).  
     • offset: the byte offset into video RAM where the write should begin.  
     • mem_value: an 8‑bit value (in a 32‑bit container) whose bits drive which pixel pairs get set.  
   - The offset is first masked with s->cirrus_addr_mask to wrap or clamp it into the valid VRAM range.  
   - dst is set to point into s->vga.vram_ptr at that masked offset.  
   - The code then iterates 8 times, once per bit in the high-to-low direction of the original mem_value:  
     • If the current bit is 1, it writes two bytes at dst and dst+1, pulling values from two “shadow” registers (gr1 and gr[0x11]).  
     • Else if mode == 5 (and the bit is 0), it writes two alternative bytes sourced from shadow_gr0 and gr[0x10].

   - Null or uninitialized pointers: s->vga.vram_ptr and the register shadows are assumed valid, as in a correctly initialized VGA device. There is no dereference of unvalidated external data.  
   - Race conditions: This is a single-threaded or externally serialized access pattern in QEMU’s device emulation. There is no concurrent VRAM access in this snippet.  
   - Side-channel or code-injection: The writes are pure memory operations driven by internal VGA state. No user data is executed or misdirected.  
   - Conclusion: There is no evidence of buffer overflows, out-of-bounds writes, uninitialized reads, or other typical vulnerabilities in this tightly constrained looping and masking logic.

   No, the function does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It safely masks its offset, bounds VRAM writes, and uses only internal state for its operations.

original_information.commit_message:
CVE-2013-6401: Change hash function, randomize hashes

Thanks to Florian Weimer and Eric Sesterhenn for reporting, reviewing
and testing.

+static uint32_t buf_to_uint32(char *data) {
+    size_t i;
+    uint32_t result = 0;
+
+    for (i = 0; i < sizeof(uint32_t); i++)
+        result = (result << 8) | (unsigned char)data[i];
+
+    return result;
+}
+
+

+/* /dev/urandom */
+#if !defined(_WIN32) && defined(USE_URANDOM)
+static int seed_from_urandom(uint32_t *seed) {
+    /* Use unbuffered I/O if we have open(), close() and read(). Otherwise
+       fall back to fopen() */
+
+    char data[sizeof(uint32_t)];
+    int ok;
+
+#if defined(HAVE_OPEN) && defined(HAVE_CLOSE) && defined(HAVE_READ)
+    int urandom;

+        return 1;
+

+    close(urandom);
+#else
+    FILE *urandom;
+
+    urandom = fopen("/dev/urandom", "rb");
+    if (!urandom)
+        return 1;
+
+    ok = fread(data, 1, sizeof(uint32_t), urandom) == sizeof(uint32_t);
+    fclose(urandom);
+#endif
+
+    if (!ok)
+        return 1;
+
+    *seed = buf_to_uint32(data);
+    return 0;
+}

+/* Windows Crypto API */

+typedef BOOL (WINAPI *CRYPTRELEASECONTEXT)(HCRYPTPROV hProv, DWORD dwFlags);

+static int seed_from_windows_cryptoapi(uint32_t *seed)
+{
+    HINSTANCE hAdvAPI32 = NULL;
+    CRYPTACQUIRECONTEXTA pCryptAcquireContext = NULL;
+    CRYPTGENRANDOM pCryptGenRandom = NULL;
+    CRYPTRELEASECONTEXT pCryptReleaseContext = NULL;
+    HCRYPTPROV hCryptProv = 0;
+    BYTE data[sizeof(uint32_t)];
+    int ok;
+
+    hAdvAPI32 = GetModuleHandle("advapi32.dll");
+    if(hAdvAPI32 == NULL)

+
+    pCryptAcquireContext = (CRYPTACQUIRECONTEXTA)GetProcAddress(hAdvAPI32, "CryptAcquireContextA");
+    if (!pCryptAcquireContext)

+
+    pCryptGenRandom = (CRYPTGENRANDOM)GetProcAddress(hAdvAPI32, "CryptGenRandom");
+    if (!pCryptGenRandom)

+
+    pCryptReleaseContext = (CRYPTRELEASECONTEXT)GetProcAddress(hAdvAPI32, "CryptReleaseContext");
+    if (!pCryptReleaseContext)
+        return 1;
+
+    if (!pCryptAcquireContext(&hCryptProv, NULL, NULL, PROV_RSA_FULL, CRYPT_VERIFYCONTEXT))
+        return 1;
+
+    ok = CryptGenRandom(hCryptProv, sizeof(uint32_t), data);
+    pCryptReleaseContext(hCryptProv, 0);
+
+    if (!ok)
+        return 1;
+
+    *seed = buf_to_uint32((char *)data);
+    return 0;
+}

+/* gettimeofday() and getpid() */
+static int seed_from_timestamp_and_pid(uint32_t *seed) {
+#ifdef HAVE_GETTIMEOFDAY

+    struct timeval tv;
+    gettimeofday(&tv, NULL);
+    *seed = (uint32_t)tv.tv_sec ^ (uint32_t)tv.tv_usec;
+#else
+    /* Seconds only */
+    *seed = (uint32_t)time(NULL);
+#endif
+

+#if defined(_WIN32)
+    *seed ^= (uint32_t)_getpid();
+#elif defined(HAVE_GETPID)
+    *seed ^= (uint32_t)getpid();
+#endif
+
+    return 0;
+}

+static uint32_t generate_seed() {
+    uint32_t seed;
+    int done = 0;
+
+#if !defined(_WIN32) && defined(USE_URANDOM)
+    if (!done && seed_from_urandom(&seed) == 0)
+        done = 1;
+#endif
+
+#if defined(_WIN32) && defined(USE_WINDOWS_CRYPTOAPI)
+    if (!done && seed_from_windows_cryptoapi(&seed) == 0)
+        done = 1;
+#endif
+

+        /* Fall back to timestamp and PID if no better randomness is
+           available */
+        seed_from_timestamp_and_pid(&seed);
+    }
+
+    /* Make sure the seed is never zero */
+    if (seed == 0)
+        seed = 1;
+
+    return seed;
+}

+

+    }
+}
+#elif defined(HAVE_SYNC_BUILTINS) && (defined(HAVE_SCHED_YIELD) || !defined(_WIN32))

+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+lookup3.c, by Bob Jenkins, May 2006, Public Domain.
+
+These are functions for producing 32-bit hashes for hash table lookup.
+hashword(), hashlittle(), hashlittle2(), hashbig(), mix(), and final() 
+are externally useful functions.  Routines to test the hash are included 
+if SELF_TEST is defined.  You can use this free for any purpose.  It's in
+the public domain.  It has no warranty.
+
+You probably want to use hashlittle().  hashlittle() and hashbig()
+hash byte arrays.  hashlittle() is is faster than hashbig() on
+little-endian machines.  Intel and AMD are little-endian machines.
+On second thought, you probably want hashlittle2(), which is identical to
+hashlittle() except it returns two 32-bit hashes for the price of one.  
+You could implement hashbig2() if you wanted but I haven't bothered here.
+
+If you want to find a hash of, say, exactly 7 integers, do
+  a = i1;  b = i2;  c = i3;
+  mix(a,b,c);
+  a += i4; b += i5; c += i6;
+  mix(a,b,c);
+  a += i7;
+  final(a,b,c);
+then use c as the hash value.  If you have a variable length array of
+4-byte integers to hash, use hashword().  If you have a byte array (like
+a character string), use hashlittle().  If you have several byte arrays, or
+a mix of things, see the comments above hashlittle().  
+
+Why is this so big?  I read 12 bytes at a time into 3 4-byte integers, 
+then mix those integers.  This is fast (you can do a lot more thorough
+mixing with 12*3 instructions on 3 integers than you can with 3 instructions
+on 1 byte), but shoehorning those bytes into integers efficiently is messy.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+
+#include <stdlib.h>
+
+#ifdef HAVE_CONFIG_H
+#include <config.h>
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_STDINT_H
+#include <stdint.h>     /* defines uint32_t etc */
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_SYS_PARAM_H
+#include <sys/param.h>  /* attempt to define endianness */
+#endif
+
+#ifdef HAVE_ENDIAN_H
+# include <endian.h>    /* attempt to define endianness */
+#endif
+
+/*
+ * My best guess at if you are big-endian or little-endian.  This may
+ * need adjustment.
+ */
+#if (defined(__BYTE_ORDER) && defined(__LITTLE_ENDIAN) && \
+     __BYTE_ORDER == __LITTLE_ENDIAN) || \
+    (defined(i386) || defined(__i386__) || defined(__i486__) || \
+     defined(__i586__) || defined(__i686__) || defined(vax) || defined(MIPSEL))
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 1
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 0
+#elif (defined(__BYTE_ORDER) && defined(__BIG_ENDIAN) && \
+       __BYTE_ORDER == __BIG_ENDIAN) || \
+      (defined(sparc) || defined(POWERPC) || defined(mc68000) || defined(sel))
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 0
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 1
+#else
+# define HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN 0
+# define HASH_BIG_ENDIAN 0
+#endif
+
+#define hashsize(n) ((uint32_t)1<<(n))
+#define hashmask(n) (hashsize(n)-1)
+#define rot(x,k) (((x)<<(k)) | ((x)>>(32-(k))))
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+mix -- mix 3 32-bit values reversibly.
+
+This is reversible, so any information in (a,b,c) before mix() is
+still in (a,b,c) after mix().
+
+If four pairs of (a,b,c) inputs are run through mix(), or through
+mix() in reverse, there are at least 32 bits of the output that
+are sometimes the same for one pair and different for another pair.
+This was tested for:
+* pairs that differed by one bit, by two bits, in any combination
+  of top bits of (a,b,c), or in any combination of bottom bits of
+  (a,b,c).
+* "differ" is defined as +, -, ^, or ~^.  For + and -, I transformed
+  the output delta to a Gray code (a^(a>>1)) so a string of 1's (as
+  is commonly produced by subtraction) look like a single 1-bit
+  difference.
+* the base values were pseudorandom, all zero but one bit set, or 
+  all zero plus a counter that starts at zero.
+
+Some k values for my "a-=c; a^=rot(c,k); c+=b;" arrangement that
+satisfy this are
+    4  6  8 16 19  4
+    9 15  3 18 27 15
+   14  9  3  7 17  3
+Well, "9 15 3 18 27 15" didn't quite get 32 bits diffing
+for "differ" defined as + with a one-bit base and a two-bit delta.  I
+used http://burtleburtle.net/bob/hash/avalanche.html to choose 
+the operations, constants, and arrangements of the variables.
+
+This does not achieve avalanche.  There are input bits of (a,b,c)
+that fail to affect some output bits of (a,b,c), especially of a.  The
+most thoroughly mixed value is c, but it doesn't really even achieve
+avalanche in c.
+
+This allows some parallelism.  Read-after-writes are good at doubling
+the number of bits affected, so the goal of mixing pulls in the opposite
+direction as the goal of parallelism.  I did what I could.  Rotates
+seem to cost as much as shifts on every machine I could lay my hands
+on, and rotates are much kinder to the top and bottom bits, so I used
+rotates.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+#define mix(a,b,c) \
+{ \
+  a -= c;  a ^= rot(c, 4);  c += b; \
+  b -= a;  b ^= rot(a, 6);  a += c; \
+  c -= b;  c ^= rot(b, 8);  b += a; \
+  a -= c;  a ^= rot(c,16);  c += b; \
+  b -= a;  b ^= rot(a,19);  a += c; \
+  c -= b;  c ^= rot(b, 4);  b += a; \
+}
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+final -- final mixing of 3 32-bit values (a,b,c) into c
+
+Pairs of (a,b,c) values differing in only a few bits will usually
+produce values of c that look totally different.  This was tested for
+* pairs that differed by one bit, by two bits, in any combination
+  of top bits of (a,b,c), or in any combination of bottom bits of
+  (a,b,c).
+* "differ" is defined as +, -, ^, or ~^.  For + and -, I transformed
+  the output delta to a Gray code (a^(a>>1)) so a string of 1's (as
+  is commonly produced by subtraction) look like a single 1-bit
+  difference.
+* the base values were pseudorandom, all zero but one bit set, or 
+  all zero plus a counter that starts at zero.
+
+These constants passed:
+ 14 11 25 16 4 14 24
+ 12 14 25 16 4 14 24
+and these came close:
+  4  8 15 26 3 22 24
+ 10  8 15 26 3 22 24
+ 11  8 15 26 3 22 24
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+#define final(a,b,c) \
+{ \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,14); \
+  a ^= c; a -= rot(c,11); \
+  b ^= a; b -= rot(a,25); \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,16); \
+  a ^= c; a -= rot(c,4);  \
+  b ^= a; b -= rot(a,14); \
+  c ^= b; c -= rot(b,24); \
+}
+
+/*
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+hashlittle() -- hash a variable-length key into a 32-bit value
+  k       : the key (the unaligned variable-length array of bytes)
+  length  : the length of the key, counting by bytes
+  initval : can be any 4-byte value
+Returns a 32-bit value.  Every bit of the key affects every bit of
+the return value.  Two keys differing by one or two bits will have
+totally different hash values.
+
+The best hash table sizes are powers of 2.  There is no need to do
+mod a prime (mod is sooo slow!).  If you need less than 32 bits,
+use a bitmask.  For example, if you need only 10 bits, do
+  h = (h & hashmask(10));
+In which case, the hash table should have hashsize(10) elements.
+
+If you are hashing n strings (uint8_t **)k, do it like this:
+  for (i=0, h=0; i<n; ++i) h = hashlittle( k[i], len[i], h);
+
+By Bob Jenkins, 2006.  bob_jenkins@burtleburtle.net.  You may use this
+code any way you wish, private, educational, or commercial.  It's free.
+
+Use for hash table lookup, or anything where one collision in 2^^32 is
+acceptable.  Do NOT use for cryptographic purposes.
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
+*/
+
+static uint32_t hashlittle(const void *key, size_t length, uint32_t initval)
+{
+  uint32_t a,b,c;                                          /* internal state */
+  union { const void *ptr; size_t i; } u;     /* needed for Mac Powerbook G4 */
+
+  /* Set up the internal state */
+  a = b = c = 0xdeadbeef + ((uint32_t)length) + initval;
+
+  u.ptr = key;
+  if (HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN && ((u.i & 0x3) == 0)) {
+    const uint32_t *k = (const uint32_t *)key;         /* read 32-bit chunks */
+
+#ifdef VALGRIND
+    const uint8_t  *k8;
+#endif
+
+    /*------ all but last block: aligned reads and affect 32 bits of (a,b,c) */
+    while (length > 12)
+    {
+      a += k[0];
+      b += k[1];
+      c += k[2];
+      mix(a,b,c);
+      length -= 12;
+      k += 3;
+    }
+
+    /*----------------------------- handle the last (probably partial) block */
+    /* 
+     * "k[2]&0xffffff" actually reads beyond the end of the string, but
+     * then masks off the part it's not allowed to read.  Because the
+     * string is aligned, the masked-off tail is in the same word as the
+     * rest of the string.  Every machine with memory protection I've seen
+     * does it on word boundaries, so is OK with this.  But VALGRIND will
+     * still catch it and complain.  The masking trick does make the hash
+     * noticably faster for short strings (like English words).
+     */
+#ifndef VALGRIND
+
+    switch(length)
+    {
+    case 12: c+=k[2]; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 11: c+=k[2]&0xffffff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 10: c+=k[2]&0xffff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 9 : c+=k[2]&0xff; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 8 : b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 7 : b+=k[1]&0xffffff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 6 : b+=k[1]&0xffff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 5 : b+=k[1]&0xff; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 4 : a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 3 : a+=k[0]&0xffffff; break;
+    case 2 : a+=k[0]&0xffff; break;
+    case 1 : a+=k[0]&0xff; break;
+    case 0 : return c;              /* zero length strings require no mixing */
+    }
+
+#else /* make valgrind happy */
+
+    k8 = (const uint8_t *)k;
+    switch(length)
+    {
+    case 12: c+=k[2]; b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 11: c+=((uint32_t)k8[10])<<16;  /* fall through */
+    case 10: c+=((uint32_t)k8[9])<<8;    /* fall through */
+    case 9 : c+=k8[8];                   /* fall through */
+    case 8 : b+=k[1]; a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 7 : b+=((uint32_t)k8[6])<<16;   /* fall through */
+    case 6 : b+=((uint32_t)k8[5])<<8;    /* fall through */
+    case 5 : b+=k8[4];                   /* fall through */
+    case 4 : a+=k[0]; break;
+    case 3 : a+=((uint32_t)k8[2])<<16;   /* fall through */
+    case 2 : a+=((uint32_t)k8[1])<<8;    /* fall through */
+    case 1 : a+=k8[0]; break;
+    case 0 : return c;
+    }
+
+#endif /* !valgrind */
+
+  } else if (HASH_LITTLE_ENDIAN && ((u.i & 0x1) == 0)) {
+    const uint16_t *k = (const uint16_t *)key;         /* read 16-bit chunks */
+    const uint8_t  *k8;
+
+    /*--------------- all but last block: aligned reads and different mixing */
+    while (length > 12)
+    {
+      a += k[0] + (((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+      b += k[2] + (((uint32_t)k[3])<<16);
+      c += k[4] + (((uint32_t)k[5])<<16);
+      mix(a,b,c);
+      length -= 12;
+      k += 6;
+    }
+
+    /*----------------------------- handle the last (probably partial) block */
+    k8 = (const uint8_t *)k;
+    switch(length)
+    {
+    case 12: c+=k[4]+(((uint32_t)k[5])<<16);
+             b+=k[2]+(((uint32_t)k[3])<<16);
+             a+=k[0]+(((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+             break;
+    case 11: c+=((uint32_t)k8[10])<<16;     /* fall through */
+    case 10: c+=k[4];
+             b+=k[2]+(((uint32_t)k[3])<<16);
+             a+=k[0]+(((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+             break;
+    case 9 : c+=k8[8];                      /* fall through */
+    case 8 : b+=k[2]+(((uint32_t)k[3])<<16);
+             a+=k[0]+(((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+             break;
+    case 7 : b+=((uint32_t)k8[6])<<16;      /* fall through */
+    case 6 : b+=k[2];
+             a+=k[0]+(((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+             break;
+    case 5 : b+=k8[4];                      /* fall through */
+    case 4 : a+=k[0]+(((uint32_t)k[1])<<16);
+             break;
+    case 3 : a+=((uint32_t)k8[2])<<16;      /* fall through */
+    case 2 : a+=k[0];
+             break;
+    case 1 : a+=k8[0];
+             break;
+    case 0 : return c;                     /* zero length requires no mixing */
+    }
+
+  } else {                        /* need to read the key one byte at a time */
+    const uint8_t *k = (const uint8_t *)key;
+
+    /*--------------- all but the last block: affect some 32 bits of (a,b,c) */
+    while (length > 12)
+    {
+      a += k[0];
+      a += ((uint32_t)k[1])<<8;
+      a += ((uint32_t)k[2])<<16;
+      a += ((uint32_t)k[3])<<24;
+      b += k[4];
+      b += ((uint32_t)k[5])<<8;
+      b += ((uint32_t)k[6])<<16;

- Both underlying functions compare characters from `s1` and `s2` after mapping them to a common case, returning:
  • 0 if the strings are equal (ignoring case)  
  • A negative value if `s1` is lexicographically less than `s2`  
  • A positive value if `s1` is lexicographically greater than `s2`

- There is no memory allocation, no format strings, no buffer writes, and no user‐controlled length parameters in this wrapper.

3. Decision

No, the code is safe. It simply provides a cross‐platform alias for standard case‐insensitive string comparison without introducing additional risk.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `postFillThisBuffer(BufferInfo *info)` is called to hand off an input buffer for downstream processing.
- It first checks whether end-of-stream (EOS) has already been signaled on the input port; if so, it returns immediately.
- It verifies via `CHECK_EQ` that the buffer’s status is currently `OWNED_BY_US`, ensuring the codec indeed holds the buffer before posting it.
- It clones (`dup()`) the codec’s notification message (`mNotify`) and populates it with two fields:
  • `"what" = kWhatFillThisBuffer` (a message identifier)  
  • `"buffer-id" = info->mBufferID` (to track which buffer is being filled)  
- It clears any existing metadata in the buffer (`info->mData->meta()->clear()`), then attaches the buffer itself to the notification under the key `"buffer"`.
- It constructs a reply message (`kWhatInputBufferFilled`) destined back at the codec, embeds the same `"buffer-id"`, and adds it to the notification under `"reply"`.
- It posts the assembled notification (`notify->post()`), signaling the upstream component that data is ready.
- Finally, it updates the buffer’s status to `OWNED_BY_UPSTREAM`, transferring ownership out of the codec.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no direct processing of untrusted input data in this routine.  
- The only buffer manipulation is metadata clearing (`meta()->clear()`), which is a safe operation that resets internal fields rather than parsing or copying unvalidated content.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix hash overflow handling

The handling for directory crc hash overflows was fairly obscure,
split_leaf returns EOVERFLOW when we try to extend the item and that is
supposed to bubble up to userland.  For a while it did so, but along the
way we added better handling of errors and forced the FS readonly if we
hit IO errors during the directory insertion.

Along the way, we started testing only for EEXIST and the EOVERFLOW case
was dropped.  The end result is that we may force the FS readonly if we
catch a directory hash bucket overflow.

This fixes a few problem spots.  First I add tests for EOVERFLOW in the
places where we can safely just return the error up the chain.

btrfs_rename is harder though, because it tries to insert the new
directory item only after it has already unlinked anything the rename
was going to overwrite.  Rather than adding very complex logic, I added
a helper to test for the hash overflow case early while it is still safe
to bail out.

Snapshot and subvolume creation had a similar problem, so they are using
the new helper now too.

Signed-off-by: Chris Mason <chris.mason@fusionio.com>
Reported-by: Pascal Junod <pascal@junod.info>

      d. Queries the address family–specific code for the proper sockaddr length.  
      e. Calls `copy_to_user(to, &temp, addrlen)` to copy that many bytes into user space; on failure returns –EFAULT immediately.  
      f. Advances the user-space pointer `to` by `addrlen` and increments `cnt`.

     The function only advances `to` by known lengths (`addrlen`) and stops once `cnt == max_addrs`. original_information.commit_message:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function Type_MPE_Write serializes a multi-part “MPE” (multi-process element) pipeline (cmsPipeline) into a binary I/O stream.  
- It begins by computing a BaseOffset (the current file position minus the size of the tag header) for later back-patching.  
- It queries the pipeline’s number of input channels, output channels, and stage count (ElemCount).  
- It allocates two arrays of length ElemCount:  
   • ElementOffsets – to record, for each stage, the offset (relative to BaseOffset) at which that stage’s block begins in the file  
   • ElementSizes   – to record the size of each stage block  
- It writes the input- and output-channel counts (16-bit each) and the stage count (32-bit), then reserves ElemCount directory entries (each entry is two 32-bit zeros: one for offset, one for size).  
- It loops over each pipeline stage in turn:  
   • Records the stage’s start position (Tell – BaseOffset) into ElementOffsets[i].  
   • Looks up the stage’s type signature and finds the corresponding type-handler.  
   • Writes the type signature (32 bits).  
   • Calls the handler’s WritePtr function to serialize that stage.  
   • Pads to alignment, measures the bytes written, and records that in ElementSizes[i].  
- After all stages are written, it seeks back to the directory, emits the real offsets and sizes, then returns to the end-of-file and frees the two arrays.  
- On any failure (allocation, write, seek, unknown type, etc.) it jumps to Error, frees any allocated arrays, and returns FALSE.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory allocation sizing: ElementOffsets and ElementSizes are allocated with “ElemCount * sizeof(cmsUInt32Number)” without checking for integer overflow on the product. If an attacker could supply a very large ElemCount, the multiplication could wrap, leading to under-allocation and then a write-past when populating the arrays. In practice, ElemCount is the number of stages in a pipeline loaded from an ICC profile, and upstream code typically constrains that count to reasonable limits.  
- Data truncation: The code writes the pipeline’s stage count as a 32-bit number but casts it to a 16-bit type (`(cmsUInt16Number) ElemCount`) before passing it to the write function. If ElemCount ever exceeded 65535, the written value would wrap, causing a mismatch between the actual number of stages and the recorded count in the file. That could yield an incorrect file that later reading code might misinterpret. Again, in typical use the number of stages is small and this truncation never occurs.  
- Bounds checking on channel counts: Similarly, inputChan and outputChan are cast to 16 bits. If a pipeline had more than 65535 channels (unrealistic in color-management), that would wrap.  
- Error handling and cleanup: The code properly checks every I/O call, seeks, and memory allocation and jumps to an error path that frees the arrays. No memory leaks or double frees on error.  
- Buffer overruns: Aside from the array-allocation issue above, all writes occur via well-defined I/O routines that take explicit sizes; there are no raw memcpy’s or pointer arithmetic beyond offset bookkeeping.

3. Decision

No. The code correctly follows a serialization pattern with checks on every I/O operation and proper cleanup. The only theoretical concerns are an unchecked multiplication when allocating the offset/size arrays and 16-bit truncations on counts—but in normal usage (where stage and channel counts are small) those issues do not lead to exploitable vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
timerfd: Protect the might cancel mechanism proper

The handling of the might_cancel queueing is not properly protected, so
parallel operations on the file descriptor can race with each other and
lead to list corruptions or use after free.

Protect the context for these operations with a seperate lock.

The wait queue lock cannot be reused for this because that would create a
lock inversion scenario vs. the cancel lock. Replacing might_cancel with an
atomic (atomic_t or atomic bit) does not help either because it still can
race vs. the actual list operation.

sfc: Fix maximum number of TSO segments and minimum TX queue size

[ Upstream commit 7e6d06f0de3f74ca929441add094518ae332257c ]

Currently an skb requiring TSO may not fit within a minimum-size TX
queue.  The TX queue selected for the skb may stall and trigger the TX
watchdog repeatedly (since the problem skb will be retried after the
TX reset).  This issue is designated as CVE-2012-3412.

Set the maximum number of TSO segments for our devices to 100.  This
should make no difference to behaviour unless the actual MSS is less
than about 700.  Increase the minimum TX queue size accordingly to
allow for 2 worst-case skbs, so that there will definitely be space
to add an skb after we wake a queue.

To avoid invalidating existing configurations, change
efx_ethtool_set_ringparam() to fix up values that are too small rather
than returning -EINVAL.

original_information.commit_message:
Sched: fix skip_clock_update optimization

idle_balance() drops/retakes rq->lock, leaving the previous task
vulnerable to set_tsk_need_resched().  Clear it after we return
from balancing instead, and in setup_thread_stack() as well, so
no successfully descheduled or never scheduled task has it set.

Need resched confused the skip_clock_update logic, which assumes
that the next call to update_rq_clock() will come nearly immediately
after being set.  Make the optimization robust against the waking
a sleeper before it sucessfully deschedules case by checking that
the current task has not been dequeued before setting the flag,
since it is that useless clock update we're trying to save, and
clear unconditionally in schedule() proper instead of conditionally
in put_prev_task().

original_information.commit_message:
dentry name snapshots

take_dentry_name_snapshot() takes a safe snapshot of dentry name;
if the name is a short one, it gets copied into caller-supplied
structure, otherwise an extra reference to external name is grabbed
(those are never modified).  In either case the pointer to stable
string is stored into the same structure.

dentry must be held by the caller of take_dentry_name_snapshot(),
but may be freely dropped afterwards - the snapshot will stay
until destroyed by release_dentry_name_snapshot().

Intended use:
	struct name_snapshot s;

	take_dentry_name_snapshot(&s, dentry);
	...
	access s.name
	...
	release_dentry_name_snapshot(&s);

Replaces fsnotify_oldname_...(), gets used in fsnotify to obtain the name
to pass down with event.

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>

original_information.Summary: The Framework UI permission-dialog implementation in Android 6.x before 2016-06-01 allows attackers to conduct tapjacking attacks and access arbitrary private-storage files by creating a partially overlapping window, aka internal bug 26677796.
original_information.commit_message:
Add new MotionEvent flag for partially obscured windows.

Due to more complex window layouts resulting in lots of overlapping
windows, the policy around FLAG_WINDOW_IS_OBSCURED has changed to
only be set when the point at which the window was touched is
obscured. Unfortunately, this doesn't prevent tapjacking attacks that
overlay the dialog's text, making a potentially dangerous operation
seem innocuous. To avoid this on particularly sensitive dialogs,
introduce a new flag that really does tell you when your window is
being even partially overlapped.

We aren't exposing this as API since we plan on making the original
flag more robust. This is really a workaround for system dialogs
since we generally know their layout and screen position, and that
they're unlikely to be overlapped by other applications.

- allow tearing down and recreating the UI parent context without
losing the renderer contexts

creating the GLSurfaceHandle

the frontbuffer textures are now owned by RWHV where they are refcounted

mailbox names for the front- and backbuffer textures by
associating them with a surface_handle (1 or 2) in the AcceleratedSurfaceNew message.
During SwapBuffers() or PostSubBuffer() cycles, it then uses 
produceTextureCHROMIUM() and consumeTextureCHROMIUM()

 - HasSingleSecurityOrigin
 - DidPassCORSAccessCheck

original_information.commit_message:
netfilter: add back stackpointer size checks

The rationale for removing the check is only correct for rulesets
generated by ip(6)tables.

In iptables, a jump can only occur to a user-defined chain, i.e.
because we size the stack based on number of user-defined chains we
cannot exceed stack size.

However, the underlying binary format has no such restriction,
and the validation step only ensures that the jump target is a
valid rule start point.

IOW, its possible to build a rule blob that has no user-defined
chains but does contain a jump.

If this happens, no jump stack gets allocated and crash occurs
because no jumpstack was allocated.

Fixes: 7814b6ec6d0d6 ("netfilter: xtables: don't save/restore jumpstack offset")

original_information.commit_message:
Fix up non-directory creation in SGID directories

sgid directories have special semantics, making newly created files in
the directory belong to the group of the directory, and newly created
subdirectories will also become sgid.  This is historically used for
group-shared directories.

But group directories writable by non-group members should not imply
that such non-group members can magically join the group, so make sure
to clear the sgid bit on non-directories for non-members (but remember
that sgid without group execute means "mandatory locking", just to
confuse things even more).

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix truncation of compressed and inlined extents

When truncating a file to a smaller size which consists of an inline
extent that is compressed, we did not discard (or made unusable) the
data between the new file size and the old file size, wasting metadata
space and allowing for the truncated data to be leaked and the data
corruption/loss mentioned below.
We were also not correctly decrementing the number of bytes used by the
inode, we were setting it to zero, giving a wrong report for callers of
the stat(2) syscall. The fsck tool also reported an error about a mismatch
between the nbytes of the file versus the real space used by the file.

Now because we weren't discarding the truncated region of the file, it
was possible for a caller of the clone ioctl to actually read the data
that was truncated, allowing for a security breach without requiring root
access to the system, using only standard filesystem operations. The
scenario is the following:

   1) User A creates a file which consists of an inline and compressed
      extent with a size of 2000 bytes - the file is not accessible to
      any other users (no read, write or execution permission for anyone
      else);

   2) The user truncates the file to a size of 1000 bytes;

   3) User A makes the file world readable;

   4) User B creates a file consisting of an inline extent of 2000 bytes;

   5) User B issues a clone operation from user A's file into its own
      file (using a length argument of 0, clone the whole range);

   6) User B now gets to see the 1000 bytes that user A truncated from
      its file before it made its file world readbale. User B also lost
      the bytes in the range [1000, 2000[ bytes from its own file, but
      that might be ok if his/her intention was reading stale data from
      user A that was never supposed to be public.

Note that this contrasts with the case where we truncate a file from 2000
bytes to 1000 bytes and then truncate it back from 1000 to 2000 bytes. In
this case reading any byte from the range [1000, 2000[ will return a value
of 0x00, instead of the original data.

This problem exists since the clone ioctl was added and happens both with
and without my recent data loss and file corruption fixes for the clone
ioctl (patch "Btrfs: fix file corruption and data loss after cloning
inline extents").

So fix this by truncating the compressed inline extents as we do for the
non-compressed case, which involves decompressing, if the data isn't already
in the page cache, compressing the truncated version of the extent, writing
the compressed content into the inline extent and then truncate it.

The following test case for fstests reproduces the problem. In order for
the test to pass both this fix and my previous fix for the clone ioctl
that forbids cloning a smaller inline extent into a larger one,
which is titled "Btrfs: fix file corruption and data loss after cloning
inline extents", are needed. Without that other fix the test fails in a
different way that does not leak the truncated data, instead part of
destination file gets replaced with zeroes (because the destination file
has a larger inline extent than the source).

  seq=`basename $0`
  seqres=$RESULT_DIR/$seq
  echo "QA output created by $seq"
  tmp=/tmp/$$
  status=1	# failure is the default!
  trap "_cleanup; exit \$status" 0 1 2 3 15

  # and consists of a single inline extent with an uncompressed size of 512 bytes,
  # while file bar consists of a single inline extent with an uncompressed size of
  # 256 bytes. For our test's purpose, it's important that file bar has an inline
  # extent with a size smaller than foo's inline extent.

          -c "pwrite -S 0x2a 128 384" \
          $SCRATCH_MNT/foo | _filter_xfs_io
  $XFS_IO_PROG -f -c "pwrite -S 0xbb 0 256" $SCRATCH_MNT/bar | _filter_xfs_io

  # on disk an inline extent with a size of 512 bytes for file foo.
  sync

  # compressed and inline extent, btrfs did not shrink the inline extent to the
  # new size (if the extent was not compressed, btrfs would shrink it to 128
  # bytes), it only updates the inode's i_size to 128 bytes.

  # inline extents), resulting in copying the full inline extent from the source
  # file into the destination file.

1. Functional Analysis

  This function computes the total output length of an SSL/TLS record given the plaintext data size (`data_size`), the MAC/hash size (`hash_size`), whether it is a stream or block cipher, the block size, and whether to add random padding.

  – It takes a session pointer, the number of data bytes, the MAC/hash size, a pointer to an 8-bit pad-length (`pad`), a flag `random_pad`, the cipher type, and the block size.  
  – It initializes `*pad = 0`.  
  – For CIPHER_STREAM:  
    • It sets `length = data_size + hash_size`.  
  – For CIPHER_BLOCK:  
    1. It draws one random byte `rnd` via `_gnutls_rnd(RND_NONCE, &rnd, 1)`.  
    2. If the protocol version is SSL3 or `random_pad == 0`, it forces `rnd = 0`.  
    3. Otherwise it reduces `rnd` to a multiple of the block size by `(rnd/blocksize)*blocksize`, and if that result exceeds one block, it subtracts one block to ensure the extra padding is strictly less than two blocks.  
    4. It computes the “mandatory” padding needed so that `(data_size + hash_size + pad) % blocksize == 0`, namely  
       pad = blocksize – ((data_size+hash_size) % blocksize)  
    5. It adds the extra randomized multiple-of-blocksize padding:  
       *pad = pad + rnd  
    6. It increments `length` by `*pad`.  
    7. For TLS1.1 or higher, it also adds one blocksize to account for the explicit IV.  
  – It returns the total `length`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  a) Random-pad logic  
    – The code ensures padding is nonzero and aligned to the block size, adding a small randomized multiple of the block size (0 or 1×blocksize). That conforms to the TLS 1.0+ randomized padding extension.  
    – For SSL3 or if `random_pad == 0`, `rnd` is forced to 0, yielding only the minimal padding, as SSL3 does not define random padding beyond the minimal.  

  b) Integer overflow  
    – All intermediate lengths (`data_size + hash_size + pad + blocksize`) are computed in signed `int` without explicit overflow checks. In extreme cases where inputs are near `INT_MAX`, these additions could overflow. In practice GnuTLS bounds record sizes well below that limit, so this is not generally exploitable.  

  c) Missing pointer or session checks  
    – The code assumes `session` is non-NULL and that `session->security_parameters.version` is valid. These are invariants elsewhere in GnuTLS.  

  d) No direct padding oracle or side-channel in this routine  
    – This function only computes lengths; it does not perform or verify padding on decryption, so it is not itself the site of a padding-oracle leak.  

3. Decision

No, the snippet does not itself contain a practical vulnerability. It correctly computes padded lengths (with optional random padding) for TLS records, subject only to the usual integer-overflow checks enforced by the surrounding library.

The function `Read` is a deserializer for a Mojo data view of type `gfx::mojom::BufferUsageAndFormatDataView`.  It takes two parameters:  
- `data`: a Mojo data‐view object that holds serialized fields “usage” and “format.”  
- `out`: a pointer to a `gfx::BufferUsageAndFormat` struct, whose fields are to be filled in.  

Internally it does the following:  
  a. Calls `data.ReadUsage(&out->usage)`, which attempts to parse and validate the serialized “usage” enum value and store it in `out->usage`. It returns `true` on success, `false` on invalid data.  
  b. Calls `data.ReadFormat(&out->format)`, which does the same for the “format” enum.  
  c. Returns the logical AND of both calls—i.e. `true` only if both fields were successfully read and validated.

- Enum‐Validation Safety: Mojo’s `ReadXXX` helpers check that the incoming integer values map to known enum members. Invalid or out‐of‐range values cause the calls to return `false` rather than writing bad data.  
- Memory Safety: There is no raw buffer manipulation, no loops, and no direct pointer arithmetic. The only mutation is writing to `out->usage` and `out->format` via their addresses, and that is guarded by the return values of the `Read*` methods.  
- Null‐Pointer Consideration: The function does not explicitly check whether `out` is non‐null. If a caller ever passed a null pointer for `out`, this routine would dereference it, leading to undefined behavior. However, in typical Mojo patterns the callee is responsible for providing a valid `out` pointer.  

Given these points, there is no buffer overflow, integer‐overflow, injection, or other common serialization‐related flaw. The only potential issue would be misuse by passing a null `out` pointer, but that is a contract‐level requirement, not an inherent vulnerability in the code itself.

No, the code is not vulnerable. It safely deserializes two enum fields, validating each, and only writes to `out` when validation succeeds.

Commit 503358ae01b70ce6909d19dd01287093f6b6271c ("ext4: avoid divide by
zero when trying to mount a corrupted file system") fixes CVE-2009-4307
by performing a sanity check on s_log_groups_per_flex, since it can be
set to a bogus value by an attacker.

	sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex = sbi->s_es->s_log_groups_per_flex;
	groups_per_flex = 1 << sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex;

	if (groups_per_flex < 2) { ... }

This patch fixes two potential issues in the previous commit.

On x86, 5 bits are used for the shifting amount.  That means, given a
large s_log_groups_per_flex value like 36, groups_per_flex = 1 << 36
is essentially 1 << 4 = 16, rather than 0.  This will bypass the check,
leaving s_log_groups_per_flex and groups_per_flex inconsistent.

2) The sanity check relies on undefined behavior, i.e., oversized shift.
A standard-confirming C compiler could rewrite the check in unexpected
ways.  Consider the following equivalent form, assuming groups_per_flex
is unsigned for simplicity.

	groups_per_flex = 1 << sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex;
	if (groups_per_flex == 0 || groups_per_flex == 1) {

We compile the code snippet using Clang 3.0 and GCC 4.6.  Clang will
completely optimize away the check groups_per_flex == 0, leaving the
patched code as vulnerable as the original.  GCC keeps the check, but
there is no guarantee that future versions will do the same.

     – the format string

floppy: fix div-by-zero in setup_format_params

This fixes a divide by zero error in the setup_format_params function of
the floppy driver.

Two consecutive ioctls can trigger the bug: The first one should set the
drive geometry with such .sect and .rate values for the F_SECT_PER_TRACK
to become zero.  Next, the floppy format operation should be called.

A floppy disk is not required to be inserted.  An unprivileged user
could trigger the bug if the device is accessible.

The patch checks F_SECT_PER_TRACK for a non-zero value in the
set_geometry function.  The proper check should involve a reasonable
upper limit for the .sect and .rate fields, but it could change the
UAPI.

The patch also checks F_SECT_PER_TRACK in the setup_format_params, and
cancels the formatting operation in case of zero.

The bug was found by syzkaller.
