2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Reflected Input: The code reflects a header value directly in the HTTP response body without any escaping or encoding. In a browser context, if the test server emits a content-type of HTML (rather than plain text), this could allow a malicious client to inject JavaScript or HTML via a crafted header name/value, leading to cross‑site scripting (XSS).  
   - HTTP Response Splitting: The code does not inject user‑controlled data into response headers or the status line; it only places the value into the body. Standard HTTP header value rules disallow raw CR or LF in header values, so response splitting is not a concern here.  
   - Denial of Service / Performance: There is no input length check on the header name or value; an extremely long header could consume excessive memory, but most HTTP servers clamp header sizes, and this is a test server scenario.

  • If the PTE is present (mapping a normal page), it looks up the struct page, optionally filters by a user-provided mapping, then atomically clears the PTE, removes the TLB entry, updates dirty/accessed bits and RSS counters, tears down the reverse mapping (rmap), and unregisters the page from the TLB batch.

- Use-After-Free / Double-Free: Clearing a PTE together with ptep_get_and_clear_full or pte_clear_not_present_full both remove the sole page reference from the table before any free or rmap teardown.  Page references are owned by mm_struct and taken care of by the PTE-clearing primitives, so the code does not dereference freed pages nor free them twice.  
- Integer Overflows: Addr and end are unsigned long aligned to page boundaries; stepping by PAGE_SIZE will not wrap if end ≥ addr and the caller supplies sane bounds.  
- Special-Case Handling: Optional “details” filters short-circuit the swap-free path but never fail to clear the PTE, so there’s no stale entry left behind.

No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It correctly unmaps and frees PTEs, handles races via locking and lazy-MMU batching, and updates all accounting safely.

original_information.commit_message:
mm: avoid setting up anonymous pages into file mapping

Reading page fault handler code I've noticed that under right
circumstances kernel would map anonymous pages into file mappings: if
the VMA doesn't have vm_ops->fault() and the VMA wasn't fully populated
on ->mmap(), kernel would handle page fault to not populated pte with
do_anonymous_page().

Let's change page fault handler to use do_anonymous_page() only on
anonymous VMA (->vm_ops == NULL) and make sure that the VMA is not
shared.

For file mappings without vm_ops->fault() or shred VMA without vm_ops,
page fault on pte_none() entry would lead to SIGBUS.

   - Next it reads a 16‐bit count of authentication key management (AKM) suites, bounds‐checks again, loops over them, validates the OUI, and sets bits in `wpa_auth` corresponding to NONE, PSK, SHA256, etc., distinguishing WPA vs. RSN.

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a practical exploitable vulnerability. It performs adequate length checks around every variable‐length field and fails safely on malformed IEs.

original_information.Summary: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.
original_information.commit_message:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

1. Functional Analysis  
- The method `PendingFrameReadbackComplete` is called when a frame readback operation finishes.  
- It records a trace event with the frame’s sequence number and the readback response code.  
- If the response indicates success (`READBACK_SUCCESS`), it makes a heap‐allocated copy of the provided `SkBitmap` and stores it in the pending frame’s `bitmap` field. Otherwise, it logs a warning with the failure code.  
- It clears the `wait_for_copy_result` flag on the pending frame to signal that the readback has completed.  
- It calls `MaybeRunCallback()` on the pending frame; if that returns true (meaning the user callback has run and the frame is done), it removes that frame from the `pending_frames_` container by erasing the unique_ptr whose raw pointer matches `pending_frame`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
- Memory Safety: All bitmap storage is done through `std::unique_ptr<SkBitmap>`, preventing double deletes. The code makes a full copy of the bitmap, so there is no aliasing of client buffers.  
- Use-After-Free: The lambda passed to `EraseIf` captures only the raw `pending_frame` pointer but is invoked only after `MaybeRunCallback()` returns, at which point the pending frame object is still alive in `pending_frames_`. There is no evidence of a callback deleting or invalidating the frame before `EraseIf` runs.  
- Null Dereferences: The code never dereferences user‐provided pointers. `pending_frame` is guaranteed valid by being taken from `pending_frames_`.  
- Concurrency: This callback appears to run on a single thread (the compositor or UI thread), and there’s no interleaving with other removal logic shown, so there is no obvious data race on `pending_frames_`.  
- Logging: The only external output is a warning log; it does not expose sensitive data beyond an integer response code.  
- Resource Exhaustion/Flooding: If many frames fail readback, logs could be spammed, but that’s an operational issue rather than a memory or code‐execution vulnerability.

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain a security vulnerability. It correctly manages ownership, copies data, clears state, invokes callbacks, and erases completed entries without risking double‐free, use‐after‐free, or null‐pointer dereference.

   • It calls `blk_aio_get(&trim_aiocb_info, blk, cb, opaque)` to allocate or obtain a `TrimAIOCB` structure for tracking the operation.

   • Finally, it returns a pointer to the generic `BlockAIOCB` portion of the structure so that the caller can track completion.

   • Out‑of‑bounds or integer overflow: No loops or arithmetic are performed here on `sector_num` or `nb_sectors`, so there is no direct risk of buffer overrun or overflow in this snippet. Those parameters are simply passed on and will be validated in deeper layers if needed.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function GetPortFieldFromSockaddr takes a generic `sockaddr*` pointer and its length.  
   - It checks the `sa_family` field to see if the address is IPv4 (AF_INET) or IPv6 (AF_INET6).  
     - If AF_INET, it verifies (in debug builds) that the buffer is at least as large as `sockaddr_in`, then casts to `sockaddr_in*` and returns the address of its `sin_port` member.  
     - If AF_INET6, it similarly verifies size against `sockaddr_in6`, casts, and returns the address of `sin6_port`.  
   - If `sa_family` is neither AF_INET nor AF_INET6, it hits a NOTREACHED() marker (indicating this branch should never occur) and returns NULL.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Null Input: There is no explicit check for `address == NULL`. Passing a NULL pointer will lead to undefined behavior on access to `address->sa_family`.  
   - Length Validation: The code uses `DCHECK_LE` to assert that `address_len` is sufficient for the expected struct size, but `DCHECK_LE` is typically compiled out in release builds. In a release build there is no runtime guard against a too-small `address_len`, so a malicious or malformed input could be shorter than expected. Subsequent code will still cast and take the port field address, which can lead to out-of-bounds memory access if the caller then dereferences that pointer.  
   - Family Mismatch: If the family is neither AF_INET nor AF_INET6, the function returns NULL. A caller that does not check for NULL before dereferencing will crash.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a direct buffer overflow or memory corruption bug in its current form. However, it does rely on debug-only checks for buffer size and doesn’t validate its inputs in release builds, which can lead to undefined behavior if misused.

1. Functional Analysis

   - The function ovl_copy_xattr takes two dentry pointers, old and new, and attempts to copy all extended attributes (xattrs) from the inode behind old to the inode behind new.
   - It first checks whether both inodes implement the getxattr operation; if not, it returns success (0) because there is nothing to copy.
   - It calls vfs_listxattr with a NULL buffer to query the total size of the xattr name list.  
     • If the return value is 0 or negative:  
       – If it is –EOPNOTSUPP, it means xattrs aren’t supported by this filesystem, so it returns 0.  
       – Otherwise it returns that error code directly.
   - It allocates a buffer of that size to hold the xattr names, plus a fixed buffer of size XATTR_SIZE_MAX for the attribute values.
   - It re‑invokes vfs_listxattr to fill the names buffer.  
     • If that fails (≤ 0), it bails out with the error.
   - It then iterates over all null‑terminated attribute names in the buffer:  
     • For each name:  
       – Calls vfs_getxattr(old, name, value, XATTR_SIZE_MAX) to fetch the attribute’s value into the fixed buffer.  
       – If that succeeds (size > 0), calls vfs_setxattr(new, name, value, size, 0) to write it to the new inode.  
       – On any failure it breaks out and returns the error.
   - Finally it frees both buffers and returns either 0 (success) or the first negative error encountered.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   - Buffer overruns:  
     • The code allocates exactly list_size bytes for the name list as reported by vfs_listxattr, and iterates only within those bounds.  
     • The value buffer is a fixed XATTR_SIZE_MAX; if an attribute is larger, vfs_getxattr will return –ERANGE (≤0) and the code will abort rather than overflow.
   - Use-after-free or double-free:  
     • All allocated buffers are freed exactly once on every path (success or error).
   - Error handling:  
     • Every syscall return is checked (listxattr, getxattr, setxattr), and negative returns are propagated.
   - Race conditions:  
     • Changes to the old inode’s xattrs during the copy could cause the second listxattr or getxattr to fail; that just triggers a controlled abort. No memory corruption results.
   - Denial‑of‑service:  
     • A filesystem could supply an extremely large list_size, causing kzalloc to fail, but the code handles that by returning –ENOMEM. This only denies the copy operation, not compromise integrity.
   - Privilege escalation:  
     • The code does not elevate privileges or bypass any security checks. vfs_setxattr will enforce the usual xattr permissions on the new inode.
   - In summary, all data lengths are bounded, error paths are handled, and no unchecked pointer arithmetic occurs.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any evident vulnerabilities. It properly bounds all buffers, checks all return values, and cleans up on error.

original_information.commit_message:
ovl: fix dentry reference leak

In ovl_copy_up_locked(), newdentry is leaked if the function exits through
out_cleanup as this just to out after calling ovl_cleanup() - which doesn't
actually release the ref on newdentry.

The out_cleanup segment should instead exit through out2 as certainly
newdentry leaks - and possibly upper does also, though this isn't caught
given the catch of newdentry.

Without this fix, something like the following is seen:

	BUG: Dentry ffff880023e9eb20{i=f861,n=#ffff880023e82d90} still in use (1) [unmount of tmpfs tmpfs]
	BUG: Dentry ffff880023ece640{i=0,n=bigfile}  still in use (1) [unmount of tmpfs tmpfs]

when unmounting the upper layer after an error occurred in copyup.

original_information.commit_message:
sctp: do not peel off an assoc from one netns to another one

Now when peeling off an association to the sock in another netns, all
transports in this assoc are not to be rehashed and keep use the old
key in hashtable.

As a transport uses sk->net as the hash key to insert into hashtable,
it would miss removing these transports from hashtable due to the new
netns when closing the sock and all transports are being freeed, then
later an use-after-free issue could be caused when looking up an asoc
and dereferencing those transports.

This is a very old issue since very beginning, ChunYu found it with
syzkaller fuzz testing with this series:

  socket$inet6_sctp()
  bind$inet6()
  sendto$inet6()
  unshare(0x40000000)
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_GET_ASSOC_ID_LIST()
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_SOCKOPT_PEELOFF()

This patch is to block this call when peeling one assoc off from one
netns to another one, so that the netns of all transport would not
go out-sync with the key in hashtable.

Note that this patch didn't fix it by rehashing transports, as it's
difficult to handle the situation when the tuple is already in use
in the new netns. Besides, no one would like to peel off one assoc
to another netns, considering ipaddrs, ifaces, etc. are usually
different.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `cdf_read_short_sector_chain` is designed to read a series of “short sectors” out of an OLE-style compound file. 
- It takes as inputs:
  • `h` – the compound‐file header (gives the short‐sector size)  
  • `ssat` – the short‐sector allocation table (maps one short‐sector ID to the next)  
  • `sst` – the raw short‐sector stream (from which actual bytes are copied)  
  • `sid` – the starting short‐sector ID  
  • `len` – the logical length of the overall short‐stream directory  
  • `scn` – an output structure into which the concatenated short‐sector data will be placed  

- First the code computes:  
  • `ss = CDF_SHORT_SEC_SIZE(h)` – the size of each short sector in bytes  
  • `scn->sst_len = cdf_count_chain(ssat, sid, CDF_SEC_SIZE(h))` – how many sectors are in the chain, by walking the SAT for full‐sector sized links  
  • `scn->sst_dirlen = len` – copy out the requested logical length  

- It then checks that the input stream table is present and that the chain‐length computation did not return “error” (`(size_t)-1`).  
- It allocates a buffer of `scn->sst_len * ss` bytes with `calloc`.  
- It walks the chain a second time, guarded by two bounds checks per iteration:  
  • a loop‐limit counter `j` to prevent infinite cycles  
  • a check that the loop index `i` remains below the previously computed `scn->sst_len`.  
- On each iteration it calls `cdf_read_short_sector` to copy one short‐sector’s worth of data into the allocated buffer at offset `i * ss`, then follows the next‐sector pointer from `ssat->sat_tab[sid]`.  
- If anything fails (allocation failure, loop‐limit exceeded, read failure, out-of-bounds), it frees the buffer and returns –1. Otherwise, it returns 0 on success.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer‐overrun on the read loop?  
  Each iteration checks `i < scn->sst_len` before writing at `i*ss`, so ordinary out‐of‐bounds writes are prevented, assuming `scn->sst_len` is correct.
- Infinite loop?  
  A separate counter `j` is capped by `CDF_LOOP_LIMIT`, so even a malicious cyclic SAT chain cannot loop forever.
- Allocation‐size integer overflow?  
  The code calls `calloc(scn->sst_len, ss)` without explicitly verifying that `scn->sst_len * ss` does not exceed `SIZE_MAX`.  If both operands are large enough, some libc implementations might wrap the multiplication and return a smaller buffer than intended.  A subsequent write at `i*ss` could then exceed the (wrapped) allocation size, leading to a heap‐based overflow.  That said, common modern allocators (e.g. glibc) do check for overflow in `calloc` and will fail the call rather than wrap.  If using an allocator that does not check, there is a theoretical integer‐overflow → buffer‐overflow risk.
- Denial‐of‐service (OOM) attack?  
  If `cdf_count_chain` reports an extremely large `scn->sst_len`, the caller will try to `calloc` a huge buffer and may exhaust memory.  This is not a memory‐safety bug per se but can be used to crash or hang a process by feeding it a malicious SSAT.
- Other issues (signedness, use‐after‐free, double‐free)?  
  No obvious problems: `sid` is tested for `>= 0`, the buffer pointer is only freed after a failed allocation or read, and there’s no reuse of freed memory.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a concrete memory‐safety vulnerability under typical allocators.  
Summary: The read loop is properly bounded and protected against cycles. The only possible concern is a theoretical integer‐overflow in the `calloc` call if it does not detect oversized products, but most modern C libraries will catch that and fail the allocation instead of wrapping.

original_information.commit_message:
Don't treat the packet length as unsigned.

The scanf family of functions are as annoyingly bad at handling unsigned
numbers as strtoul() is - both of them are perfectly willing to accept a
value beginning with a negative sign as an unsigned value.  When using
strtoul(), you can compensate for this by explicitly checking for a '-'
as the first character of the string, but you can't do that with
sscanf().

So revert to having pkt_len be signed, and scanning it with %d, but
check for a negative value and fail if we see a negative value.

    • Syncs the scanline (SyncAuthenticPixels) and updates progress.

    • Destroys the OpenJPEG codec, image structure, and any codestream index.  
    • Closes the blob and returns the fully populated Image (or only the header if ping was set).

original_information.commit_message:
Make MediaStreamDispatcherHost per-request instead of per-frame.

Instead of having RenderFrameHost own a single MSDH to handle all
requests from a frame, MSDH objects will be owned by a strong binding.

A consequence of this is that an additional requester ID is added to
requests to MediaStreamManager, so that an MSDH is able to cancel only
requests generated by it.

In practice, MSDH will continue to be per frame in most cases since
each frame normally makes a single request for an MSDH object.

This fixes a lifetime issue caused by the IO thread executing tasks
after the RenderFrameHost dies.

- It checks whether there is already a pending wallpaper stored in the member pointer pending_inactive_.

    • It allocates a new PendingWallpaper object with that delay and the given account_id.

    • No synchronization is shown; if multiple threads call this concurrently, a data race could occur on pending_inactive_ or loading_. But absent any threading context in the snippet, this is not a code-level flaw by itself.

    • No unbounded buffers or string operations.

1. Functional Analysis  
- The function ixheaacd_inv_modulation_lp takes four inputs:  
  • qmf_real: pointer to time–frequency data (WORD32 array)  
  • filter_states: history buffer used across calls (WORD16 array)  
  • syn_qmf: parameters for the QMF synthesis filter bank, including the number of channels (no_channels)  
  • qmf_dec_tables_ptr: precomputed tables needed by the inverse DCT routines  

- It reads syn_qmf->no_channels into L and computes M = L/2.  
- It alias-casts qmf_real to dct_in for the upcoming inverse DCT.  
- It allocates a local stack buffer time_out of size 2*NO_SYNTHESIS_CHANNELS WORD32s.  
- It computes ui_rem = address_of(time_out) mod 8 to figure out how far the stack buffer is from an 8-byte boundary, then advances a byte pointer into time_out by (8 − ui_rem) to produce ptime_out, which is guaranteed 8-byte aligned.  
- It selects one of two inverse-DCT functions based on L:  
    • If L==64, calls ixheaacd_dct2_64(dct_in, ptime_out, …, filter_states+M).  
    • Otherwise calls ixheaacd_dct2_32(dct_in, time_out, …, filter_states).  
- Finally it zeroes out filter_states[3*M] before returning.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
- Stack-buffer bounds: time_out is a compile-time array of 2*NO_SYNTHESIS_CHANNELS WORD32s. Aligning ptime_out can advance the pointer by up to 7 bytes, but ptime_out still points within the original array, so unless NO_SYNTHESIS_CHANNELS is grossly undersized relative to the DCT output, standard DCT output writes will remain in bounds.  
- filter_states indexing: writing to filter_states[3*M] assumes the caller supplied at least 3*M+1 entries. If the caller’s array is too small, that would be an out-of-bounds write—but that depends on the contract of the caller, not on this function itself.  
- Pointer casts and alignment: the code casts via integer arithmetic and pVOID/WORD8* to realign; this is a common pattern and not inherently unsafe.  
- No use of unbounded memcpy/memcpy-like calls, no format-string/log injection, no integer underflows or overflows in control logic.  

Conclusion: the function itself does not introduce any obvious buffer overflow or memory‐safety issues, provided its inputs meet the documented size requirements.  

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It correctly aligns its internal buffer and uses indexed accesses consistent with its intended array sizes.

- The function ParaNdis_AllocateMemoryRaw takes two parameters:
  • MiniportHandle: an opaque handle representing an NDIS miniport driver context.  
  • ulRequiredSize: the number of bytes to allocate.  
- It calls NdisAllocateMemoryWithTagPriority, passing along:  
  • the same miniport handle,  
  • the requested size,  
  • a predefined tag (PARANDIS_MEMORY_TAG) to label the allocation for debugging/tracking,  
  • and a NormalPoolPriority to indicate the allocation priority.  
- The return value is whatever NdisAllocateMemoryWithTagPriority returns—either a valid pointer to the allocated block or NULL on failure.

- Integer overflow: There is no explicit check for ulRequiredSize overflow. If ulRequiredSize were near ULONG_MAX, an addition inside the allocator could wrap, but the NDIS allocator itself typically checks size and returns NULL on unreasonable requests.  
- Zero-size allocation: ulRequiredSize == 0 is passed through; most allocators either return a minimum-size buffer or NULL. Handlers downstream must check for NULL.  
- Uncontrolled allocation size: A malicious caller could request very large memory and exhaust system resources (denial-of-service). This wrapper does not impose a maximum size limit. However, running out of pool memory simply causes the allocator to fail rather than corrupt memory.  
- No buffer overflow: This function does not write to the allocated memory or copy data in. It merely requests memory. Any overflow would be the caller’s responsibility once memory is used.  
- No direct return-of-stack-pointer or use-after-free issues: It only returns heap memory or NULL.

3. Decision

No, the code itself contains no direct memory corruption or security flaw. It is a straightforward allocation wrapper that defers checks and failures to the underlying NDIS allocator.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `process_ellipse` takes a data stream `s`, an output structure `os`, a bitmask `present`, and a flag `delta`.  
   - For each bit in `present`, it conditionally reads one of:  
     • left coordinate (bit 0x01)  
     • top coordinate (bit 0x02)  
     • right coordinate (bit 0x04)  
     • bottom coordinate (bit 0x08)  
     using `rdp_in_coord(s, &os->…, delta)`.  
   - If bit 0x10 is set, it reads an 8-bit opcode into `os->opcode`.  
   - If bit 0x20 is set, it reads an 8-bit fill mode into `os->fillmode`.  
   - If bit 0x40 is set, it reads a 32-bit color into `os->fgcolour`.  
   - It logs all seven parameters (left, top, right, bottom, opcode, fillmode, fgcolour).  
   - Finally it calls `ui_ellipse`, passing the opcode−1, fillmode, the x/y position, the computed width (`right−left`) and height (`bottom−top`), plus the color.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflows: All reads are fixed-size (`rdp_in_coord`, `in_uint8`, `rdp_in_colour`) and write into known structure fields. No arbitrary-length copy operations occur.  
   - Integer under/overflow: Coordinates and color are read into signed or unsigned integers of the expected size. Computing `right−left` or `bottom−top` could underflow if the peer sent out-of-order values, but that only yields a (possibly negative) width or height. There’s no heap or stack corruption risk.  
   - Opcode/fillmode range: The code does not explicitly validate that `os->opcode` falls within the UI layer’s permitted range. If the peer sends an opcode of 0, `ui_ellipse` is called with index −1; if it sends a very large byte, `ui_ellipse` could receive an unexpected opcode value. In practice the UI backend should sanitize or clamp invalid opcodes and modes.  
   - Denial of Service: A malicious server could stream extremely large coordinate values, causing the client to attempt to render a gigantic ellipse, but this is a resource-consumption issue, not a memory‐corruption flaw.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any direct memory-corruption or buffer-overflow vulnerabilities. It reads fixed-size fields under a presence mask and passes them to the UI. Potential out-of-range opcodes or enormous dimensions should be handled (or clamped) at the UI layer but do not by themselves introduce a low-level exploit.

have .get and .set methods, but not necessarily .active methods.

      - Optionally emits a MoveTo (if `MOVETOFLAG`) with X/Y offsets: it computes the minimum signed‐bit width (`nBits`) needed, writes a 5-bit length header, then the two signed values.

      - Emits the 2-bit code for “straight edge.”  
      - If dx==0 → vertical line: computes bits for dy, writes a 4-bit length (`nBits–2`), 2-bit subtype “vertical,” then the signed delta.  
      - Else if dy==0 → horizontal line: does the same for dx.  
      - Else → general straight line: picks the max bit width of dx, dy; writes length, a 1-bit “general line” flag, and both signed deltas.

      - Computes the max signed‐bit width of controlX, controlY, anchorX, anchorY (minimum of 2 bits), asserts <18, then writes the 2-bit “curved edge” code, a 4-bit length (`nBits–2`), and the four signed coordinates.

   c. If `enc_enable == 1`:

      – It logs the updated key masks, then, if any local key bit remains set, it dispatches a SMP_BOND_REQ_EVT to start bonding; otherwise it posts an SMP_AUTH_CMPL_EVT with the encryption‐fail or success reason.  
   d. If `enc_enable == 0`:

original_information.commit_message:
sched/fair: Fix infinite loop in update_blocked_averages() by reverting a9e7f6544b9c

Zhipeng Xie, Xie XiuQi and Sargun Dhillon reported lockups in the
scheduler under high loads, starting at around the v4.18 time frame,
and Zhipeng Xie tracked it down to bugs in the rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

   - It retrieves the filesystem-specific info (`sbi`) from the superblock pointer.  
   - It locks the `s_alloc_mutex` to serialize access to allocation‐related fields.  
   - If the flag `s_lvid_dirty` is set, indicating that the Logical Volume Integrity Descriptor (LVID) buffer needs to be written:  
     • It marks the buffer head `s_lvid_bh` dirty via `mark_buffer_dirty()`, so that the block layer’s writeout path will pick it up later.  
     • It clears the superblock’s dirty flag (`sb->s_dirt = 0`).  
     • It clears the `s_lvid_dirty` flag to reflect that the buffer has now been scheduled for writeback.  
   - Finally, it releases the mutex and returns success (0).

   - Memory Safety:  
     • There is no dynamic allocation or indexing here that could overflow or underflow.  
     • The code assumes `s_lvid_bh` is non-NULL when `s_lvid_dirty` is true; upstream code should only set `s_lvid_dirty` when `s_lvid_bh` has been properly initialized.

     • The use of `s_alloc_mutex` around both the flag check and the state updates prevents concurrent threads from racing on `s_lvid_dirty`, `s_lvid_bh`, and `sb->s_dirt`.  
   - Locking Discipline:  
     • The mutex is always released in the same function path that acquires it, so there is no deadlock risk internal to this function.  
   - Error Handling:  
     • The function always returns 0; there is no error path here. Any I/O errors will surface asynchronously when the buffer is actually written out by the block layer, not in this sync callback.

3. Decision

- vrend_resource_reference(&query->res, NULL):  
  Decrements or clears the reference to the resource stored in query->res, potentially releasing it if no other references remain.

- list_del(&query->waiting_queries):  
  Removes the query’s waiting_queries list node from whatever linked list it’s in, so it is no longer queued or tracked.

- glDeleteQueries(1, &query->id):  
  Informs the GL driver to delete the GPU query object identified by query->id.

- free(query):  
  Frees the heap memory occupied by the vrend_query structure itself.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Null-pointer dereference  
  The function assumes `query` is non-NULL. If someone calls vrend_destroy_query(NULL), it will crash when dereferencing `query`. In most codebases the caller is responsible for not passing NULL here.

- list_del on an untracked node  
  If `query->waiting_queries` is not in a list or was already removed, list_del may corrupt memory. Proper usage requires that the list node was initialized and linked exactly once.

- Double-free  
  If vrend_destroy_query is called more than once on the same query pointer, `free(query)` will be invoked twice, leading to undefined behavior. There is no internal guard against double-destruction.

- Use-after-free  
  All operations on `query` happen before `free(query)`, so there is no immediate use-after-free within the function itself. After returning, the caller must not use the freed pointer.

- Resource lifecycle  
  The call to glDeleteQueries is synchronous with respect to the function call. There is no outward use of `query` afterward, so no dangling-GL handle issues arise here.

Overall, none of these are exploitable vulnerabilities if the calling code guarantees:
  1. It never passes NULL to vrend_destroy_query.  
  2. It only destroys each query once.  
  3. Each query’s waiting_queries node was properly initialized and linked before removal.

3. Decision

No, the snippet itself does not contain a vulnerability so long as it is used according to its intended lifecycle rules.

  `PDFiumEngine::GetVisibleRect() const` returns a `pp::Rect` describing the visible region of the PDF page in document coordinates.

- Local variable  
  Declares `pp::Rect rv` as the return value.

- Calculating X and Y  
  - `position_.x()` and `.y()` are the pixel offsets of the top‑left of the viewport within the PDF page at the current zoom.  
  - Dividing by `current_zoom_` converts those pixel offsets back into page (document) coordinates.  
  - `static_cast<int>` truncates to integer page coordinates for the rectangle’s origin.

- Calculating width and height  
  - `plugin_size_.width()` and `.height()` give the viewport size in pixels.  
  - Dividing by `current_zoom_` converts that size into document units.  
  - `ceil(...)` ensures that any fractional portion of a page unit is included so that the viewport fully covers partial pixels at the edges.  
  - The result is cast to `int` for the rectangle’s dimensions.

- Return  
  Returns `rv`, the visible-page rectangle in document coordinates, for use in rendering or hit‑testing.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Division by zero  
  If `current_zoom_` were ever zero, the divisions (`… / current_zoom_`) would be invalid. The code does not explicitly guard against `current_zoom_ == 0`. In practice, a PDF viewer’s zoom factor should never be zero, and elsewhere in the class it is initialized and constrained to positive, nonzero values. If an out‑of‑range zoom did occur, you could get an infinite or undefined result, but that would represent a logic flaw upstream rather than a memory or security issue here.

- Negative or extreme values  
  - If `position_` or `plugin_size_` fields contained negative or extremely large values, the resulting `int` conversions could underflow, overflow, or produce unexpected rectangles. In a well‑behaved plugin environment, those member variables are constrained to valid viewport ranges.  
  - No buffer overruns or memory corruption are possible here: the function merely does floating‑point arithmetic and populates an object of fixed size.

- Rounding and truncation  
  Use of `static_cast<int>` truncates negative results toward zero, and `ceil` rounds up positive results. There is no out‑of‑bounds memory access, just potential off‑by‑one in viewport coverage, which is typically harmless or even desirable (to avoid visual artifacts by dropping fractional pixels).

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any exploitable security vulnerabilities. It simply converts pixel coordinates and sizes to document-space integers, relying on upstream invariants (nonzero zoom, valid sizes).

original_information.commit_message:
[pdf] Defer page unloading in JS callback.

One of the callbacks from PDFium JavaScript into the embedder is to get the
current page number. In Chromium, this will trigger a call to
CalculateMostVisiblePage that method will determine the visible pages and unload
any non-visible pages. But, if the originating JS is on a non-visible page
we'll delete the page and annotations associated with that page. This will
cause issues as we are currently working with those objects when the JavaScript
returns.

This Cl defers the page unloading triggered by getting the most visible page
until the next event is handled by the Chromium embedder.

original_information.commit_message:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

- Lookup and initial bookkeeping  
  - Retrieve `struct perf_event *event` from the VMA’s private_data.  
  - Acquire a pointer to the associated ring buffer (`rb = ring_buffer_get(event)`), its `mmap_user`, and record how many pages were “locked” in the mmap (`mmap_locked`) and the total buffer `size`.

- Decrement mmap counts  
  - Atomically decrement the ring‑buffer’s own `mmap_count`.  
  - Atomically decrement the perf_event’s `mmap_count`, locking `event->mmap_mutex` if that count reaches zero. If the count did not hit zero, skip ahead to final cleanup.

- Detach primary event  
  - Call `ring_buffer_attach(event, NULL)` under `mmap_mutex` so this event no longer writes into the mmap–ed buffer.  
  - Unlock `event->mmap_mutex`.  
  - If other mmaps remain on the same buffer (`rb->mmap_count` > 0), skip to final cleanup.

- Detach all other events on this buffer  
  - Iterate (under RCU protection) the `rb->event_list` of all events pointing to the same ring buffer.  
    - For each event, attempt to bump its refcount with `atomic_long_inc_not_zero`. If it fails, the event is racing with free and will clean itself up later—skip it.  
    - Drop RCU lock, lock that event’s `mmap_mutex`, re-verify that it still points at our `rb`, and call `ring_buffer_attach(event, NULL)` to detach it.  
    - Unlock, put the event (decrement its refcount), and restart the iteration (to avoid list corruption races).

- Undo VM accounting once fully detached  
  - Subtract the number of pages mapped (`(size>>PAGE_SHIFT) + 1`) from the user’s `locked_vm`.  
  - Subtract `mmap_locked` from the process’s `pinned_vm`.  
  - Release the reference on `mmap_user` (`free_uid`).

- Final tear-down  
  - `out_put:` calls `ring_buffer_put(rb)` to balance the initial `ring_buffer_get`, possibly freeing the buffer if this was the last reference.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Reference‐counting and use‐after‐free  
  - The code uses `atomic_long_inc_not_zero` to prevent resurrecting freed events and pairs each increment with a `put_event()`.  
  - The ring buffer is kept alive by `ring_buffer_get()`/`ring_buffer_put()`. No obvious use‐after‐free remains.

- Locking and race conditions  
  - The `event->mmap_mutex` serializes modifications of `event->rb` and `event->mmap_count`.  
  - RCU read‐side protects the event list traversal, and the iteration properly restarts if the list is modified.  
  - The two‐stage atomic decrement for `event->mmap_count` (`atomic_dec_and_mutex_lock`) avoids races between multiple closers.

- Deadlocks  
  - Lock ordering is consistent: `event->mmap_mutex` is not taken under any other lock that could re-enter it. The RCU read‐lock is dropped before acquiring the mutex.

- Resource accounting  
  - VM and UID accounting are undone exactly once, only after all mmaps of the buffer have closed.

There is no evidence of unbalanced reference or lock operations, nor any misuse of kernel primitives that would introduce UAF, double‐free, or deadlock.

3. Decision

No, the code appears free of memory‐safety or concurrency vulnerabilities.

  • tmpl->share    ← XFRM_SHARE_UNIQUE    (indicates per-SA uniqueness)

  • tmpl->aalgos  ← ALGO_MASK_AUTH_ALL    (allow all auth algorithms)  
  • tmpl->ealgos  ← ALGO_MASK_CRYPT_ALL   (allow all encryption algorithms)

original_information.commit_message:
Set optlen for UDP-encap check in XfrmController

When setting the socket owner for an encap socket XfrmController will
first attempt to verify that the socket has the UDP-encap socket option
set. When doing so it would pass in an uninitialized optlen parameter
which could cause the call to not modify the option value if the optlen
happened to be too short. So for example if the stack happened to
contain a zero where optlen was located the check would fail and the
socket owner would not be changed.

Fix this by setting optlen to the size of the option value parameter.

original_information.commit_message:
net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

This prevents numerous uninitialized memory leaks we had in the
recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

Optimize for the case recvfrom is called with NULL as address. We don't
need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Also document these changes in include/linux/net.h as suggested by David
Miller.

Changes since RFC:

Set msg->msg_name = NULL if user specified a NULL in msg_name but had a
non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "
if (!uaddr || msg_sys->msg_namelen == 0)
	msg->msg_name = NULL
".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

Also remove two unnecessary curly brackets in ___sys_recvmsg and change
comments to netdev style.

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function RangeThresholdImage applies a two-stage threshold (range threshold) to each pixel in an image.  
  - It first ensures the image is in “DirectClass” storage (one sample per pixel) and that grayscale images are moved into sRGB color space.  
  - It acquires a thread-safe cache view for pixel reads/writes and then, in parallel across rows, does:  
    • Fetch one scanline of pixels (`GetCacheViewAuthenticPixels`).  
    • For each pixel, compute its intensity.  
    • For each channel of that pixel (respecting the image’s channel mask and traits):  
      – If intensity < low_black, set channel to 0.  
      – If low_black ≤ intensity < low_white, linearly ramp from 0 to max (QuantumRange).  
      – If low_white ≤ intensity ≤ high_white, set channel to QuantumRange.  
      – If high_white < intensity ≤ high_black, linearly ramp from max back to 0.  
      – If intensity > high_black, set channel to 0.  
    • Write the modified scanline back (`SyncCacheViewAuthenticPixels`).  
    • Update a progress counter and invoke the progress monitor callback.  
  - Finally it destroys the cache view and returns success/failure.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Memory safety: All pixel accesses use MagickCore cache APIs (`GetCacheViewAuthenticPixels` and `SyncCacheViewAuthenticPixels`) which ensure valid buffers; indexing is bounded by `image->columns * channels`.  
  - Integer overflow: Loop bounds use `ssize_t` for rows and columns; there is no arithmetic that could overflow between 0 and the image dimensions.  
  - Division by zero: The code calls `PerceptibleReciprocal(low_white-low_black)` and similarly for `(high_black-high_white)`. In ImageMagick this routine returns a safe reciprocal even when the difference is zero, preventing an actual divide-by-zero fault.  
  - Thread safety: The loop is parallelized with OpenMP. The shared `status` flag is only ever set from true→false (safe under concurrent writes), and the `progress` counter is updated atomically. Each thread writes distinct scanlines.  
  - No user data is used to index out of bounds or to execute code paths that would corrupt memory.  

3. Decision

  No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It properly bounds pixel access, handles zero denominators safely, and uses thread-safe cache operations.

original_information.commit_message:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

original_information.commit_message:
nEPT: Nested INVEPT

If we let L1 use EPT, we should probably also support the INVEPT instruction.

In our current nested EPT implementation, when L1 changes its EPT table
for L2 (i.e., EPT12), L0 modifies the shadow EPT table (EPT02), and in
the course of this modification already calls INVEPT. But if last level
of shadow page is unsync not all L1's changes to EPT12 are intercepted,
which means roots need to be synced when L1 calls INVEPT. Global INVEPT
should not be different since roots are synced by kvm_mmu_load() each
time EPTP02 changes.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function fib6_lookup_1(root, args) searches an IPv6 prefix tree (a binary radix tree) for the longest‐matching route entry corresponding to args->addr.
- It first checks if args->offset is zero; if so, it aborts early (returns NULL).
- It then “descends” the tree starting from root:
  • At each node fn, it tests bit fn->fn_bit of args->addr.
  • If that bit is 1, it follows fn->right; otherwise fn->left.
  • It repeats until it reaches a node with no further matching child (“next” is NULL).
- Once the descent finishes at fn, it walks back up the parent chain:
  • For each fn, if it represents a subtree root or contains RTN_RTINFO, it computes a pointer  
    key = (rt6key *)(fn->leaf + args->offset)  
    and checks whether key->addr matches args->addr for the stored prefix length.
  • If fn has a subtree (CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES) and the match passes, it recursively calls  
    fib6_lookup_1(fn->subtree, args+1) to continue in the next subtable.
  • If fn carries RTN_RTINFO (i.e. a valid route) it returns fn.
  • Otherwise it moves fn = fn->parent until it hits RTN_ROOT, then exits with NULL.
- The function thus implements a longest‐prefix IPv6 lookup with support for optional subtree stages.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- The only pointer arithmetic that might go out of bounds is `(u8 *)fn->leaf + args->offset`.  
  • In principle, if args->offset were arbitrarily large or incorrect, `key` could point outside the `leaf` block, leading to an out‐of‐bounds read in `ipv6_prefix_equal()`.  
  • However, in the IPv6 FIB implementation, args->offset is internally assigned at route‐insertion time to the exact byte offset of the rt6key within fn->leaf. Callers of fib6_lookup_1 never supply an external offset.  
- All other branches and loops are bounded by the tree structure:
  • The descent loop exits when no child exists.
  • The climb loop stops at the root marker (RTN_ROOT).
  • Bit tests and flag checks do not dereference invalid memory.
- No user‐supplied data (other than the IPv6 address, which is only read) can influence memory layout or offsets. There is no unchecked index or untrusted pointer arithmetic beyond the internally controlled offset.

3. Decision

No, the code contains no exploitable vulnerability. It only performs safe, internally validated pointer arithmetic and tree traversal.

original_information.commit_message:
net: fib: fib6_add: fix potential NULL pointer dereference

When the kernel is compiled with CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES, and we return
with an error in fn = fib6_add_1(), then error codes are encoded into
the return pointer e.g. ERR_PTR(-ENOENT). In such an error case, we
write the error code into err and jump to out, hence enter the if(err)
condition. Now, if CONFIG_IPV6_SUBTREES is enabled, we check for:

  if (pn != fn && pn->leaf == rt)
    ...
  if (pn != fn && !pn->leaf && !(pn->fn_flags & RTN_RTINFO))
    ...

Since pn is NULL and fn is f.e. ERR_PTR(-ENOENT), then pn != fn
evaluates to true and causes a NULL-pointer dereference on further
checks on pn. Fix it, by setting both NULL in error case, so that
pn != fn already evaluates to false and no further dereference
takes place.

This was first correctly implemented in 4a287eba2 ("IPv6 routing,
NLM_F_* flag support: REPLACE and EXCL flags support, warn about
missing CREATE flag"), but the bug got later on introduced by
188c517a0 ("ipv6: return errno pointers consistently for fib6_add_1()").

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis

- The function `fcs_len` accepts a pointer `s` to an `E1000State` structure.  
- It reads the `RCTL` register value from the `mac_reg` array inside `s`.  
- It tests the `E1000_RCTL_SECRC` bit in that register:  
  - If the bit is set, it returns 0.  
  - If the bit is clear, it returns 4.  
- In other words, it chooses whether to include a 4-byte FCS (Frame Check Sequence) based on whether the “Strip CRC” control bit is enabled.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no user‐supplied data parsing, no loops or recursion, no pointer arithmetic, no memory allocation or copying, and no formatted I/O—so classic buffer overflows, format‐string bugs, integer overflows, or similar issues do not arise.  
- The only indirect safety consideration is that the pointer `s` must be non-NULL and valid; if a caller passed a null or invalid pointer, this code would dereference it and crash. However, that is a caller‐side precondition, not an inherent flaw in this simple bit test.  
- No uninitialized data is read; all operations are on existing fields of the provided struct.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It simply returns 0 or 4 based on a single register bit.

original_information.Summary: Buffer overflow in the e1000_receive function in the e1000 device driver (hw/e1000.c) in QEMU 1.3.0-rc2 and other versions, when the SBP and LPE flags are disabled, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest OS crash) and possibly execute arbitrary guest code via a large packet.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function t2p_pdf_tifftime tries to read the TIFFTAG_DATETIME field (a string) from the TIFF handle.  
   - If the field exists and its length is at least 19 characters, it re-formats selected characters into the PDF date format “D:YYYYMMDDHHMMSS” stored in t2p->pdf_datetime, then NUL-terminates it.  
   - If the TIFF tag is absent or shorter than 19 bytes, it calls t2p_pdf_currenttime(t2p) to generate a “current time” timestamp instead.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflow: The code checks strlen(datetime) ≥ 19 before indexing datetime[0..18], so it will not read past the source buffer. Assuming t2p->pdf_datetime is allocated with at least 17+1 bytes, there is no overflow on the destination side.  
   - Null termination: The function explicitly writes a terminating '\0' at position 16, ensuring t2p->pdf_datetime is properly terminated.  
   - Integer overflow or format issues: None are present; all index calculations are constants and safe.  
   - Reliance on TIFFGetField: It assumes the library returns a valid, NUL-terminated datetime string, which is standard TIFF behavior.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code correctly bounds its reads and writes and does not contain a vulnerability.

original_information.Summary: tools/tiffcrop.c in libtiff 4.0.6 has out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities in buffers. Reported as MSVR 35093, MSVR 35096, and MSVR 35097.
original_information.commit_message:
* tools/tiffcrop.c: fix various out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities
in heap or stack allocated buffers. Reported as MSVR 35093,
MSVR 35096 and MSVR 35097. Discovered by Axel Souchet and Vishal
Chauhan from the MSRC Vulnerabilities & Mitigations team.
* tools/tiff2pdf.c: fix out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities in
heap allocate buffer in t2p_process_jpeg_strip(). Reported as MSVR
35098. Discovered by Axel Souchet and Vishal Chauhan from the MSRC
Vulnerabilities & Mitigations team.
* libtiff/tif_pixarlog.c: fix out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities
in heap allocated buffers. Reported as MSVR 35094. Discovered by
Axel Souchet and Vishal Chauhan from the MSRC Vulnerabilities &
Mitigations team.
* libtiff/tif_write.c: fix issue in error code path of TIFFFlushData1()
that didn't reset the tif_rawcc and tif_rawcp members. I'm not
completely sure if that could happen in practice outside of the odd
behaviour of t2p_seekproc() of tiff2pdf). The report points that a
better fix could be to check the return value of TIFFFlushData1() in
places where it isn't done currently, but it seems this patch is enough.
Reported as MSVR 35095. Discovered by Axel Souchet & Vishal Chauhan &
Suha Can from the MSRC Vulnerabilities & Mitigations team.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
   - The method `Document::enqueuePageshowEvent` takes a `PageshowEventPersistence` argument named `persisted`.  
   - Inside the method, it calls `PageTransitionEvent::create`, passing in the event name for a “pageshow” event (obtained via `eventNames().pageshowEvent`) and the `persisted` flag.  
   - The newly created `PageTransitionEvent` object is then dispatched to the window (or document) context via `dispatchWindowEvent`, with `this` as the target.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no direct handling of untrusted input in this snippet: `persisted` is an internal enum/flag, and `eventNames().pageshowEvent` is a static string.  
   - `PageTransitionEvent::create` and `dispatchWindowEvent` are framework APIs responsible for correctly constructing and queuing the event. Assuming they perform their usual validation and memory management, no buffer overflows, injection flaws, or use-after-free conditions are introduced here.  
   - Because the code merely wraps and forwards a known event type with a Boolean-like persistence flag—and does not interpolate user data into scripts or HTML—it is not susceptible to DOM-based XSS, script injection, or similar client-side attacks.

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities; it safely constructs and dispatches a pageshow event.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The method `HandleClientRequest` processes an incoming client request on a promised (pushed) stream in a QUIC session.  
   - It first checks whether the stream identified by `id_` has already been closed (`session_->IsClosedStream(id_)`). If so, it calls `session_->DeletePromised(this)` to remove the promise and returns a failure status.  
   - Next, it checks whether this promise is already in a validation state (`is_validating()`). If it is, it immediately returns failure.  
   - It then records the caller’s delegate pointer (`client_request_delegate_ = delegate`) and makes a deep copy of the incoming headers (`client_request_headers_.reset(new SpdyHeaderBlock(request_headers.Clone()))`).  
   - If there is not yet a corresponding set of response headers (`!response_headers_`), it defers final processing by returning `QUIC_PENDING`.  
   - Once the response headers are available, it proceeds with `FinalValidation()` to complete the interaction.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Use‑after‑free: Deleting `this` via `session_->DeletePromised(this)` and then immediately returning prevents further member access in this function. The caller must respect the `QUIC_FAILURE` return and not touch the object again. As long as that contract is honored, there is no built‑in use‑after‑free in this snippet.  
   - Null‑pointer dereference:  
     • `session_` and `response_headers_` are assumed valid or state‑managed elsewhere in the class. If `session_` were null, it would crash, but typical QUIC session setup ensures `session_` is non‑null.  
     • `delegate` is stored blindly; if a null delegate is later invoked, that would be an issue, but this code does not dereference `delegate` here.  
   - Race conditions: The code does not show locks around `response_headers_` or `is_validating()`. In a multithreaded context, concurrent updates could require external synchronization, but that is outside this method’s scope.  
   - Resource leaks: The header clone is managed by a smart pointer (`unique_ptr` or similar via `reset`), so no explicit leak is evident here.  
   - Injection or boundary issues: The code merely copies header data and does not parse it or write it into fixed‑size buffers, so no buffer overflow or injection risk is introduced at this level.

3. Decision  
   No, the snippet does not contain any direct vulnerabilities. It correctly manages its control flow, resource ownership, and failure paths.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function ext4_end_io_unwritten is an end‑I/O callback invoked when an unwritten (delayed‑allocation) buffer completes its I/O.
- It retrieves the associated inode from bh->b_assoc_map->host.
- It computes the file‑offset “offset” of this buffer by taking bh->b_private (which holds the logical block number), casting it to loff_t, and shifting left by inode->i_blkbits (i.e. multiplying by the block size).
- If the I/O did not complete successfully (uptodate == 0), the function simply returns without further action.
- It emits a WARN_ON if the buffer is unexpectedly not marked as “unwritten.”
- Finally it calls ext4_convert_unwritten_extents(NULL, inode, offset, bh->b_size) to convert the range covered by this buffer from unwritten into written extents in the file’s metadata.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer overflow on 32‑bit architectures?  
  There is a known comment (“XXX: breaks on 32‑bit > 16TB”) indicating that casting and shifting bh->b_private may overflow the 32‑bit intermediate if the file is extremely large. In practice ext4 on 32‑bit kernels cannot reliably handle files that big anyway, so this is a limitation rather than a security hole.  
- Memory safety  
  All pointer dereferences (bh, bh->b_assoc_map, host) are internal kernel structures allocated and managed by ext4; there is no unchecked user pointer or user–kernel boundary here.  
- Error handling  
  The return value err from ext4_convert_unwritten_extents is ignored, so a conversion failure won’t be reported to the caller. This may lead to data‑consistency issues but again is not a direct memory‑corruption or privilege‑escalation flaw.

Overall, there is no sign of buffer overrun, use‑after‑free, or other classic exploitable memory corruption. The only “issue” is a large‑file arithmetic limitation on 32‑bit, which is documented in the comment.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain a security vulnerability. It may exhibit data‑consistency or correctness limitations on very large files on 32‑bit kernels, but it is not exploitable as a memory‑corruption or privilege‑escalation flaw.

original_information.Summary: Multiple race conditions in the ext4 filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.5 allow local users to cause a denial of service (disk corruption) by writing to a page that is associated with a different user's file after unsynchronized hole punching and page-fault handling.
original_information.commit_message:
ext4: fix races between page faults and hole punching

Currently, page faults and hole punching are completely unsynchronized.
This can result in page fault faulting in a page into a range that we
are punching after truncate_pagecache_range() has been called and thus
we can end up with a page mapped to disk blocks that will be shortly
freed. Filesystem corruption will shortly follow. Note that the same
race is avoided for truncate by checking page fault offset against
i_size but there isn't similar mechanism available for punching holes.

Fix the problem by creating new rw semaphore i_mmap_sem in inode and
grab it for writing over truncate, hole punching, and other functions
removing blocks from extent tree and for read over page faults. We
cannot easily use i_data_sem for this since that ranks below transaction
start and we need something ranking above it so that it can be held over
the whole truncate / hole punching operation. Also remove various
workarounds we had in the code to reduce race window when page fault
could have created pages with stale mapping information.

Signed-off-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function `GetSkRegion` takes two parameters:
    • `JNIEnv* env`: a pointer to the JNI environment, used for calling JNI functions.  
    • `jobject regionObject`: a Java object which is expected to wrap a native `SkRegion*`.  
  - It calls `env->GetLongField(regionObject, gRegion_nativeInstanceFieldID)` to read a `long` field named by `gRegion_nativeInstanceFieldID` from the Java object. This field is presumed to hold the native pointer value.  
  - It then reinterpret‑casts that `jlong` (64‑bit integer) back into a `SkRegion*`.  
  - An assertion (`SkASSERT(region != NULL)`) checks at runtime (in debug builds) that the resulting pointer is not null.  
  - Finally it returns the `SkRegion*`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Pointer integrity: The code assumes that the Java field truly holds a valid, live `SkRegion*`. If that field has been overwritten or never properly initialized, the cast yields an invalid pointer. Any subsequent use of that pointer can crash or corrupt memory.  
  - Missing validation: Beyond checking for null, there is no safeguards against bogus or out‑of‑bounds pointers. In a hostile environment, a malicious Java layer could provide an arbitrary long value and induce arbitrary‐memory reads or writes in native code.  
  - Lifecycle management: If the native `SkRegion` was freed on the native side but the Java wrapper still holds its old pointer value, calling `GetSkRegion` would return a dangling pointer, leading to use‑after‑free.  
  - Field lookup errors: If the field ID `gRegion_nativeInstanceFieldID` is invalid or uninitialized, `GetLongField` can crash. Proper JNI error checks are not shown here.

3. Decision

No, the snippet itself does not mitigate risks around pointer validity or object lifetime. It merely retrieves and asserts non‑null. Without higher‑level checks, it is susceptible to invalid or malicious pointer injection and use‑after‑free.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis

   The function `get_data(FILE *pnm_file, int depth)` reads successive pixel values of a specified bit‐depth from a PNM‐style file stream, one group of bits at a time, and returns each sample as a 32-bit unsigned integer.  Here is what each part does:

   • Static variables  
     – `bits_left`: how many unused bits remain in the current byte buffer (`old_value`).  
     – `old_value`: the last byte fetched from the file, used as a shifting bit-source.  
     – `mask`: a bitmask that isolates `depth` bits in `old_value`.

   • Mask initialization  
     If `mask` is zero (first invocation), a loop generates a mask with exactly `depth` high bits set in the most significant positions.  

   • Replenish buffer  
     If no bits remain (`bits_left <= 0`), the next byte is read from `pnm_file` via `fgetc`, stored in `old_value`, and `bits_left` is reset to 8.

   • Extract bits  
     – `ret_value = old_value & mask;` isolates the top `depth` bits of `old_value`.  
     – The loop `for (i = 1; i < (8/depth); i++) ret_value = ret_value || (ret_value >> depth);` is intended to replicate or pack those bits into a full sample.  

   • Shift buffer  
     The code then shifts `old_value` left by `depth` bits, masks to a byte, and decrements `bits_left` by `depth`.

   • Return  
     The accumulated value of that `depth`-bit field is returned.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Integer divide-by-zero  
     – If `depth` ≤ 0, the expression `8 / depth` is undefined or will raise a runtime error.  

   • Missing EOF check  
     – The return of `fgetc` is not checked for `EOF` (–1). An `old_value` of –1 propagates through bit-operations in unexpected ways.  

   • Logical bug vs. bitwise intent  
     – The code uses the C logical-OR operator `||` instead of the bitwise OR operator `|`. This causes `ret_value` to collapse to 0 or 1, not to the intended bit pattern.  

   • Static state  
     – The use of function-local `static` variables makes the function non-reentrant and not thread-safe. Concurrent calls or different `depth` values across calls can corrupt its internal state.  

   • No memory or buffer overflow  
     – There is no heap allocation or buffer indexing by untrusted lengths. No direct risk of classic buffer overrun or memory corruption.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not exhibit a memory‐corruption or injection vulnerability, but it does suffer from input validation issues (divide-by-zero, unchecked EOF), a logical operator bug (`||` vs `|`), and lack of reentrancy/thread‐safety.

+  Fixed an error in handling of bad zlib CMINFO field in pngfix, found by
+    American Fuzzy Lop, reported by Brian Carpenter.  inflate() doesn't
+    immediately fault a bad CMINFO field; instead a 'too far back' error
+    happens later (at least some times).  pngfix failed to limit CMINFO to
+    the allowed values but then assumed that window_bits was in range,
+    triggering an assert. The bug is mostly harmless; the PNG file cannot
+    be fixed.
+  In libpng 1.6 zlib initialization was changed to use the window size
+    in the zlib stream, not a fixed value. This causes some invalid images,
+    where CINFO is too large, to display 'correctly' if the rest of the
+    data is valid.  This provides a workaround for zlib versions where the
+    error arises (ones that support the API change to use the window size

+VIII. Configuring libpng for 16-bit platforms
+
+You will want to look into zconf.h to tell zlib (and thus libpng) that
+it cannot allocate more than 64K at a time.  Even if you can, the memory
+won't be accessible.  So limit zlib and libpng to 64K by defining MAXSEG_64K.
+
+IX. Configuring for DOS
+
+For DOS users who only have access to the lower 640K, you will
+have to limit zlib's memory usage via a png_set_compression_mem_level()
+call.  See zlib.h or zconf.h in the zlib library for more information.
+
+X. Configuring for Medium Model
+
+Libpng's support for medium model has been tested on most of the popular
+compilers.  Make sure MAXSEG_64K gets defined, USE_FAR_KEYWORD gets
+defined, and FAR gets defined to far in pngconf.h, and you should be
+all set.  Everything in the library (except for zlib's structure) is
+expecting far data.  You must use the typedefs with the p or pp on
+the end for pointers (or at least look at them and be careful).  Make
+note that the rows of data are defined as png_bytepp, which is
+an "unsigned char far * far *".
+
+XI. Prepending a prefix to exported symbols
+
+Starting with libpng-1.6.0, you can configure libpng (when using the
+"configure" script) to prefix all exported symbols by means of the
+configuration option "--with-libpng-prefix=FOO_", where FOO_ can be any
+string beginning with a letter and containing only uppercase
+and lowercase letters, digits, and the underscore (i.e., a C language
+identifier).  This creates a set of macros in pnglibconf.h, so this is
+transparent to applications; their function calls get transformed by
+the macros to use the modified names.
+
+XII. Configuring for compiler xxx:
+
+All includes for libpng are in pngconf.h.  If you need to add, change
+or delete an include, this is the place to do it.
+The includes that are not needed outside libpng are placed in pngpriv.h,
+which is only used by the routines inside libpng itself.
+The files in libpng proper only include pngpriv.h and png.h, which
+in turn includes pngconf.h and, as of libpng-1.5.0, pnglibconf.h.
+As of libpng-1.5.0, pngpriv.h also includes three other private header
+files, pngstruct.h, pnginfo.h, and pngdebug.h, which contain material
+that previously appeared in the public headers.
+
+XIII. Removing unwanted object code
+
+There are a bunch of #define's in pngconf.h that control what parts of
+libpng are compiled.  All the defines end in _SUPPORTED.  If you are
+never going to use a capability, you can change the #define to #undef
+before recompiling libpng and save yourself code and data space, or
+you can turn off individual capabilities with defines that begin with
+PNG_NO_.
+
+In libpng-1.5.0 and later, the #define's are in pnglibconf.h instead.
+
+You can also turn all of the transforms and ancillary chunk capabilities
+off en masse with compiler directives that define
+PNG_NO_READ[or WRITE]_TRANSFORMS, or PNG_NO_READ[or WRITE]_ANCILLARY_CHUNKS,
+or all four, along with directives to turn on any of the capabilities that
+you do want.  The PNG_NO_READ[or WRITE]_TRANSFORMS directives disable the
+extra transformations but still leave the library fully capable of reading
+and writing PNG files with all known public chunks. Use of the
+PNG_NO_READ[or WRITE]_ANCILLARY_CHUNKS directive produces a library
+that is incapable of reading or writing ancillary chunks.  If you are
+not using the progressive reading capability, you can turn that off
+with PNG_NO_PROGRESSIVE_READ (don't confuse this with the INTERLACING
+capability, which you'll still have).
+
+All the reading and writing specific code are in separate files, so the
+linker should only grab the files it needs.  However, if you want to
+make sure, or if you are building a stand alone library, all the
+reading files start with "pngr" and all the writing files start with "pngw".
+The files that don't match either (like png.c, pngtrans.c, etc.)
+are used for both reading and writing, and always need to be included.
+The progressive reader is in pngpread.c
+
+If you are creating or distributing a dynamically linked library (a .so
+or DLL file), you should not remove or disable any parts of the library,
+as this will cause applications linked with different versions of the
+library to fail if they call functions not available in your library.
+The size of the library itself should not be an issue, because only
+those sections that are actually used will be loaded into memory.

+XIV. Changes to the build and configuration of libpng in libpng-1.5.x
+
+Details of internal changes to the library code can be found in the CHANGES
+file and in the GIT repository logs.  These will be of no concern to the vast
+majority of library users or builders; however, the few who configure libpng
+to a non-default feature set may need to change how this is done.
+
+There should be no need for library builders to alter build scripts if
+these use the distributed build support - configure or the makefiles -
+however, users of the makefiles may care to update their build scripts
+to build pnglibconf.h where the corresponding makefile does not do so.
+
+Building libpng with a non-default configuration has changed completely.
+The old method using pngusr.h should still work correctly even though the
+way pngusr.h is used in the build has been changed; however, library
+builders will probably want to examine the changes to take advantage of
+new capabilities and to simplify their build system.
+
+A. Specific changes to library configuration capabilities
+
+The exact mechanism used to control attributes of API functions has
+changed.  A single set of operating system independent macro definitions
+is used and operating system specific directives are defined in
+pnglibconf.h
+
+As part of this the mechanism used to choose procedure call standards on
+those systems that allow a choice has been changed.  At present this only
+affects certain Microsoft (DOS, Windows) and IBM (OS/2) operating systems
+running on Intel processors.  As before, PNGAPI is defined where required
+to control the exported API functions; however, two new macros, PNGCBAPI
+and PNGCAPI, are used instead for callback functions (PNGCBAPI) and
+(PNGCAPI) for functions that must match a C library prototype (currently
+only png_longjmp_ptr, which must match the C longjmp function.)  The new
+approach is documented in pngconf.h
+
+Despite these changes, libpng 1.5.0 only supports the native C function
+calling standard on those platforms tested so far (__cdecl on Microsoft
+Windows).  This is because the support requirements for alternative
+calling conventions seem to no longer exist.  Developers who find it
+necessary to set PNG_API_RULE to 1 should advise the mailing list
+(png-mng-implement) of this and library builders who use Openwatcom and
+therefore set PNG_API_RULE to 2 should also contact the mailing list.
+
+B. Changes to the configuration mechanism
+
+Prior to libpng-1.5.0 library builders who needed to configure libpng
+had either to modify the exported pngconf.h header file to add system
+specific configuration or had to write feature selection macros into
+pngusr.h and cause this to be included into pngconf.h by defining
+PNG_USER_CONFIG. The latter mechanism had the disadvantage that an
+application built without PNG_USER_CONFIG defined would see the
+unmodified, default, libpng API and thus would probably fail to link.
+
+These mechanisms still work in the configure build and in any makefile
+build that builds pnglibconf.h, although the feature selection macros
+have changed somewhat as described above.  In 1.5.0, however, pngusr.h is
+processed only once, at the time the exported header file pnglibconf.h is
+built.  pngconf.h no longer includes pngusr.h; therefore, pngusr.h is ignored
+after the build of pnglibconf.h and it is never included in an application
+build.
+
+The formerly used alternative of adding a list of feature macros to the
+CPPFLAGS setting in the build also still works; however, the macros will be
+copied to pnglibconf.h and this may produce macro redefinition warnings
+when the individual C files are compiled.
+
+All configuration now only works if pnglibconf.h is built from
+scripts/pnglibconf.dfa.  This requires the program awk.  Brian Kernighan
+(the original author of awk) maintains C source code of that awk and this
+and all known later implementations (often called by subtly different
+names - nawk and gawk for example) are adequate to build pnglibconf.h.
+The Sun Microsystems (now Oracle) program 'awk' is an earlier version
+and does not work; this may also apply to other systems that have a
+functioning awk called 'nawk'.
+
+Configuration options are now documented in scripts/pnglibconf.dfa.  This
+file also includes dependency information that ensures a configuration is
+consistent; that is, if a feature is switched off, dependent features are
+also switched off.  As a recommended alternative to using feature macros in
+pngusr.h a system builder may also define equivalent options in pngusr.dfa
+(or, indeed, any file) and add that to the configuration by setting
+DFA_XTRA to the file name.  The makefiles in contrib/pngminim illustrate
+how to do this, and also illustrate a case where pngusr.h is still required.
+
+After you have built libpng, the definitions that were recorded in
+pnglibconf.h are available to your application (pnglibconf.h is included
+in png.h and gets installed alongside png.h and pngconf.h in your
+$PREFIX/include directory).  Do not edit pnglibconf.h after you have built
+libpng, because than the settings would not accurately reflect the settings
+that were used to build libpng.

+XV. Setjmp/longjmp issues
+
+Libpng uses setjmp()/longjmp() for error handling.  Unfortunately setjmp()
+is known to be not thread-safe on some platforms and we don't know of
+any platform where it is guaranteed to be thread-safe.  Therefore, if
+your application is going to be using multiple threads, you should
+configure libpng with PNG_NO_SETJMP in your pngusr.dfa file, with
+-DPNG_NO_SETJMP on your compile line, or with
+
+  #undef PNG_SETJMP_SUPPORTED
+
+in your pnglibconf.h or pngusr.h.

+Starting with libpng-1.6.0, the library included a "simplified API".
+This requires setjmp/longjmp, so you must either build the library
+with PNG_SETJMP_SUPPORTED defined, or with PNG_SIMPLIFIED_READ_SUPPORTED
+and PNG_SIMPLIFIED_WRITE_SUPPORTED undefined.

-	  || $(CSCOPE) -b -q $(AM_CSCOPEFLAGS) $(CSCOPEFLAGS) -i cscope.files $(CSCOPE_ARGS)
