- It obtains a pointer to the algorithm payload `algp = nla_data(rt)`.  
- It checks that the provided attribute length (`nla_len(rt)`) is at least as large as the minimum expected size for that algorithm payload (`xfrm_alg_len(algp)`). If the payload is too short, it returns –EINVAL.  
- It verifies that `type` is one of the three allowed algorithm attribute types (`XFRMA_ALG_AUTH`, `XFRMA_ALG_CRYPT`, or `XFRMA_ALG_COMP`). Any other type is rejected with –EINVAL.

- On success, it returns 0.

  The only write performed is `algp->alg_name[sizeof(algp->alg_name)-1] = '\0';`. Whether this can stray past the buffer depends entirely on the correctness of the previous length check

Under normal definitions of `xfrm_alg_len()` (which is typically `offsetof(xfrm_algo, alg_key) + algp->alg_key_len`), that check guarantees the entire `alg_name` array lies within the provided netlink payload. In that case, the NUL-termination write is safe.  
  A maliciously large or specially crafted `alg_key_len` could in theory cause an integer-overflow in the computation of `xfrm_alg_len(algp)`, making the test pass spuriously and permitting an out-of-bounds write.   Beyond length and type checks, there is no further inspection of key bytes or name contents. But that is outside the scope of “verification” and not inherently unsafe.

Separate repaint and layout requirements of StyleDifference (Step 1)

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies
StyleDifferenceRepaint). This causes unnecessary repaints in some cases
on layout change.

Convert StyleDifference to a structure containing relatively independent
flags.

This change doesn't directly improve the result, but can make further
repaint optimizations possible.

Step 1 doesn't change any functionality. RenderStyle still generate the
legacy StyleDifference enum when comparing styles and convert the result
to the new StyleDifference. Implicit requirements are not handled during
the conversion.

Converted call sites to use the new StyleDifference according to the
following conversion rules:
- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceLayout => diff.needsFullLayout()

original_information.commit_message:
nEPT: Nested INVEPT

If we let L1 use EPT, we should probably also support the INVEPT instruction.

In our current nested EPT implementation, when L1 changes its EPT table
for L2 (i.e., EPT12), L0 modifies the shadow EPT table (EPT02), and in
the course of this modification already calls INVEPT. But if last level
of shadow page is unsync not all L1's changes to EPT12 are intercepted,
which means roots need to be synced when L1 calls INVEPT. Global INVEPT
should not be different since roots are synced by kvm_mmu_load() each
time EPTP02 changes.

- It declares a local variable `ksm_pages_volatile` of type `long`.
- It computes `ksm_pages_volatile` by subtracting three counters (`ksm_pages_shared`, `ksm_pages_sharing`, `ksm_pages_unshared`) from the total reverse‑map item count (`ksm_rmap_items`).
- A comment explains that these counters are read without locking, so the result might occasionally go negative; the following `if` clause forces any negative result to zero.

  • Sysfs “show” buffers are allocated at `PAGE_SIZE` (4 KB or larger), so the small formatted string cannot overflow the buffer.  
- Format‑string issue:  
  • The format string is a constant `"%ld\n"`, so there is no user‑controlled formatting.  
- Integer underflow/overflow:  
  • The subtraction could underflow or overflow a `long`, but the code clamps negative results to zero.  
  • On systems where `long` wraps, an extremely large underflow could produce a positive value, but in practice the statistics involved remain far below the limits of a `long`.  
- Concurrency/data race:  
  • The counters are read without locking, so the reported value might be slightly out of date or briefly negative (hence the clamp). This is a design trade‑off, not a security flaw.  
- Return‑value correctness:  
  • The function returns an `ssize_t` equal to the number of bytes printed, which is the convention expected by sysfs.  

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly clamps negative results, uses a safe fixed format string, and writes far less data than the sysfs buffer size.

ipv4: Don't do expensive useless work during inetdev destroy.

is removed.  And in this scenerio we do two pointless things which can
be very expensive if the number of assigned interfaces is large:

x86,kvm,vmx: Preserve CR4 across VM entry

like it's correct.

extremely likely that consecutive entries into the same vcpu will have

original_information.commit_message:
ipv6: addrconf: validate new MTU before applying it

Currently we don't check if the new MTU is valid or not and this allows
one to configure a smaller than minimum allowed by RFCs or even bigger
than interface own MTU, which is a problem as it may lead to packet
drops.

If you have a daemon like NetworkManager running, this may be exploited
by remote attackers by forging RA packets with an invalid MTU, possibly
leading to a DoS. (NetworkManager currently only validates for values
too small, but not for too big ones.)

The fix is just to make sure the new value is valid. That is, between
IPV6_MIN_MTU and interface's MTU.

Note that similar check is already performed at
ndisc_router_discovery(), for when kernel itself parses the RA.

- It first retrieves the bookmark’s title:
  - Calls `FPDFBookmark_GetTitle` to get the required buffer size.
  - Allocates a `base::string16` of that size via `PDFiumAPIStringBufferSizeInBytesAdapter`.
  - Calls `FPDFBookmark_GetTitle` again to fill the buffer, then converts from UTF‑16 to UTF‑8.
  - Stores the UTF‑8 title under key `"title"` in a `pp::VarDictionary`.
- It then tries to locate a destination (`FPDF_DEST`) for the bookmark:
  - If present, it gets the page index via `FPDFDest_GetDestPageIndex`.
  - Checks the page index is in bounds, and if so stores `"page"` and, via `GetPageXYTarget`, stores a `"y"` coordinate if available.
- If no explicit destination is found, it looks for an action of type URI:
  - Calls `FPDFAction_GetURIPath` first to get the buffer size, then to fill a `std::string`.
  - Stores the URI under key `"uri"`.
- Finally, it enumerates child bookmarks:
  - It enforces a maximum recursion depth of 128.
  - For each child returned by `FPDFBookmark_GetFirstChild` / `FPDFBookmark_GetNextSibling`, it:
    - Tracks seen child pointers in a local `std::set` to break on immediate cycles.
    - Recursively calls `TraverseBookmarks` with `depth+1`.
    - Appends each child’s dictionary to a `pp::VarArray`.
  - Associates this array under key `"children"` in the dictionary.
- The function returns the populated `pp::VarDictionary`, representing one bookmark and its subtree.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer handling for titles and URIs uses the two‑step “get size then get content” pattern. This prevents classic buffer over‑reads or -overflows as long as `buffer_size` is correct and the PDFium API obeys its contract.
- The recursion depth is capped at `kMaxDepth = 128`, so deep or maliciously cyclic bookmark trees cannot cause unbounded recursion or stack overflow.
- The per-node `seen_bookmarks` set stops infinite loops in the immediate sibling chain. Cross‑level cycles (child pointing back to an ancestor) would only recurse until the depth cap, so there is no uncontrolled infinite recursion.
- There is no explicit limit on the total number of siblings or total nodes processed, so an extremely large bookmark tree (millions of entries) could in theory exhaust memory or CPU time. However, this is a resource‑exhaustion/DoS concern rather than a code execution or memory‐corruption vulnerability.
- No user data is executed or interpolated without sanitization; titles and URIs are treated as plain strings in a dictionary.
- There is no use of unsafe string operations (e.g., `strcpy`) or unchecked arithmetic.

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities. It properly bounds buffers and recursion depth. At worst, a very large bookmark tree could incur high CPU/memory usage, but there is no memory corruption or denial of service beyond natural resource usage.

1. Functional Analysis  
   
   - The function `ipgre_rcv` is the GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) packet-reception handler in the Linux IPv4 stack. It processes an incoming `sk_buff` (socket buffer) from the GRE device.  
   - It first ensures at least 16 contiguous bytes of the linear part of the packet (`pskb_may_pull(skb, 16)`) to cover the maximum GRE header length it will parse.  
   - It extracts the outer IP header (`iph = ip_hdr(skb)`) and a pointer `h = skb->data` to the start of the GRE header.  
   - It reads the 16-bit GRE flags field (`flags = *(__be16*)h`) and rejects the packet if it carries unsupported version or routing bits.  
   - For each supported GRE optional field present (checksum, key, sequence), it:  
     • Adjusts `offset` by 4 bytes per optional field.  
     • If there is a checksum, it computes or verifies it and stores it in `csum`.  
     • If there is a key, it reads it into `key`.  
     • If there is a sequence number, it reads it into `seqno`.  
   - It reads the GRE protocol field (`gre_proto = *(__be16*)(h + 2)`) to know what is encapsulated: IPv4, Ethernet, WCCP, etc.  
   - Under an RCU read-lock it looks up a matching GRE tunnel instance by ingress device, IP addresses, key, and protocol (`ipgre_tunnel_lookup`).  
     • If no such tunnel is found, it sends back an ICMP Destination Unreachable (Port Unreachable) and frees the packet.  
   - Once a tunnel is found, it:  
     • Resets any existing security path (`secpath_reset`).  
     • Sets the packet’s `protocol` to the GRE payload’s Ethertype. Special-cases WCCP to treat it like IP and skip an extra 4 bytes when needed.  
     • Rebase the MAC header, strip (`__pskb_pull`) the GRE header bytes, and adjust checksums accordingly (`skb_postpull_rcsum`).  
     • Marks the packet as destined for local host (`PACKET_HOST`), with a possible promotion to broadcast if the tunnel is multicast and broadcast reception is enabled.  
     • Verifies or enforces checksum and sequence constraints against the tunnel’s configuration, dropping on mismatch or replay.  
     • If the tunnel is an Ethernet-over-GRE type, it again pulls in an Ethernet header, runs `eth_type_trans` to set up L2 header parsing, and updates checksums.  
     • Updates per-CPU statistics for packets and bytes.  
     • Calls `__skb_tunnel_rx` to account for tunnel-related metrics, resets network header pointers, handles ECN decapsulation, and finally enqueues the packet to the network stack (`netif_rx`).  
   - In all error or drop paths it cleans up by releasing the RCU read lock (if held) and freeing the skb (`kfree_skb`).  
   
2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   
   - Input validation and buffer bounds:  
     • The code always calls `pskb_may_pull(skb, X)` before reading up to X bytes, so GRE headers and optional fields are not read out of bounds.  
     • Strip operations via `__pskb_pull` and corresponding checksum adjustments are protected by prior length checks.  
   - Integer overflows or mis-offsetting:  
     • `offset` begins at 4 and increments by exactly 4 per GRE optional field; the maximum is 16 bytes, matching the initial `pskb_may_pull(skb, 16)` check, so there is no offset overflow.  
   - Double-free or use-after-free:  
     • The code paths clearly separate the point where the skb is consumed by `netif_rx` (and ownership is passed on) from the error paths, where `kfree_skb` is called exactly once.  
     • `icmp_send` does not free the original skb (in Linux’s ICEP code it just builds and sends a new skb), so the subsequent `kfree_skb` is correct.  
   - Alignment and unaligned accesses:  
     • The code casts `h` to `__be16*` and `__be32*` to read GRE fields; on architectures without unaligned support this could fault. However, the Linux networking stack assumes unaligned loads via these casts are acceptable, and production kernels build with support or use wrappers—so this is intentional, not an undiscovered bug here.  
   - Concurrency and RCU usage:  
     • `rcu_read_lock`/`rcu_read_unlock` bracket the tunnel lookup and the “fast path” that invokes the tunnel’s data structures. All error paths release the lock correctly.  
   - Special-case WCCP handling:  
     • The extra offset for WCCP does not exceed the available data because it only applies when `flags == 0` (so offset == 4) and the check inspects one byte (`*(h + offset)`) without advancing beyond the initial pull.  
   - Denial-of-service considerations:  
     • Excessive GRE packet floods could consume CPU but are no worse than any other packet-handler path; no unbounded loops or recursive calls exist.  
   
   In summary, the code defends against out-of-bounds access, dropping malformed or unsupported headers, enforces checksum/sequence requirements, and properly manages skb ownership. No buffer overflows, double frees, integer-overflow attacks, or RCU misuse are evident.  
   
3. Decision  
   
   No, the code does not contain any obvious security vulnerabilities. It performs correct bounds checking, checksum and sequence validation, and resource management.

original_information.commit_message:
net: don't allow CAP_NET_ADMIN to load non-netdev kernel modules

Since a8f80e8ff94ecba629542d9b4b5f5a8ee3eb565c any process with
CAP_NET_ADMIN may load any module from /lib/modules/.  This doesn't mean
that CAP_NET_ADMIN is a superset of CAP_SYS_MODULE as modules are
limited to /lib/modules/**.  However, CAP_NET_ADMIN capability shouldn't
allow anybody load any module not related to networking.

This patch restricts an ability of autoloading modules to netdev modules
with explicit aliases.  This fixes CVE-2011-1019.

Arnd Bergmann suggested to leave untouched the old pre-v2.6.32 behavior
of loading netdev modules by name (without any prefix) for processes
with CAP_SYS_MODULE to maintain the compatibility with network scripts
that use autoloading netdev modules by aliases like "eth0", "wlan0".

original_information.commit_message:
net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

This prevents numerous uninitialized memory leaks we had in the
recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

Optimize for the case recvfrom is called with NULL as address. We don't
need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Also document these changes in include/linux/net.h as suggested by David
Miller.

Changes since RFC:

Set msg->msg_name = NULL if user specified a NULL in msg_name but had a
non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "
if (!uaddr || msg_sys->msg_namelen == 0)
	msg->msg_name = NULL
".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

Also remove two unnecessary curly brackets in ___sys_recvmsg and change
comments to netdev style.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `aio_read_events` attempts to read asynchronous I/O completion events from a context ring into a user‐space buffer.
- It takes:
  • `ctx`      – a pointer to the AIO context  
  • `min_nr`   – the minimum number of events the caller wants before returning  
  • `nr`       – the maximum number of events that can be read in this invocation  
  • `event`    – a user‐space pointer to an array of `struct io_event`  
  • `i`        – a pointer to a counter tracking how many events have already been filled  
- It first calls `aio_read_events_ring(ctx, event + *i, nr - *i)` and stores the result in `ret`.  A positive `ret` means that many events were copied, a zero means no events ready, and a negative indicates an error.
- If `ret > 0`, it increments `*i` by `ret` to account for newly read events.
- It then checks whether the context has been marked “dead” (via `atomic_read(&ctx->dead)`).  If so, it forces `ret = -EINVAL` to indicate the context is no longer usable.
- If no events have yet been reported (`*i == 0`), it writes `ret` back into `*i`.  This way, on the very first call, the caller sees either the positive event count, zero, or a negative error code in `*i`.
- Finally, it returns a boolean indicating whether one of these conditions holds:
  • an error was encountered (`ret < 0`), or  
  • the caller’s minimum requirement has been met or exceeded (`*i >= min_nr`).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer bounds:  The ring‐reader is told to copy at most `nr - *i` entries into `event + *i`.  As long as `nr` accurately reflects the user‐provided buffer length, no overflow occurs here.
- User‐space access:  Any actual copy to/from user memory must be performed safely inside `aio_read_events_ring`; this wrapper does not directly dereference the user pointer except in pointer arithmetic, which is safe as long as `*i` ≤ `nr`.
- Dead‐context handling:  By checking `atomic_read(&ctx->dead)` after reading, the code ensures that once the context is torn down, further calls will return `-EINVAL`.  One minor quirk is that if events were already added to `*i` before detecting `dead`, those counts are not rolled back, but the error code is still delivered.  This reflects a design choice, not a memory safety flaw.
- Race conditions:  There is a small window where new events could arrive just as `ctx->dead` is set, but that only affects whether the caller sees them or an error; it does not introduce corruption.
- Return logic:  The final boolean return and the use of `*i` to carry either counts or an initial error code follows common kernel idioms.  No unchecked use of uninitialized data or mishandled pointers is visible.

Conclusion: No memory‐safety or misuse vulnerabilities are present in this wrapper, provided its callee (`aio_read_events_ring`) correctly bounds and copies user data.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any apparent vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
ALSA: pcm : Call kill_fasync() in stream lock

Currently kill_fasync() is called outside the stream lock in
snd_pcm_period_elapsed().  This is potentially racy, since the stream
may get released even during the irq handler is running.  Although
snd_pcm_release_substream() calls snd_pcm_drop(), this doesn't
guarantee that the irq handler finishes, thus the kill_fasync() call
outside the stream spin lock may be invoked after the substream is
detached, as recently reported by KASAN.

As a quick workaround, move kill_fasync() call inside the stream
lock.  The fasync is rarely used interface, so this shouldn't have a
big impact from the performance POV.

Ideally, we should implement some sync mechanism for the proper finish
of stream and irq handler.  But this oneliner should suffice for most
cases, so far.

original_information.commit_message:
tcp: fix SCM_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS for normal skbs

__sock_recv_timestamp can be called for both normal skbs (for
receive timestamps) and for skbs on the error queue (for transmit
timestamps).

Commit 1c885808e456
(tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING)
assumes any skb passed to __sock_recv_timestamp are from
the error queue, containing OPT_STATS in the content of the skb.
This results in accessing invalid memory or generating junk
data.

To fix this, set skb->pkt_type to PACKET_OUTGOING for packets
on the error queue. This is safe because on the receive path
on local sockets skb->pkt_type is never set to PACKET_OUTGOING.
With that, copy OPT_STATS from a packet, only if its pkt_type
is PACKET_OUTGOING.

Fixes: 1c885808e456 ("tcp: SOF_TIMESTAMPING_OPT_STATS option for SO_TIMESTAMPING")

original_information.Summary: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 ignores unreachable code, even though it would still be processed by JIT compilers. This behavior, also considered an improper branch-pruning logic issue, could possibly be used by local users for denial of service.
original_information.commit_message:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

original_information.Summary: The sctp_do_peeloff function in net/sctp/socket.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14 does not check whether the intended netns is used in a peel-off action, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and system crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted system calls.
original_information.commit_message:
sctp: do not peel off an assoc from one netns to another one

Now when peeling off an association to the sock in another netns, all
transports in this assoc are not to be rehashed and keep use the old
key in hashtable.

As a transport uses sk->net as the hash key to insert into hashtable,
it would miss removing these transports from hashtable due to the new
netns when closing the sock and all transports are being freeed, then
later an use-after-free issue could be caused when looking up an asoc
and dereferencing those transports.

This is a very old issue since very beginning, ChunYu found it with
syzkaller fuzz testing with this series:

  socket$inet6_sctp()
  bind$inet6()
  sendto$inet6()
  unshare(0x40000000)
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_GET_ASSOC_ID_LIST()
  getsockopt$inet_sctp6_SCTP_SOCKOPT_PEELOFF()

This patch is to block this call when peeling one assoc off from one
netns to another one, so that the netns of all transport would not
go out-sync with the key in hashtable.

Note that this patch didn't fix it by rehashing transports, as it's
difficult to handle the situation when the tuple is already in use
in the new netns. Besides, no one would like to peel off one assoc
to another netns, considering ipaddrs, ifaces, etc. are usually
different.

Remove the Simple Default Stylesheet, it's just a foot-gun.

We've been bitten by the Simple Default Stylesheet being out
of sync with the real html.css twice this week.

The Simple Default Stylesheet was invented years ago for Mac:
http://trac.webkit.org/changeset/36135
It nicely handles the case where you just want to create
a single WebView and parse some simple HTML either without
styling said HTML, or only to display a small string, etc.

Note that this optimization/complexity *only* helps for the
very first document, since the default stylesheets are
all static (process-global) variables.  Since any real page
on the internet uses a tag not covered by the simple default
stylesheet, not real load benefits from this optimization.
Only uses of WebView which were just rendering small bits
of text might have benefited from this.  about:blank would
also have used this sheet.

This was a common application for some uses of WebView back
in those days.  These days, even with WebView on Android,
there are likely much larger overheads than parsing the
html.css stylesheet, so making it required seems like the
right tradeoff of code-simplicity for this case.

original_information.commit_message:
xfs: fix directory hash ordering bug

Commit f5ea1100 ("xfs: add CRCs to dir2/da node blocks") introduced
in 3.10 incorrectly converted the btree hash index array pointer in
xfs_da3_fixhashpath(). It resulted in the the current hash always
being compared against the first entry in the btree rather than the
current block index into the btree block's hash entry array. As a
result, it was comparing the wrong hashes, and so could misorder the
entries in the btree.

For most cases, this doesn't cause any problems as it requires hash
collisions to expose the ordering problem. However, when there are
hash collisions within a directory there is a very good probability
that the entries will be ordered incorrectly and that actually
matters when duplicate hashes are placed into or removed from the
btree block hash entry array.

This bug results in an on-disk directory corruption and that results
in directory verifier functions throwing corruption warnings into
the logs. While no data or directory entries are lost, access to
them may be compromised, and attempts to remove entries from a
directory that has suffered from this corruption may result in a
filesystem shutdown.  xfs_repair will fix the directory hash
ordering without data loss occuring.

original_information.commit_message:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

manipulation.

Do a (manual) revert of:

  a9e7f6544b9c ("sched/fair: Fix O(nr_cgroups) in load balance path")

It turns out that the list_del_leaf_cfs_rq() introduced by this commit
is a surprising property that was not considered in followup commits
such as:

  9c2791f936ef ("sched/fair: Fix hierarchical order in rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list")

As Vincent Guittot explains:

 "I think that there is a bigger problem with commit a9e7f6544b9c and
  cfs_rq throttling:

  Let take the example of the following topology TG2 --> TG1 --> root:

   1) The 1st time a task is enqueued, we will add TG2 cfs_rq then TG1
      cfs_rq to leaf_cfs_rq_list and we are sure to do the whole branch in
      one path because it has never been used and can't be throttled so
      tmp_alone_branch will point to leaf_cfs_rq_list at the end.

   2) Then TG1 is throttled

   3) and we add TG3 as a new child of TG1.

   4) The 1st enqueue of a task on TG3 will add TG3 cfs_rq just before TG1
      cfs_rq and tmp_alone_branch will stay  on rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.

  With commit a9e7f6544b9c, we can del a cfs_rq from rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list.
  So if the load of TG1 cfs_rq becomes NULL before step 2) above, TG1
  cfs_rq is removed from the list.
  Then at step 4), TG3 cfs_rq is added at the beginning of rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list
  but tmp_alone_branch still points to TG3 cfs_rq because its throttled
  parent can't be enqueued when the lock is released.
  tmp_alone_branch doesn't point to rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list whereas it should.

  So if TG3 cfs_rq is removed or destroyed before tmp_alone_branch
  points on another TG cfs_rq, the next TG cfs_rq that will be added,
  will be linked outside rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list - which is bad.

  In addition, we can break the ordering of the cfs_rq in
  rq->leaf_cfs_rq_list but this ordering is used to update and
  propagate the update from leaf down to root."

Instead of trying to work through all these cases and trying to reproduce
the very high loads that produced the lockup to begin with, simplify
the code temporarily by reverting a9e7f6544b9c - which change was clearly
not thought through completely.

This (hopefully) gives us a kernel that doesn't lock up so people
can continue to enjoy their holidays without worrying about regressions. ;-)

Fix null deref in SPNEGO acceptor [CVE-2014-4344]

When processing a continuation token, acc_ctx_cont was dereferencing
the initial byte of the token without checking the length.  This could
result in a null dereference.

CVE-2014-4344:

In MIT krb5 1.5 and newer, an unauthenticated or partially
authenticated remote attacker can cause a NULL dereference and
application crash during a SPNEGO negotiation by sending an empty
token as the second or later context token from initiator to acceptor.
The attacker must provide at least one valid context token in the
security context negotiation before sending the empty token.  This can
be done by an unauthenticated attacker by forcing SPNEGO to
renegotiate the underlying mechanism, or by using IAKERB to wrap an
unauthenticated AS-REQ as the first token.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function vmx_update_pi_irte() is called when KVM wants to enable or disable posted-interrupt (PI) mode for a given MSI-based guest interrupt.
- It first checks three global capabilities/conditions (assigned-device support, IRQ-posting capability, and active APICv) and aborts early if any are missing.
- It takes an SRCU read-lock around the IRQ-routing table and looks up the list of routing entries for the specified guest IRQ.
- For each MSI-type entry:
  • It builds up a local “struct kvm_lapic_irq” to represent the MSI delivery.  
  • If the MSI can’t be bound to exactly one vCPU, it calls irq_set_vcpu_affinity(host_irq, NULL) to “fall back” to remapped (non-posted) mode, then continues.  
  • If the MSI is destined for exactly one vCPU, it computes the physical address of the vCPU’s PI descriptor and the delivery vector, traces the operation, and then either calls irq_set_vcpu_affinity(host_irq, &vcpu_info) (to enable PI) or, if disabling, does a small ping suppression dance (pi_set_sn/clear_sn) around a call to irq_set_vcpu_affinity(host_irq, NULL).
- It releases the SRCU lock and returns 0 on success or a negative errno on failure.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety: All pointers used (the IRQ-routing table, linked-list entries, vCPU structures) are standard kernel objects protected by SRCU locking. There is no unbounded copy or user-supplied pointer arithmetic.
- Concurrency: The use of srcu_read_lock()/srcu_read_unlock() correctly synchronizes traversal of irq_routing. The calls into irq_set_vcpu_affinity are atomic with respect to IRQ core paths.
- Bounds checking: The code does BUG_ON(guest_irq >= nr_rt_entries). That is an internal assertion which would panic if violated, but guest_irq is maintained by KVM and not directly by untrusted user code.
- Integer overflows or underflows: No arithmetic on sizes; vector and addresses are taken from fixed-size fields.
- Error paths: All calls that can fail return a negative code, which the function propagates (and prints an info-level message). No silent ignoring of errors.
- Summary: There is no evidence of buffer overflows, use-after-free, integer overflows, or race conditions. The intentional BUG_ON enforces an invariant rather than introducing memory corruption.

3. Decision

No, the code contains no evident security vulnerability. It properly validates its inputs, uses SRCU locking for safety, and handles error paths without risk of corrupting memory or leaking data.

original_information.Summary: arch/x86/kvm/vmx.c in the Linux kernel through 4.9 mismanages the #BP and #OF exceptions, which allows guest OS users to cause a denial of service (guest OS crash) by declining to handle an exception thrown by an L2 guest.

were forwarded to L1.

1. Functional Analysis

- The method menuListDefaultEventHandler handles various DOM events (keydown, keypress, mousedown, blur) on a <select> element’s menu list.
- For keydown events:
  • It ignores non‐renderer or non‐keyboard events.  
  • It first lets the platform handle the key.  
  • If spatial navigation is on and the element is not in “active selection” mode, it returns.  
  • It reads the keyIdentifier (“Up”, “Down”, “PageUp”, “PageDown”, “Home”, “End”, “Left”, “Right”) and computes a new list index via nextValidIndex.  
  • If the computed index is in range, it calls selectOption() with flags to deselect other options, dispatch a change event, and mark it user‐driven.  
  • If any of these cases handled the key, it marks the event default‐handled.

- For keypress events:
  • It ignores non‐renderer or non‐keyboard events.  
  • If SPACE is pressed while spatial navigation is enabled, it toggles an “active selection” flag and marks the event handled.  
  • Otherwise, it queries the RenderTheme to see if SPACE/RETURN or arrow keys should pop open the menu.  
    – If so, it focuses the element, saves the last selection, and calls showPopup() on the RenderMenuList.  
    – In the RETURN case (when popsMenuByArrowKeys() is false), it may submit the form implicitly and dispatch a change event.  
  • If any of these consumed the key, it marks the event handled.

- For mousedown events:
  • On left‐button clicks it focuses the element.  
  • If the popup is visible it hides it; otherwise it saves the current selection and shows the popup.  
  • It marks the event handled.

- For blur events:
  • If the popup is visible, it hides it.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no direct user‐supplied data being parsed, evaluated, or executed—only navigation keys, mouse buttons, and a known options list are handled.
- Index computations go through nextValidIndex and are validated by comparing against listItems.size() before calling selectOption.
- There is no string‐based lookup, no dynamic code evaluation (e.g. no exec/eval), no uncontrolled memory access, and no use of untrusted inputs in rendering or DOM insertion.
- Event default handling is consistently prevented when the code intends to consume an event, avoiding duplicate or unexpected event processing.
- Focus management and popup show/hide logic are cleanly scoped and do not introduce race conditions or leaks.

No buffer overflows, injection risks, or unsafe pointer operations are present.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any apparent vulnerabilities. It safely handles navigation and user interaction without processing untrusted inputs in an unsafe manner.

1. Functional Analysis

- Signature and parameters  
  The function `Browser::AddNewContents` takes:  
  • `WebContents* source` – the originating contents (may be null).  
  • `std::unique_ptr<WebContents> new_contents` – the new tab or popup to add.  
  • `WindowOpenDisposition disposition` – how to open it (new tab, new window, popup, etc.).  
  • `const gfx::Rect& initial_rect` – initial bounds for a popup window.  
  • `bool user_gesture` – whether this was initiated by a user action.  
  • `bool* was_blocked` – out‑parameter to indicate popup blocking.

- macOS fullscreen handling  
  On macOS only, if the request is for a popup (`NEW_POPUP`) while the browser is in fullscreen mode, it downgrades the disposition to `NEW_FOREGROUND_TAB`. This ensures popups don’t unexpectedly open new windows over a fullscreen app.

- Popup blocking  
  If there is a source WebContents and the disposition qualifies for popup blocking (`ConsiderForPopupBlocking(disposition)`), it attaches a `PopupTracker` to the new contents. That tracker works with the `PopupBlockerTabHelper` to decide if the popup should be blocked.

- Final addition  
  It calls `chrome::AddWebContents`, passing ownership of `new_contents` (via `std::move`), along with the source, disposition, and initial bounds, to actually insert the new tab or window into the browser.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety  
  Uses `std::unique_ptr` for `new_contents` and always `std::move`s it into `chrome::AddWebContents`. There are no raw heap allocations or buffer operations here, so common memory-safety issues (use-after-free, double-free, buffer overflow) are avoided.

- Popup abuse  
  The code explicitly hooks into the existing popup‑blocking framework (`PopupBlockerTabHelper::ConsiderForPopupBlocking` and `PopupTracker`), so unwanted popups can be detected and suppressed. This prevents a common UI abuse.

- Privilege or focus escalation  
  The macOS fullscreen branch actually reduces privilege (forcing a tab instead of a popup window), which is a security/usability hardening rather than a vulnerability.

- Parameter validation  
  There is no direct user input parsing here—`disposition` and `initial_rect` come from higher‑level navigation code that itself enforces invariants. This layer simply forwards parameters, trusting the browser’s internal validation.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly manages ownership, integrates with popup blocking, and applies a security-sensitive workaround in macOS fullscreen mode.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function takes a pointer `local` to an `nfc_llcp_local` structure, which contains at least:
  - A bitmask `local_sdp` tracking which SDP SAPs (Service Access Points) are in use.
  - A mutex `sdp_lock` to serialize access to that bitmask.

- It locks `local->sdp_lock` to ensure exclusive access.

- It calls `find_first_zero_bit(&local->local_sdp, LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP)`  
  • This scans the first `LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP` bits of the bitmask and returns the index of the first zero bit (an unused SAP).  
  • If no zero bit is found, it returns `LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP`.

- It checks whether the returned index equals `LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP`.  
  • If so, that means all SDP SAPs are already in use.  
  • In that case it unlocks the mutex and returns `LLCP_SAP_MAX` to indicate failure/“no SAP available.”

- If a free SAP was found:  
  • It logs a debug message with the actual SAP number it will assign: `LLCP_WKS_NUM_SAP + ssap`.  
  • It marks that bit in `local->local_sdp` as used by calling `set_bit(ssap, &local->local_sdp)`.  
  • It unlocks the mutex.  
  • It returns the assigned SAP number: `LLCP_WKS_NUM_SAP + ssap`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Concurrency/race conditions: Access to the shared bitmask is properly protected by the mutex. No race here.
- Bounds checking:  
  • `find_first_zero_bit` is given the correct maximum (`LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP`), and the return value is checked against that same constant.  
  • All arithmetic (`LLCP_WKS_NUM_SAP + ssap`) stays within expected small integer ranges.  
- Integer truncation: The return of `find_first_zero_bit` (an unsigned long) is stored in a `u8`, but since `LLCP_SDP_NUM_SAP` is well below 256, no overflow/truncation occurs in practice.
- NULL-pointer: The code assumes `local` is valid; in its usage context, `local` is never NULL.
- Return-value semantics: Returning `LLCP_SAP_MAX` on exhaustion is the documented design for “no available SAP.”

No buffer overflows, no unchecked user input, no integer-overflow issues, and proper locking. The function behaves correctly and is not susceptible to race conditions or memory corruption.

3. Decision

No, the code is safe and does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function GetProfilesFromResourceBlock reads and parses a Photoshop resource block (StringInfo) attached to an image.  
- It obtains a byte pointer `datum` and a length `length` from the resource block.  
- It then iterates over the block in a for‐loop, looking for resource entries prefixed by the ASCII tag “8BIM”.  
- For each entry it:  
  • Reads a 2‐byte resource ID (`id`).  
  • Reads a 1‐byte name length (`length_byte`) and skips over the name (including a pad byte if the name length is even).  
  • Reads a 4‐byte data size (`value`), casts it to `ssize_t count`, and then ensures that `count` is non‐negative, not larger than the remaining buffer, and that reading it will not overrun `length`.  
  • Switches on `id` to handle specific resource types:  
     – 0x03ed: parses horizontal/vertical resolution and unit type and stores them into the `image->resolution` and `image->units`.  
     – 0x0404, 0x040f, 0x0422, 0x0424: for IPTC, ICC, EXIF, and XMP profiles respectively:  
         * Allocates a new StringInfo of size `count`.  
         * Sets its data pointer to the next `count` bytes in the resource block.  
         * Calls SetImageProfileInternal(...) to attach the profile to the image.  
         * Destroys the temporary StringInfo.  
     – 0x040c (thumbnail) or any other ID: simply skips over `count` bytes of data.  
  • If the data size `count` is odd, it skips one extra padding byte.  
- The loop repeats until it either hits a non-8BIM tag, exhausts the buffer (with safety checks), or breaks on malformed fields.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

The code employs multiple explicit bounds checks before reading or skipping data, but a few edge‐cases remain:

 a) Initial loop bound underflow  
    - The for‐loop condition is `for (p=datum; p < (datum+length-16); )`.  
    - If `length < 16`, then `length-16` underflows (because `length` is unsigned), turning into a huge value.  
    - That makes the loop condition true even when there is not enough data for the first “8BIM” comparison, leading to an out‐of‐bounds read in `LocaleNCompare((char *) p,"8BIM",4)`.

 b) Post‐skip padding  
    - After skipping `count` bytes, the code does `if ((count & 0x01) != 0) p++;` to skip one pad byte.  
    - Although the code earlier checked that `p + count <= datum + length`, it does *not* separately check `p + count + 1 <= datum + length` before that extra `p++`.  
    - In a corner case where `count` exactly reaches the end of the buffer and is odd, `p++` advances the pointer one past the buffer, which is formally undefined behavior, even though it may not immediately crash.

 c) Pointer arithmetic vs. signed/unsigned  
    - The check `(p > (datum+length-count))` guards against `p+count` going past the buffer, but it compares pointers after casting `count` to `ssize_t`.  
    - If `count` were maliciously large but still ≤ `length`, this comparison would pass, yet `p + count` could still overflow the address space in pointer arithmetic (unlikely on modern flat‐address systems but theoretically UB).

In typical usage with well-formed resource blocks, these corner‐cases are unlikely to be triggered. The developer has been careful with bounds checks on `count` vs. `length` and breaks out on most malformed fields. However, they did not guard the very first comparison for small buffers and did not check the pad‐byte advance against the buffer end.

3. Decision

No—the code is not free of issues.  
Summary: The code contains bounds‐checking for the bulk of its parsing, but (a) its initial loop limit `length-16` underflows when `length<16`, leading to out-of-bounds reads, and (b) it advances the pointer by one for odd‐length padding without re-validating the buffer boundary.

  The function `ipip6_err` handles incoming IPv4 ICMP error messages on an IPv4‑in‑IPv6 tunnel device (`skb->dev`). Its steps are:

  a. Parse the IPv4 header and ICMP header  
    - `iph` points at the IPv4 header in `skb->data`  
    - `type` and `code` are extracted from the ICMP header  

  b. Determine which ICMP error types to process  
    - ICMP_PARAMETERPROB: early return (ignored)  
    - ICMP_DEST_UNREACH: unless `ICMP_SR_FAILED`, treat all codes as “host unreachable”  
    - ICMP_TIME_EXCEEDED: only TTL‐expired (`ICMP_EXC_TTL`) messages are processed; compute `data_len = reserved[1] * 4` per RFC4884  
    - ICMP_REDIRECT: handled later  

  c. Look up the corresponding tunnel (`t`)  
    - Determine the source interface index (`sifindex`) based on whether `skb->dev` is an L3 master  
    - Call `ipip6_tunnel_lookup` with the tunnel’s remote/local addresses and `sifindex`  
    - If no tunnel is found, return `-ENOENT`  

  d. Handle special cases  
    - “Fragmentation needed”: invoke `ipv4_update_pmtu`, clear error, return  
    - “Redirect”: invoke `ipv4_redirect`, clear error, return  

  e. Possibly generate an ICMPv6 unreachable back to the sender  
    - If the underlying IPv6 device exists and `ip6_err_gen_icmpv6_unreach` says “do not continue,” stop processing  

  f. Update tunnel error state  
    - If the tunnel has no configured remote (`daddr == 0`) or TTL=0 on a TTL‐expired error, stop  
    - Otherwise increment or reset `t->err_count` based on a timeout, and record `t->err_time`  

  g. Return `0` on success or the last `err` value (default `-ENOENT` if no tunnel was found)

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Buffer/Boundary checks:  
    • The code reads the IPv4 header at `skb->data` and an ICMP extension byte (`reserved[1]`). In proper kernel context, `skb->data` is guaranteed to contain at least the standard headers by the time this error handler is invoked.  
    • The multiplication `reserved[1] * 4` is bounded by 0…255×4 = 1020, so it cannot overflow a 32‑bit `unsigned int` or exceed reasonable ICMP payload lengths.  

  - Integer overflows/underflows: none visible—arithmetic is simple and bounded.  

  - Memory safety: no unbounded loops, no pointer arithmetic beyond fixed‐size header accesses.  

  - Access control: the code only operates on a tunnel already looked up via `ipip6_tunnel_lookup`, so it cannot be tricked into operating on arbitrary state.  

  - No use of unchecked user data for indices or sizes beyond those ICMP specs already in the kernel.  

  Overall, the code follows standard kernel patterns for ICMP error handling and does not introduce new vulnerabilities.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It correctly bounds all header accesses, validates the tunnel, and safely handles each ICMP type.

original_information.commit_message:
Do not crash while reentrantly appending to style element.

When a node is inserted into a container, it is notified via
::InsertedInto. However, a node may request a second notification via
DidNotifySubtreeInsertionsToDocument, which occurs after all the children
have been notified as well. *StyleElement is currently using this
second notification.

This causes a problem, because *ScriptElement is using the same mechanism,
which in turn means that scripts can execute before the state of
*StyleElements are properly updated.

This patch avoids ::DidNotifySubtreeInsertionsToDocument, and instead
processes the stylesheet in ::InsertedInto. The original reason for using
::DidNotifySubtreeInsertionsToDocument in the first place appears to be
invalid now, as the test case is still passing.

original_information.commit_message:
ext4: fix races between page faults and hole punching

Currently, page faults and hole punching are completely unsynchronized.
This can result in page fault faulting in a page into a range that we
are punching after truncate_pagecache_range() has been called and thus
we can end up with a page mapped to disk blocks that will be shortly
freed. Filesystem corruption will shortly follow. Note that the same
race is avoided for truncate by checking page fault offset against
i_size but there isn't similar mechanism available for punching holes.

Fix the problem by creating new rw semaphore i_mmap_sem in inode and
grab it for writing over truncate, hole punching, and other functions
removing blocks from extent tree and for read over page faults. We
cannot easily use i_data_sem for this since that ranks below transaction
start and we need something ranking above it so that it can be held over
the whole truncate / hole punching operation. Also remove various
workarounds we had in the code to reduce race window when page fault
could have created pages with stale mapping information.

Signed-off-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>

No, the code itself does not introduce a significant security vulnerability under typical single‐threaded initialization use. Possible minor issues (data race on concurrent calls, repeated allocations) can be addressed by ensuring it’s called once in a controlled context.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `br_ip6_multicast_leave_group` is intended to remove (leave) an IPv6 multicast group from a bridge port.
- Parameters:
  - `br`: the bridge on which the group membership should be removed.
  - `port`: the bridge port interface associated with the group membership.
  - `group`: pointer to the IPv6 multicast address to leave.
  - `vid`: the VLAN ID associated with the multicast group.
- Steps:
  1. Declare a local `br_ip br_group` structure that will describe the multicast flow.
  2. Call `ipv6_is_transient_multicast(group)` to verify that the provided address is in a transient (non-permanent) IPv6 multicast range. If it is not, return immediately and do nothing.
  3. Populate `br_group`:
     - Copy the 128-bit IPv6 address from `*group` into `br_group.u.ip6`.
     - Set `br_group.proto` to the Ethernet protocol ID for IPv6 (`ETH_P_IPV6`), converted to network byte order.
     - Set `br_group.vid` to the provided VLAN ID.
  4. Invoke `br_multicast_leave_group(br, port, &br_group)` to perform the actual leave operation in the bridge’s multicast state machine.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Null-pointer dereference  
  - The code does not explicitly check that `group`, `br`, or `port` are non-NULL. If any of these pointers were NULL, the subsequent dereference in `ipv6_is_transient_multicast(group)` or inside `br_multicast_leave_group` would lead to a kernel panic. However, in the normal kernel call paths, these pointers should always be valid. This is a robustness issue rather than an attacker-controlled vulnerability.
- Buffer overrun / stack overflow  
  - The IPv6 address is copied by assignment into a fixed-size struct field (`br_group.u.ip6`). There is no unbounded copy, so no overflow.
- Integer overflow / truncation  
  - VLAN ID (`vid`) is a 16-bit value stored into a 16-bit field. No loss of precision or overflow.
- Protocol checks  
  - The transient-multicast check prevents permanent or non-multicast addresses from being used here, so the function will not inadvertently remove invalid addresses.
- Race conditions  
  - All state changes are serialized by the usual bridge locking in `br_multicast_leave_group`, so there is no immediate reentrancy or concurrent access flaw in this snippet.

Overall, the code does not expose any out-of-bounds memory access, buffer overflow, integer overflow, format-string, or use-after-free, and it performs the necessary protocol-level check on the IPv6 address. The only minor issue is the lack of explicit NULL checks, but that would assert in other layers of the kernel and is not exploitable through normal use.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a security vulnerability. It correctly validates the multicast address range and uses fixed-size assignments without unsafe memory operations.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `try_match_pkt_pointers` is called during BPF bytecode verification to detect and refine packet‐pointer bounds when the verifier sees a register‐to‐register comparison instruction.  
   - It first checks that the instruction’s source operand is a register (BPF_X).  
   - It then switches on the comparison operator (JGT, JLT, JGE, JLE). For each case it:  
     • Examines the types of the destination and source registers—specifically whether they are `PTR_TO_PACKET`, `PTR_TO_PACKET_END`, or `PTR_TO_PACKET_META` (or an initialized packet pointer).  
     • Determines which branch of the verifier state (this_branch or other_branch) represents the “truth” or “false” outcome of the comparison.  
     • Calls `find_good_pkt_pointers(...)` on that branch to tighten the known bounds of the packet pointers (e.g., enforcing that data ≤ end, or data ≥ meta).  
   - If none of the recognized pointer‐type patterns match the instruction, it returns false; if a match is found, it returns true after updating the state.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - This code is part of the in‑kernel BPF verifier’s static analysis, not a runtime path that performs memory accesses. Its sole role is to refine pointer bounds based on comparisons.  
   - It does not perform pointer arithmetic or memory dereferences itself, so there is no direct risk of a buffer overrun, out‐of‐bounds access, or integer overflow inside this function.  
   - By tightening pointer bounds on each BPF branch, it helps prevent loaders from generating unsafe memory accesses downstream.  
   - There are no missing checks (e.g., all four relational ops are handled, and unmatched patterns simply bail out) and no unguarded pointer uses.  

3. Decision  
   No, this code does not contain a vulnerability—it safely refines packet‐pointer bounds in the BPF verifier.

original_information.Summary: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 4.14.8 ignores unreachable code, even though it would still be processed by JIT compilers. This behavior, also considered an improper branch-pruning logic issue, could possibly be used by local users for denial of service.
original_information.commit_message:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

Fixes: 17a5267067f3 ("bpf: verifier (add verifier core)")

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function ath_compute_num_delims(…) calculates how many aggregation “delimiters” a hardware descriptor needs for a given MPDU (subframe) in an Atheros Wi-Fi driver.  
   - It starts by picking a baseline number of delimiters based solely on the MPDU length (ATH_AGGR_GET_NDELIM).  
   - If the MPDU is encrypted and the hardware is not in EDMA mode, it adds a fixed extra padding (ATH_AGGR_ENCRYPTDELIM).  
   - If this is the very first subframe of an aggregated frame and certain legacy hardware/OTP settings apply, it forces a minimum of 60 delimiters.  
   - If there is no rate-control density constraint (mpdudensity == 0), it returns that delimiter count.  
   - Otherwise it:  
     • Reads the chosen transmit rate index and flags for width (20/40 MHz) and GI (normal/short).  
     • Converts the desired inter-MPDU density from microseconds to a minimum interim-frame byte length at that rate (using macros to estimate symbols/µs, streams, bits per symbol, etc.).  
     • If the actual MPDU is shorter than that minimum, it computes how many delimiters are needed to pad it up to the density requirement and takes the max of that and the earlier value.  
   - Finally it returns the computed number of delimiters.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - All arithmetic macros and constants (e.g. BITS_PER_BYTE, ATH_AGGR_DELIM_SZ) are fixed nonzero values, so there is no division by zero.  
   - Array indexing of bits_per_symbol is guarded by rix % 8, so it cannot go out of bounds.  
   - Intermediate results are kept in sufficiently wide integer types (u32 for symbol/bit counts, u16 or int for final lengths), and operands are nonnegative in contexts where subtraction occurs (the code checks frmlen < minlen before doing minlen-frmlen).  
   - There is no unbounded memory access, no unchecked user input driving pointers or lengths, and no multiplication chains large enough to overflow the 32-bit temporaries in any realistic rate-control setting.  
   - Null pointers for sc, tid, bf and their subfields would be a programming error upstream; this function assumes valid, initialized arguments, as is normal in a tightly coupled driver.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It properly bounds its arithmetic, guards array indexing, and makes no dangerous assumptions about untrusted inputs.

1. Functional Analysis

   The function `png_get_oFFs` retrieves image offset information stored in a PNG info structure.  
   - It takes five parameters:  
     • `png_ptr`: pointer to the main PNG processing struct  
     • `info_ptr`: pointer to the PNG info struct that holds metadata  
     • `offset_x`, `offset_y`: output pointers for the horizontal and vertical offsets  
     • `unit_type`: output pointer for the unit type of the offsets  
   - It logs a debug message indicating entry into the “oFFs” retrieval routine.  
   - It checks that none of the provided pointers are NULL, and that the info struct’s `valid` flag includes `PNG_INFO_oFFs`.  
   - If all checks pass, it writes `info_ptr->x_offset` and `info_ptr->y_offset` into the user-provided destinations, casts and writes `info_ptr->offset_unit_type` to `unit_type`, and returns the flag `PNG_INFO_oFFs`.  
   - If any check fails, it returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Null-pointer protection  
     – The code verifies `png_ptr`, `info_ptr`, `offset_x`, `offset_y`, and `unit_type` are non-NULL before dereferencing them.  
   • Valid-data check  
     – It requires `info_ptr->valid & PNG_INFO_oFFs` to be true, ensuring offsets have been set in the metadata before use.  
   • Type handling  
     – Offsets are stored in `png_int_32` and directly assigned; no buffer copies or arithmetic occur here.  
   • Integer overflow/underflow  
     – There is no arithmetic on the offset values other than assignment; no risk of overflow.  
   • Memory safety  
     – The function only reads from `info_ptr` and writes to caller-provided integer pointers of known, fixed size.  

   No exploitable buffer overflows, use-after-free, format-string, integer-overflow, or other common vulnerabilities are present in this snippet.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It safely checks pointers, validates presence of data, and performs simple assignments.

original_information.Summary: Multiple buffer overflows in the (1) png_set_PLTE and (2) png_get_PLTE functions in libpng before 1.0.64, 1.1.x and 1.2.x before 1.2.54, 1.3.x and 1.4.x before 1.4.17, 1.5.x before 1.5.24, and 1.6.x before 1.6.19 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a small bit-depth value in an IHDR (aka image header) chunk in a PNG image.

- HB_OBJECT_DO_DESTROY (buffer)  
  Likely performs any object‑lifecycle bookkeeping associated with `buffer` (e.g., reference‑count decrement, destructor callbacks).

- hb_unicode_funcs_destroy (buffer->unicode)  
  Cleans up or frees resources associated with the `unicode` field inside the buffer.

- free (buffer->info)  
  Releases the heap memory previously allocated for the `info` array/member.

- free (buffer->pos)  
  Releases the heap memory previously allocated for the `pos` array/member.

- free (buffer)  
  Releases the heap memory for the `hb_buffer_t` structure itself.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Null pointer handling  
  Calling `free(NULL)` is defined well in C and is a no‑op, so if any of `buffer`, `buffer->info`, `buffer->pos`, or `buffer->unicode` were NULL, the frees/destroy calls would not crash by themselves. The code does not explicitly check for NULL, but that is acceptable for `free()`.

- Double‑free / dangling pointer  
  The function assumes that it is the sole owner of all these allocations. If client code were to call `hb_buffer_destroy` twice on the same pointer (or use the buffer after destruction), that would be a double‑free or use‑after‑free, but that misuse lies outside this function’s logic.

- Buffer overflow / out‑of‑bounds  
  This snippet only performs deallocation; it does not read or write into the buffer’s memory areas, so there is no direct overflow risk here.

- Resource leaks  
  All known allocations tied to the buffer are explicitly freed. No leaks occur if each pointer is valid and was allocated.

3. Decision

No, the snippet itself does not contain an inherent vulnerability. It correctly destroys and frees all associated resources assuming it is called exactly once with a valid, fully initialized buffer.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `pcrypt_aead_encrypt` serves as the entry point for performing an AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) encryption request via a “parallel crypto” helper (pcrypt).
- It retrieves:
  • the wrapper request context (`preq`)  
  • the child AEAD request (`creq`)  
  • the padata private structure (`padata`)  
  • the underlying child cipher transform (`ctx->child`)  
  • any request flags  
- It zeroes out `padata` and assigns two function pointers:
  • `padata->parallel` points to the per‑chunk parallel encryption function  
  • `padata->serial` points to the final serial completion function  
- It configures the child AEAD request (`creq`) by setting:
  • the child transform  
  • the callback and flags (ensuring no unwanted sleep)  
  • the source/destination scatterlists, crypt length, IV  
  • the associated data length  
- Finally, it invokes `pcrypt_do_parallel`, which will break the request into chunks, run the parallel function on each, and then eventually call the serial function.  
- If `pcrypt_do_parallel` returns 0, the operation proceeds asynchronously and the function returns `-EINPROGRESS`; otherwise it returns the error code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety:  
  • `padata` is zeroed with `memset` exactly to its own size—no overflow.  
  • All pointers (`req->src`, `req->dst`, `req->iv`) are passed through the crypto AEAD API, which enforces length checks at the API boundary.  
- Concurrency/synchronization:  
  • The padata framework serializes accesses internally; the code only sets up callbacks and does not race on shared data.  
- Parameter validation:  
  • Crypt length and associated data length come from the AEAD framework, which rejects invalid inputs (e.g., lengths beyond what the cipher supports).  
- Error handling:  
  • The code propagates errors from `pcrypt_do_parallel` immediately. No ignored error paths.  
- Callback flags:  
  • Masking off `CRYPTO_TFM_REQ_MAY_SLEEP` prevents illegal sleep in atomic contexts.  

There is no sign of buffer overflows, unchecked user data, use-after-free, or logic errors introduced at this layer. All heavy lifting (bounds checks, memory grants) is done by the core crypto AEAD API and the padata framework.

3. Decision

No, the code as written does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It correctly initializes structures, delegates checks to the AEAD subsystem, and handles parallel scheduling safely.

original_information.Summary: crypto/pcrypt.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.13 mishandles freeing instances, allowing a local user able to access the AF_ALG-based AEAD interface (CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER_API_AEAD) and pcrypt (CONFIG_CRYPTO_PCRYPT) to cause a denial of service (kfree of an incorrect pointer) or possibly have unspecified other impact by executing a crafted sequence of system calls.
original_information.commit_message:
crypto: pcrypt - fix freeing pcrypt instances

pcrypt is using the old way of freeing instances, where the ->free()
method specified in the 'struct crypto_template' is passed a pointer to
the 'struct crypto_instance'.  But the crypto_instance is being
kfree()'d directly, which is incorrect because the memory was actually
allocated as an aead_instance, which contains the crypto_instance at a
nonzero offset.  Thus, the wrong pointer was being kfree()'d.

Fix it by switching to the new way to free aead_instance's where the
->free() method is specified in the aead_instance itself.

Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `RenderViewImpl::createSessionStorageNamespace` takes an unsigned integer `quota` and returns a pointer to a `WebStorageNamespace`.
- It first checks whether the current process was launched with the command-line switch `--single-process`.
  - If so, it delegates to the static method `WebStorageNamespace::createSessionStorageNamespace(quota)` and returns its result.
- If the single-process switch is not set:
  - It asserts (via `CHECK`) that `session_storage_namespace_id_` is not equal to `kInvalidSessionStorageNamespaceId`. If this condition fails, the renderer process will terminate.
  - It then constructs and returns a new `RendererWebStorageNamespaceImpl` object, passing in `DOM_STORAGE_SESSION` and the valid `session_storage_namespace_id_`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no user-supplied data being interpreted or parsed here, so classic injection (SQL, command, code, etc.) is not applicable.
- The only check is a debug/runtime assertion (`CHECK`) to prevent use of an invalid session-storage ID. Failing that assertion crashes the process; it does not expose data or enable remote exploitation.
- Memory allocation via `new` is straightforward; there is no unbounded or user-controlled allocation size, so buffer overflows or denial-of-service via huge allocations are not present.
- No pointer arithmetic, string operations, or other risky patterns appear. All parameters are either hard-coded enums or an integer quota passed straight through.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It simply dispatches between two well-defined creation paths and enforces an internal invariant with a `CHECK`.

     – Obtain the VDBE (virtual machine) object from the parse context and emit an OP_Once instruction so that the index‐creation code runs only on the first iteration of an outer loop.  
     – Initialize counters and pointers: number of key columns (`nKeyCol`), table pointer (`pTable`), WHERE‐loop object (`pLoop`), bitmasks to track which columns are used in the index, and a placeholder for any partial‐index expression (`pPartial`).

   • Scan WHERE terms  
     – Iterate over every term in the WHERE clause.  
     – If the term is a simple equality on a table column that this scan can use, record that column as part of the index key.  
     – On the first such term, also emit a warning about the automatic index.  
     – Build up `pLoop->aLTerm[]` and update `pLoop->nLTerm` and related flags to indicate that this is an automatically generated index scan on equality terms only.

   • Determine covering columns  
     – Compute which additional columns of the table are required to satisfy the rest of the query (so that no table lookup is needed).  
     – Increase `nKeyCol` by the number of these “extra” columns.

   • Allocate and initialize the transient Index object  
     – Call `sqlite3AllocateIndexObject` with capacity `nKeyCol+1` (plus space for the rowid).  
     – Fill in the new `Index` structure’s `aiColumn[]` array with the columns that drive equality, then the covering columns, and finally add the special `XN_ROWID` column.  
     – Set the index name to `"auto-index"` and link it into `pLoop->u.btree.pIndex`.

   • Open the automatic index in the VDBE  
     – Assign a new ephemeral cursor number (`iIdxCur`) and invoke `OP_OpenAutoindex`.  
     – Provide the key schema to the VDBE via `sqlite3VdbeSetP4KeyInfo`.

   • Populate the index  
     – Push a new expression cache frame.  
     – If the scan is implemented as a coroutine, initialize the coroutine and yield rows; otherwise start with `OP_Rewind` on the table’s main cursor, then loop with `OP_Next`.  
     – If there is a partial‐index predicate, branch over rows that do not satisfy it.  
     – Compute the composite key for the row by calling `sqlite3GenerateIndexKey`, storing the record in a temp register.  
     – Insert the record into the autoindex with `OP_IdxInsert`.  
     – Repeat until all rows are consumed, then restore the expression cache and free registers.

   • Finish  
     – Resolve the OP_Once jump so subsequent iterations skip the index‐creation code.  
     – Clean up any partial‐index expression tree.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Memory safety  
     – Index descriptor and expression trees are allocated via SQLite’s memory subsystem. On allocation failure the code jumps to `end_auto_index_create`, and the partial‐index expression is cleaned up at the end. No use‐after‐free or memory leak is apparent in the normal or error paths.  
   • Integer overflow / array bounds  
     – The code carefully limits the maximum number of columns (`nKeyCol`) to `nCol + 1` and loops with explicit bounds checks before writing into the `aiColumn[]` or `azColl[]` arrays. The `XN_ROWID` column is appended only after all key and extra columns.  
   • SQL Injection / Data corruption  
     – This routine uses internal expression trees and opcodes; there is no string‐concatenation of user data into SQL text. All comparisons and record insertions go through the VDBE.  
   • Resource initialization and cleanup  
     – Registers are acquired via `sqlite3GetTempReg` and released with `sqlite3ReleaseTempReg`. The OP_Once marker ensures one‐time initialization.  
   • Concurrency / reentrancy  
     – The code runs inside the normal SQLite parse/compile context. It does not introduce data races or violate invariants of the VDBE state machine.

   Overall, the code rigorously checks loop bounds, handles allocation failures, maintains proper cleanup, and uses only SQLite’s safe APIs. No vulnerability—such as buffer overflows, use‐after‐free, injection, or uninitialized memory use—is evident.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities—it safely constructs and populates an automatic index.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function sha1_sparc64_update takes three inputs:  
     • desc: a pointer to a shash_desc structure, which internally holds the SHA‑1 state  
     • data: a pointer to the input byte array to hash  
     • len: the number of bytes in that input array  
   - It retrieves the per‑descriptor SHA‑1 state (sctx), which contains:  
     • count: the total number of bytes processed so far  
     • buffer: a partial block of up to SHA1_BLOCK_SIZE bytes (typically 64)  
   - It computes partial = (sctx->count % SHA1_BLOCK_SIZE), i.e. how many bytes are already in the buffer.  
   - Fast‐path: If the new data (len) plus the existing partial bytes still do not fill a full 64‑byte block, it:  
     1. Increments the total byte count (sctx->count) by len  
     2. Copies len bytes from the input data into the buffer at offset partial  
     3. Returns immediately  
   - Slow‐path: Otherwise, it calls __sha1_sparc64_update, which handles filling the buffer, processing full 64‑byte blocks through the SHA‑1 core, and storing any remainder in the buffer for the next call.  
   - Finally, it returns 0 to indicate success.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer overflow: The function only memcpy’s up to SHA1_BLOCK_SIZE bytes into sctx->buffer, and only when partial + len < SHA1_BLOCK_SIZE, so it cannot overflow the 64‑byte buffer.  
   - Integer overflow: sctx->count is incremented by len in the fast path. In typical SHA‐1 implementations, count is a 64‑bit counter; even if it wrapped around, the implementation uses (count mod 64) for buffering and the final length is only significant mod 2^64 in the SHA‑1 padding. This matches the SHA‑1 spec, so wrapping does not introduce a security vulnerability beyond the algorithm’s inherent 2^64‑bit length limit.  
   - Side channels: This routine only buffers and dispatches to the core SHA‑1 compression; it does not introduce any new data‐dependent branches or memory accesses beyond what the core SHA‑1 already has.  
   - Other issues: There are no obvious use‐after‐free, race conditions, or other typical pitfalls here.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly handles partial blocks, prevents buffer overflows, and defers full‑block processing to the established SHA‑1 routine.

   This function computes two parameters—a signed shift (`*pshift`) and an unsigned multiplier (`*pmultiplier`)—that can be used to convert or “scale” a base timer rate (in kHz) to a desired timer rate (also in kHz).  
   - It first converts both `base_khz` and `scaled_khz` into 64-bit counts per second by multiplying by 1000 (`tps64` and `scaled64`).  
   - The first while-loop repeatedly right-shifts `tps64` (decrementing `shift`) until `tps64` fits comfortably within the same magnitude as `scaled64` (specifically, until it is ≤ twice `scaled64` and fits in 32 bits).  
   - It then casts the scaled‐down `tps64` to a 32-bit value `tps32`.  
   - The second while-loop adjusts `tps32` and `scaled64` so that `tps32` becomes strictly greater than `scaled64`—if either value would overflow when doubled, it halves the other instead—incrementing `shift` each time.  
   - Finally, it stores `shift` in `*pshift` and computes a fractional multiplier `scaled64/tps32` (via `div_frac`) into `*pmultiplier`.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Integer Overflow:  
     All 64-bit arithmetic (multiplying by 1000, shifting) remains within 64-bit limits for any 32-bit inputs. The code guards against 32-bit overflow by masking and shifting before down-casting.  
   - Division by Zero:  
     The final call `div_frac(scaled64, tps32)` could divide by zero if `tps32` became zero. In practice, however, if `scaled_khz > 0` or `base_khz > 0`, the loops should produce a nonzero `tps32` before exit.  
   - Infinite Loop / Denial of Service:  
     If `scaled_khz` is zero, then `scaled64` starts at 0. The first loop will drive `tps64` down to 0, producing `tps32 == 0`. In the second loop both branches (shifting `scaled64` or doubling `tps32`) leave both values at zero, yet the loop’s condition (`tps32 <= scaled64`) remains true. This results in an infinite loop (unbounded `shift` increments), effectively hanging the caller.  
   - Null Pointer Dereference:  
     The code does not check whether `pshift` or `pmultiplier` are null. If this function were ever called with invalid pointers, it would crash.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code is not fully safe. While it correctly avoids integer overflow in normal cases, it contains an infinite-loop / hang scenario when `scaled_khz == 0`, and it does not guard against null pointer arguments.

1. Functional Analysis

  The function `ip6_tnl_ioctl` handles IOCTL operations on IPv6 tunnel network devices. It supports four commands:

  a. SIOCGETTUNNEL  
     – If the device is the “fallback” tunnel device (`ip6n->fb_tnl_dev`), it first copies user‐supplied tunnel parameters (`struct ip6_tnl_parm p`) from user space and tries to locate an existing tunnel matching those parameters (`ip6_tnl_locate`).  
     – If that lookup fails (or the device isn’t the fallback), it simply fetches the private tunnel context from the device (`netdev_priv(dev)`).  
     – It then returns the current tunnel parameters back to user space via `copy_to_user`.

  b. SIOCADDTUNNEL / SIOCCHGTUNNEL  
     – Requires the caller to have `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, else returns `-EPERM`.  
     – Copies the new parameters (`p`) from user space and validates the protocol field (`p.proto`) against allowed values (IPv6, IPIP, or 0).  
     – Attempts to locate an existing tunnel with those parameters; for ADD it may create a new record, for CHANGE it expects one to exist.  
     – If changing a non-fallback device, it unlinks the old tunnel, applies the parameter changes, re-links it, and signals a state change on the net device.  
     – Finally, it returns the (possibly new) tunnel parameters back to user space or an error code if the operation failed.

  c. SIOCDELTUNNEL  
     – Also gated on `CAP_NET_ADMIN`.  
     – If deleting from the fallback device, it copies deletion parameters from user space and looks up the matching tunnel; it rejects attempts to delete the fallback itself.  
     – It then calls `unregister_netdevice(dev)` to remove the identified tunnel device from the system.

  d. Default  
     – Any other IOCTL command returns `-EINVAL`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  – Buffer handling: All user data transfers use `copy_from_user()` and `copy_to_user()` with the exact size of `struct ip6_tnl_parm`, preventing overruns or underruns.  
  – Privilege checks: Both add/change and delete operations are explicitly guarded by `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, so unprivileged users cannot invoke state‐modifying actions.  
  – Parameter validation: The code checks the `proto` field against a small set of valid values (IPv6, IPIP, or 0).  
  – Duplicate prevention: Tunnel lookup (`ip6_tnl_locate`) and existence checks prevent creation of conflicting tunnels.  
  – Race conditions: Tunnel linkage/unlinkage and netdevice state changes occur under the kernel’s internal locking and notifier mechanisms for network devices; there is no user‐visible race window that would lead to use‐after‐free or double‐free in this snippet.  
  – Error handling: All paths that copy data back to user space set error codes on failure (`-EFAULT`, `-EEXIST`, `-ENOENT`, etc.), so the caller is informed of failures and no silent corruption occurs.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any apparent vulnerabilities. It performs proper user‐space copying, enforces capability checks, validates inputs, and uses the kernel’s device registration routines correctly.
