1. Functional Analysis

1.1. Initialization  
- Compares `filename` and `outname` to see if they differ (`elsewhere`).  
- Declares pointers for version-control buffers (`getbuf`, `diffbuf`) and controller string (`cs`).  
- On first call (when `inerrno == -1`), calls `stat_file(filename, &instat)` to populate `instat` and set `inerrno` (error status).

1.2. Optional Version-Control Checkout  
If all of the following hold:  
  • The target is a regular file (`S_ISREG(file_type)`)  
  • Patching from version control is enabled (`patch_get`)  
  • We haven’t already failed on version control (`invc != 0`)  
  • Either the file did not stat successfully, or it does stat but nobody writable or it’s owned by someone else  
  
then the code invokes `version_controller(...)`, which returns:  
  • `cs` – a non‐null identifier of the VCS in use (e.g. “RCS” or “SCCS”), or `NULL` if no VCS found  
  • `getbuf` – a command buffer to check out or retrieve the file  
  • `diffbuf` – a buffer containing a `diff` command to compare current vs. default version  

1.2.1. After discovering a VCS controller (`cs != NULL`):  
  • If the file exists and `elsewhere == false`, checks that the file is not writable by anyone or not owned by another user; otherwise calls `fatal()`.  
  • If `diffbuf` is non‐NULL, runs `systemic(diffbuf)` to check whether the working file matches the default version. If they differ, warns and abandons version-control checkout for safety.  
  • If `dry_run` is set, also skips the checkout.  
  • Finally, if `cs` still non‐NULL, calls `version_get(...)` to fetch the file under version control, clearing `inerrno` on success.  
  • Frees `getbuf` and `diffbuf`.

1.3. Fallback for Missing or Unreadable File  
If `inerrno` is still nonzero (file missing or unreadable), sets `instat.st_mode` to world‐read/write and size zero, simulating an “empty” file to patch.

1.4. Final Type Check  
If no error and the actual file type of the existing file (`instat.st_mode & S_IFMT`) does not match the requested `file_type` (regular vs. symlink), prints an error and returns false.

1.5. Return  
Returns true on success (file ready to be patched or synthesized empty), false if the file exists but is not of the expected type.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

2.1. Shell‐Injection Risk via `system(diffbuf)`  
- The code hands `diffbuf` to `system()`. If `version_controller()` does not properly sanitize or shell‐quote user‐supplied filenames, an attacker could craft a malicious filename containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `filename="foo; rm -rf /"`).  
- Mitigation: We must assume `version_controller()` builds safe commands (e.g. escapes `filename`) or else this is a command‐injection hole.

2.2. TOCTOU / Symlink Race  
- The code does `stat_file()` early, then later invokes version‐control or compares with `diff`. An attacker who controls the filename path could swap a regular file for a symlink (or vice versa) between the `stat()` and subsequent operations, leading to patching or overwriting an unintended target.  
- Mitigation: The snippet does not re‐`stat()` or open with O_NOFOLLOW after the VCS checkout, so there is a window for race attacks.

2.3. File‐Lock/Writing Check  
- The logic verifies that, if the file is present and under version control, it is either read‐only by all or owned by the current user before checking it out.  
- This prevents overwriting someone else’s actively edited file. The check is sound given a correct `stat()`.

2.4. Memory Safety  
- Dynamically allocated `getbuf` and `diffbuf` are `free()`d in all control paths after use. No obvious buffer overflows or memory leaks in this snippet.

2.5. Permissions Hardening  
- If the file did not exist or was unreadable, the code fakes up a new file mode of 0666. This is aggressive but consistent with many patch utilities that create missing files as world‐readable/writable.

3. Decision

No; although the code takes care to avoid overwriting locked files and handles memory safely, it invokes `system(diffbuf)` on a buffer that may contain untrusted data and performs file-type and permission checks only once (leaving a TOCTOU window). Proper quoting or use of exec‐style APIs and O_NOFOLLOW would be required to eliminate these risks.

original_information.commit_message:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>

1. Functional Analysis

- The function kvm_arch_create_memslot initializes per-page-size metadata for a new KVM memory slot.
- It loops over each supported page size level (i = 0 .. KVM_NR_PAGE_SIZES–1):
  • Computes how many “large‐page units” (`lpages`) cover the slot’s GFNs:
      lpages = gfn_to_index(end_gfn, base_gfn, level) + 1
  • Allocates an array `rmap[i]` of `lpages` reverse‐map entries.
  • For levels > 0, allocates a parallel array `lpage_info[i-1]` tracking write counts on large pages.
  • Marks the first or last large‐page entry as “written” if the slot’s GFN range is not aligned to that large‐page boundary.
  • Reads the userspace address’s GFN (ugfn) and, if that ugfn isn’t aligned to the same large‐page boundary (or if large pages are globally disabled), marks every large‐page entry’s write_count to 1—effectively disabling large‐page mappings for this slot.

- If any memory allocation fails, it jumps to out_free, which frees whatever was allocated so far (all rmap[] and lpage_info[]), then returns –ENOMEM. On success it returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer arithmetic:
  • The expression `slot->base_gfn + npages - 1` can overflow if both values are large; this in turn could make `gfn_to_index()` return a small number and cause under-allocation of the arrays.  
  • The subsequent size calculation `lpages * sizeof(*…)` could overflow a `size_t` if `lpages` is huge, potentially leading `kvm_kvzalloc()` to allocate less memory than intended.

- Input validation:
  • There is no explicit range-check on `npages` or `base_gfn` inside this function. It assumes that upstream code has already verified that the guest’s memory slot size and base GFN are within valid limits.

- Out-of-bounds or use-after-free:
  • The code carefully frees all allocated arrays on error, and the two‐stage allocation pattern (rmap first, then lpage_info) avoids using uninitialized pointers. There is no evidence here of buffer over-reads or use-after-free in this snippet.

- Denial-of-Service (DoS):
  • A maliciously large `npages` could force the host to attempt to allocate huge metadata arrays, leading to resource exhaustion. Again, this typically must be guarded against by higher-level validation in KVM’s memory‐slot creation path.

3. Decision

No, there is no direct exploitable memory‐safety vulnerability in this snippet. The main risks (integer overflow in size computations and excessive allocation) should be handled by the code that invokes this function or by checks elsewhere in KVM.

original_information.commit_message:
Fix various certificate fingerprint issues.

By using non-DER or invalid encodings outside the signed portion of a
certificate the fingerprint can be changed without breaking the signature.
Although no details of the signed portion of the certificate can be changed
this can cause problems with some applications: e.g. those using the
certificate fingerprint for blacklists.

1. Reject signatures with non zero unused bits.

If the BIT STRING containing the signature has non zero unused bits reject
the signature. All current signature algorithms require zero unused bits.

2. Check certificate algorithm consistency.

Check the AlgorithmIdentifier inside TBS matches the one in the
certificate signature. NB: this will result in signature failure
errors for some broken certificates.

3. Check DSA/ECDSA signatures use DER.

Reencode DSA/ECDSA signatures and compare with the original received
signature. Return an error if there is a mismatch.

This will reject various cases including garbage after signature
(thanks to Antti Karjalainen and Tuomo Untinen from the Codenomicon CROSS
program for discovering this case) and use of BER or invalid ASN.1 INTEGERs
(negative or with leading zeroes).

original_information.commit_message:
Btrfs: fix hash overflow handling

The handling for directory crc hash overflows was fairly obscure,
split_leaf returns EOVERFLOW when we try to extend the item and that is
supposed to bubble up to userland.  For a while it did so, but along the
way we added better handling of errors and forced the FS readonly if we
hit IO errors during the directory insertion.

Along the way, we started testing only for EEXIST and the EOVERFLOW case
was dropped.  The end result is that we may force the FS readonly if we
catch a directory hash bucket overflow.

This fixes a few problem spots.  First I add tests for EOVERFLOW in the
places where we can safely just return the error up the chain.

btrfs_rename is harder though, because it tries to insert the new
directory item only after it has already unlinked anything the rename
was going to overwrite.  Rather than adding very complex logic, I added
a helper to test for the hash overflow case early while it is still safe
to bail out.

Snapshot and subvolume creation had a similar problem, so they are using
the new helper now too.

original_information.commit_message:
ipv6: addrconf: validate new MTU before applying it

Currently we don't check if the new MTU is valid or not and this allows
one to configure a smaller than minimum allowed by RFCs or even bigger
than interface own MTU, which is a problem as it may lead to packet
drops.

If you have a daemon like NetworkManager running, this may be exploited
by remote attackers by forging RA packets with an invalid MTU, possibly
leading to a DoS. (NetworkManager currently only validates for values
too small, but not for too big ones.)

The fix is just to make sure the new value is valid. That is, between
IPV6_MIN_MTU and interface's MTU.

Note that similar check is already performed at
ndisc_router_discovery(), for when kernel itself parses the RA.

Simplify "WouldTaintOrigin" concept in media/blink

Currently WebMediaPlayer has three predicates:
 - DidGetOpaqueResponseFromServiceWorker
 - HasSingleSecurityOrigin
 - DidPassCORSAccessCheck
. These are used to determine whether the response body is available
for scripts. They are known to be confusing, and actually
MediaElementAudioSourceHandler::WouldTaintOrigin misuses them.

This CL merges the three predicates to one, WouldTaintOrigin, to remove
the confusion. Now the "response type" concept is available and we
don't need a custom CORS check, so this CL removes
BaseAudioContext::WouldTaintOrigin. This CL also renames
URLData::has_opaque_data_ and its (direct and indirect) data accessors
to match the spec.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `mbedtls_ecp_curve_info_from_name` takes a C‐string `name` as input.
- It obtains a pointer to the start of a statically‐defined array of `mbedtls_ecp_curve_info` structures by calling `mbedtls_ecp_curve_list()`.
- It iterates through that array until it finds an entry whose `grp_id` is `MBEDTLS_ECP_DP_NONE`, which serves as the end‐of‐list marker.
- For each entry, it compares the entry’s `name` field against the input `name` using `strcmp`.
- If `strcmp` indicates an exact match, it returns a pointer to that `mbedtls_ecp_curve_info` entry.
- If no matching name is found by the end of the list, it returns `NULL`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflows:  
  The code only calls `strcmp` on two NUL‐terminated strings. One side (`curve_info->name`) is a compile-time constant in the library, and the other (`name`) is user-supplied. There is no attempt to write beyond any buffer, so there is no classic buffer‐overflow here.
- Out‐of‐bounds reads:  
  Iteration stops when `grp_id == MBEDTLS_ECP_DP_NONE`. Assuming the curve list is correctly terminated by the library, there is no out‐of‐bounds access.
- Null‐pointer dereference:  
  If the caller passes `name == NULL`, the call to `strcmp(curve_info->name, name)` will dereference a NULL pointer, causing undefined behavior (likely a crash). The function does not guard against a NULL input pointer.
- Timing side channels:  
  The plain `strcmp` may vary timing based on the first differing character. However, this is not a secret‐dependent operation in a cryptographic sense (the curve names are public), so timing leakage here is not a security issue.
- Denial of service / resource exhaustion:  
  The loop is bounded by the finite curve list, so it always terminates in O(N) time where N is the number of curves. There is no unbounded loop or recursion.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities in its intended use. It correctly searches a fixed list of curve names and returns the matching entry or NULL. The only minor issue is that it does not validate against `name == NULL`, which could lead to a crash if misused, but that is an input‐validation omission rather than a security flaw in normal operation.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The method begins by tracing/logging the “OnDidStartLoading” event along with two parameters: the frame tree node ID and whether the load is to a different document.  
   - It checks the boolean `to_different_document`. If true, it treats this as an unexpected condition coming from the renderer and reports a bad IPC message (`RFH_UNEXPECTED_LOAD_START`) for the renderer’s process, then returns immediately.  
   - If the load is within the same document, it queries whether the frame tree was already loading (`was_previously_loading`) and sets the member flag `is_loading_ = true`.  
   - Finally, if this `RenderFrameHostImpl` is active, it calls into the frame tree node’s `DidStartLoading` handler, passing along both the `to_different_document` flag and the prior loading state.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - The only untrusted input here is the `to_different_document` boolean, which the renderer supplies. Rather than trusting it, the code treats a “true” as a protocol violation and immediately invokes `ReceivedBadMessage`, which typically kills or isolates the misbehaving renderer. This blocks any attempt by a malicious renderer to forge an unexpected load start.  
   - There is no buffer manipulation, string formatting, pointer arithmetic, or other unsafe operations—state is simply read, a flag is flipped, and a well-defined notification call is made.  
   - No user-supplied data ever propagates into memory-unsafe operations or insecure code paths. Any protocol violation is caught and handled early by terminating the renderer.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It validates untrusted inputs, enforces protocol correctness, and performs only safe state updates.

  • Initialization  
    – Compute ldblk = (bpp * image->columns + 7) / 8: the number of bytes needed per scanline.  
    – Allocate BImgBuff of size ldblk * 8 bytes via AcquireQuantumMemory.  

  • Main decode loop (while y < image->rows)  
    – Read a control byte c = ReadBlobByte(image). If EOF, exit loop.  
    – Extract RunCount = c & 0x7F; test high bit (0x80):  
        · If high bit set (compressed run):  
            · If RunCount > 0: read one byte and repeat it RunCount times (InsertByte).  
            · Else (RunCount == 0): read next byte as RunCount, then repeat 0xFF RunCount times.  
        · If high bit clear (literal or line‑repeat):  
            · If RunCount > 0: read RunCount raw bytes and InsertByte each.  
            · Else (RunCount == 0): read new RunCount, then repeat the previous scanline RunCount times  
              – If x != 0 at this point, error out (return –3)  
              – For each repeat: reset x=0, y++, then InsertRow from the buffer of the prior line

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

original_information.Summary: OpenSSL 1.1.1 introduced a rewritten random number generator (RNG). This was intended to include protection in the event of a fork() system call in order to ensure that the parent and child processes did not share the same RNG state. However this protection was not being used in the default case. A partial mitigation for this issue is that the output from a high precision timer is mixed into the RNG state so the likelihood of a parent and child process sharing state is significantly reduced. If an application already calls OPENSSL_init_crypto() explicitly using OPENSSL_INIT_ATFORK then this problem does not occur at all. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1d (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1c).

  • Locks the parent directory inode to serialize modifications (prevents races with other rename/link/unlink operations).

  • Creation rights on the source directory are enforced (NFSD_MAY_CREATE). The target inode need only be a valid, non‐directory object; actual link permission checks are delegated to vfs_link and lower‐level inode permission routines.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

any external resources. This patch enforces these rules in

down our SVG resource handling and fixes two security bugs.

static void tcp_v4_reqsk_send_ack(const struct sock *sk, struct sk_buff *skb,
				  struct request_sock *req)
{
	/* sk->sk_state == TCP_LISTEN -> for regular TCP_SYN_RECV
	 * sk->sk_state == TCP_SYN_RECV -> for Fast Open.
	 */
	u32 seq = (sk->sk_state == TCP_LISTEN) ? tcp_rsk(req)->snt_isn + 1 :
					     tcp_sk(sk)->snd_nxt;

	/* RFC 7323 2.3
	 * The window field (SEG.WND) of every outgoing segment, with the
	 * exception of <SYN> segments, MUST be right-shifted by
	 * Rcv.Wind.Shift bits:
	 */
	tcp_v4_send_ack(sock_net(sk), skb, seq,
			tcp_rsk(req)->rcv_nxt,
			req->rsk_rcv_wnd >> inet_rsk(req)->rcv_wscale,
			tcp_time_stamp,
			req->ts_recent,
			0,
			tcp_md5_do_lookup(sk, (union tcp_md5_addr *)&ip_hdr(skb)->daddr,
					  AF_INET),
			inet_rsk(req)->no_srccheck ? IP_REPLY_ARG_NOSRCCHECK : 0,
			ip_hdr(skb)->tos);
}

The code that pushes implied names (htmlnamePush) is responsible for growing an internal stack; typical implementations ensure capacity via realloc or similar checks, so there is no obvious buffer overflow here. No integer arithmetic is done in a way that could overflow. The SAX callbacks receive only constant tag names (“html”, “head”, “body”) and a NULL attributes pointer, so there is no injection or uncontrolled data passed to callbacks.  

   Potential areas one might consider for problems—such as reentrancy, unbounded recursion, or excessive memory consumption—are all bounded by the parser’s normal limits (ctxt->nameTab capacity, ctxt->nameNr count). There is no evidence in this snippet of unguarded pointer dereferences or out‐of‐bounds access.  

   In short, the code implements standard HTML‐implied‐tag insertion logic and does not exhibit classic memory‐safety or injection vulnerabilities.  

3. Decision  
   
   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It safely handles its inputs, relies on well‐defined helper routines for string comparison and stack growth, and only works with constant tag names.

original_information.Summary: An integer overflow in xmlmemory.c in libxml2 before 2.9.5, as used in Google Chrome prior to 62.0.3202.62 and other products, allowed a remote attacker to potentially exploit heap corruption via a crafted XML file.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function stts_Write takes two arguments:
  • s: a pointer to a generic box structure (GF_Box *) that is actually a GF_TimeToSampleBox  
  • bs: a bitstream writer (GF_BitStream *)  
- It casts the generic box pointer s to a GF_TimeToSampleBox pointer (ptr).  
- It calls gf_isom_full_box_write(s, bs) to emit the full-box header (version and flags). If that call returns an error, it immediately propagates it.  
- It writes the number of time-to-sample entries (ptr->nb_entries) as a 32-bit unsigned integer.  
- It then loops over each of the nb_entries elements in ptr->entries, and for each entry writes:  
  • sampleCount (32 bits)  
  • sampleDelta (32 bits)  
- Finally, if all writes succeed, it returns GF_OK.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no unbounded string or pointer arithmetic; all writes go through a controlled bitstream API (gf_bs_write_u32).  
- The code trusts ptr->nb_entries and that ptr->entries actually point to an array of at least nb_entries elements. If the caller set these fields incorrectly, the loop could read out of bounds, but that would be a misuse of the structure rather than an internal logic bug.  
- The only “untrusted” value written is nb_entries, but writing a large count only causes more data to be emitted, not memory corruption within this routine.  
- No integer arithmetic is performed on nb_entries or the entry fields that could overflow.  
- The bitstream writes themselves may have capacity checks; this routine does not allocate or index into a buffer based on unvalidated lengths.

3. Decision

No, the snippet does not exhibit internal vulnerabilities. It safely writes a bounded number of fields to the bitstream, relying on its caller to supply a correctly populated GF_TimeToSampleBox.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `request_end` finalizes a FUSE request (`req`) associated with a connection (`fc`).
- `test_and_set_bit(FR_FINISHED, &req->flags)`: Atomically marks the request as finished; if it was already finished, jumps to release the request.
- It acquires `fiq->waitq.lock`, removes `req` from the interrupt list (`intr_entry`), and releases the lock.
- `WARN_ON` checks that the request is neither still pending nor still marked as sent.
- If the request was issued in background mode (`FR_BACKGROUND`):
  - It takes the `bg_lock`, clears the background flag, and adjusts `blocked`, `num_background`, and `active_background` counters.
  - It wakes up any threads waiting on `fc->blocked_waitq` if necessary (either because the number of in-flight background requests dropped below the maximum or there are waiters).
  - If the request was at the congestion threshold, it clears the block device’s congested flags.
  - Calls `flush_bg_queue(fc)` to send more background requests if capacity is now available.
  - Releases `bg_lock`.
- It wakes up any thread waiting on this specific request (`req->waitq`).
- If the request supplied an `end` callback, it invokes `req->end(fc, req)`.
- Finally, `fuse_put_request(fc, req)` drops the kernel’s reference to the request, potentially freeing it.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Concurrency control:
  - Atomic bit tests/sets ensure the “finished” flag is only handled once.
  - Spinlocks (`fiq->waitq.lock` and `bg_lock`) protect shared lists and counters.
  - Wake-ups are performed at safe points under or outside locks.
- Resource management:
  - The code always ends by releasing its reference to `req`, avoiding leaks.
  - Background counters and congestion flags are updated consistently under lock.
- Lack of unbounded loops, no unbounded memory allocations, no user input parsing, no string or buffer operations, and no use-after-free patterns are evident.
- WARN_ONs only issue warnings, not panics, and they guard against logic invariants rather than user-triggerable states.

Conclusion: The code correctly serializes access with atomic operations and spinlocks, updates its counters and lists safely, and always cleans up its reference. There is no obvious race condition, deadlock, or memory safety issue.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any apparent vulnerabilities. It properly uses atomic flags and locks to maintain consistency and cleans up resources reliably.

original_information.Summary: The Linux kernel before 5.1-rc5 allows page->_refcount reference count overflow, with resultant use-after-free issues, if about 140 GiB of RAM exists. This is related to fs/fuse/dev.c, fs/pipe.c, fs/splice.c, include/linux/mm.h, include/linux/pipe_fs_i.h, kernel/trace/trace.c, mm/gup.c, and mm/hugetlb.c. It can occur with FUSE requests.
original_information.commit_message:
fs: prevent page refcount overflow in pipe_buf_get

Change pipe_buf_get() to return a bool indicating whether it succeeded
in raising the refcount of the page (if the thing in the pipe is a page).
This removes another mechanism for overflowing the page refcount.  All
callers converted to handle a failure.

1. Functional Analysis  
   The function `byte2hex` takes two inputs:  
   - `data`: a pointer to a single byte (treated as an unsigned 8-bit value).  
   - `str`: a pointer to a pointer into a character buffer where the caller wants two ASCII hex digits written.  
   
   Inside the function:  
   - It reads the high nibble of `*data` (`(*data >> 4) & 0xF`) and uses it to index a global `hex_table` array of 16 ASCII characters (`'0'..'9','A'..'F'`).  
   - It writes that character at the location pointed to by `*str`, then increments the `str` pointer by one.  
   - It then reads the low nibble (`*data & 0xF`), again indexes `hex_table`, writes that character, and increments `str` again.  
   - No null terminator is written; the caller is expected to manage buffer termination if needed.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no bounds checking on the buffer pointed to by `*str`. If the caller’s buffer doesn’t have room for two more characters, this will overwrite adjacent memory, leading to a buffer overflow.  
   - The function assumes `data`, `str`, and the global `hex_table` are all non-NULL and properly initialized. Passing NULL or invalid pointers will crash or corrupt memory.

- The function `UnescapeCacheFileName` takes a percent-encoded string (e.g. URL‐style escapes like “%20”) and returns a new string with those escapes decoded.

- It loops over each character in the input `filename`.  
  - If it sees a '%' and there are at least two more characters, it calls `HexDigitToInt` on the next two characters, combines them into a byte (`(high_nibble << 4) + low_nibble`), advances the loop index by 2, and treats that byte as the decoded character.

- Embedded nulls: A “%00” sequence will insert a `'\0'` byte into the resulting C++ string. If that result is later passed to C APIs that treat `'\0'` as end-of-string, it could lead to truncation or bypass of subsequent checks. This function does not strip or guard against embedded nulls.

No, the function itself contains no direct memory-safety flaws. It correctly bounds-checks before decoding, and uses safe string operations. However, it does not validate hex input or sanitize the decoded output (e.g. against embedded nulls or “..” segments), so callers must perform any needed validation.

   The function `FreeList::CheckFreedMemoryIsZapped` takes two parameters:  
   - `address`: a pointer (of type `Address`) pointing to a region of freed memory  
   - `size`: the size (in bytes) of that region

   The macro `NEVER_INLINE` simply forces the compiler not to inline this function. Inside the function, there is a single `for` loop that iterates from `i = 0` to `i < size`.    - The check is compiled out in non-debug builds (assuming `DCHECK` is a debug-only assertion), so there is no performance or side-channel concern in release mode.

3. Decision  
No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerability. It is a straightforward debug check to verify that freed memory has been set to known zap values.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function __hwahc_dev_set_key() is responsible for sending a USB “set key” descriptor to a wireless USB host controller.
- It begins by computing the enclosing hwahc structure from the generic wusbhc pointer and retrieves the current USB interface number.
- It allocates a buffer (keyd) large enough to hold a usb_key_descriptor header plus the variable-length key data.
- It initializes the descriptor fields:
  • bLength to the total descriptor size  
  • bDescriptorType to USB_DT_KEY  
  • tTKID bytes from the 24-bit tkid argument  
  • bKeyData from the supplied key pointer and key_size  
- It issues a class-specific, interface-recipient, OUT control transfer (USB_REQ_SET_DESCRIPTOR) passing the descriptor to the device.
- Finally it kzfree()s the buffer (zeroing sensitive key bytes) and returns the result of usb_control_msg().

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory allocation and sizing  
  • keyd_len = sizeof(*keyd) + key_size ensures the buffer is sized to hold exactly key_size bytes of key data.  
  • There is a theoretical integer-overflow risk if key_size is near SIZE_MAX (wrapping keyd_len to a small value), which could lead to a buffer overrun in memcpy(). However, in practice key_size is small and controlled by upper layers (e.g. the wireless stack), and the kernel’s allocation routines and OOM killer prevent unbounded allocation.  
- Bound checking  
  • No explicit limit on key_size or bLength ≤ 255. USB specification limits descriptor length to 1 byte, but real hardware typically rejects overly long descriptors, and most key sizes (e.g. 16 or 32 bytes) are well below 255.  
  • key_idx and port_idx are not range-checked here, but they map directly to USB descriptor indices and wIndex fields; an invalid value would at worst cause the device to NAK or STALL the request.  
- Sensitive data handling  
  • The use of kzfree() zeroes the key material on free, preventing key leakage in kernel memory.  
- Denial-of-service  
  • If a malicious or buggy caller passed an extremely large key_size, the kzalloc() could fail (-ENOMEM) or trigger the OOM killer. This is a potential DoS but not a memory safety vulnerability.  

Overall, there is no direct buffer overflow or use-after-free. The only edge‐case risk is an integer overflow in computing keyd_len when key_size is absurdly large, but in realistic use key_size is small and caller-controlled.  

3. Decision

No, the code contains no exploitable memory-safety or logic vulnerability as written.

original_information.commit_message:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

original_information.commit_message:
perf: Remove the nmi parameter from the swevent and overflow interface

The nmi parameter indicated if we could do wakeups from the current
context, if not, we would set some state and self-IPI and let the
resulting interrupt do the wakeup.

For the various event classes:

  - hardware: nmi=0; PMI is in fact an NMI or we run irq_work_run from
    the PMI-tail (ARM etc.)
  - tracepoint: nmi=0; since tracepoint could be from NMI context.
  - software: nmi=[0,1]; some, like the schedule thing cannot
    perform wakeups, and hence need 0.

As one can see, there is very little nmi=1 usage, and the down-side of
not using it is that on some platforms some software events can have a
jiffy delay in wakeup (when arch_irq_work_raise isn't implemented).

The up-side however is that we can remove the nmi parameter and save a
bunch of conditionals in fast paths.

original_information.commit_message:
nfsd: check for oversized NFSv2/v3 arguments

A client can append random data to the end of an NFSv2 or NFSv3 RPC call
without our complaining; we'll just stop parsing at the end of the
expected data and ignore the rest.

Encoded arguments and replies are stored together in an array of pages,
and if a call is too large it could leave inadequate space for the
reply.  This is normally OK because NFS RPC's typically have either
short arguments and long replies (like READ) or long arguments and short
replies (like WRITE).  But a client that sends an incorrectly long reply
can violate those assumptions.  This was observed to cause crashes.

Also, several operations increment rq_next_page in the decode routine
before checking the argument size, which can leave rq_next_page pointing
well past the end of the page array, causing trouble later in
svc_free_pages.

So, following a suggestion from Neil Brown, add a central check to
enforce our expectation that no NFSv2/v3 call has both a large call and
a large reply.

As followup we may also want to rewrite the encoding routines to check
more carefully that they aren't running off the end of the page array.

We may also consider rejecting calls that have any extra garbage
appended.  That would be safer, and within our rights by spec, but given
the age of our server and the NFS protocol, and the fact that we've
never enforced this before, we may need to balance that against the
possibility of breaking some oddball client.

original_information.Summary: Inappropriate use of www mismatch redirects in browser navigation in Google Chrome prior to 61.0.3163.79 for Mac, Windows, and Linux, and 61.0.3163.81 for Android, allowed a remote attacker to potentially downgrade HTTPS requests to HTTP via a crafted HTML page. In other words, Chrome could transmit cleartext even though the user had entered an https URL, because of a misdesigned workaround for cases where the domain name in a URL almost matches the domain name in an X.509 server certificate (but differs in the initial *www.* substring).

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function tracing_readme_read is a file-read callback; when userspace reads from the associated proc or debugfs file, this routine is invoked.  
   - It takes the userspace buffer pointer (ubuf), the requested byte count (cnt), and the current file offset pointer (ppos).  
   - It calls simple_read_from_buffer, passing:  
     • The userspace buffer and requested count,  
     • The offset pointer,  
     • A kernel‐static string readme_msg and its length (strlen(readme_msg)).  
   - simple_read_from_buffer handles slicing the message based on *ppos, copies up to cnt bytes (or the remaining message length), updates *ppos, and returns the number of bytes copied (or an error if the copy_to_user fails).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - simple_read_from_buffer internally bounds the copy by the message length and the user’s requested cnt, preventing buffer overruns.  
   - It uses the safe copy_to_user mechanism to transfer data to userspace and checks for faults, returning -EFAULT on failure.  
   - There is no modifiable or external data influencing readme_msg or its length, so there is no risk of a dynamic overflow.  
   - Because readme_msg is a constant kernel string, there are no race conditions altering its size or content.  
   - No unchecked pointer dereferences or arithmetic on user-provided values beyond what simple_read_from_buffer internally manages.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code is not vulnerable. It cleanly and safely copies a fixed kernel string into userspace using the kernel-provided simple_read_from_buffer helper, which prevents overflows and handles user-space faults.

original_information.Summary: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.2. The filter parsing in kernel/trace/trace_events_filter.c could be called with no filter, which is an N=0 case when it expected at least one line to have been read, thus making the N-1 index invalid. This allows attackers to cause a denial of service (slab out-of-bounds write) or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted perf_event_open and mmap system calls.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `nfs41_check_expired_stateid` takes three arguments:  
  • `state`: a pointer to an NFSv4 state object  
  • `stateid`: a pointer to an NFSv4 stateid structure  
  • `flags`: a bitmask indicating which stateid flags to check  

- It initializes `status` to `NFS_OK`.  
- It retrieves the NFS server context from `state->inode`.  
- It checks whether any of the bits in `flags` are set in `state->flags`.  
  - If none are set, it simply returns `NFS_OK`.  
  - If at least one bit is set:  
    - It calls `nfs41_test_stateid(server, stateid)` to verify if the supplied stateid is still valid.  
    - If the test reports an error (i.e., `status != NFS_OK`):  
      • It calls `nfs41_free_stateid(server, stateid)` to release or deallocate resources associated with that stateid.  
      • It clears the corresponding bits in `state->flags` to reflect that those flags are no longer active.  
- Finally, it returns the status from the test (either `NFS_OK` or an error code).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no direct user-controlled input being parsed or copied in this small routine; it merely inspects existing kernel data structures.  
- The bitwise check and clear operations on `state->flags` are atomic with respect to this function (they do not introduce buffer overflows or pointer arithmetic).  
- The calls to `nfs41_test_stateid` and `nfs41_free_stateid` assume that those helper routines correctly validate their inputs and handle errors. This wrapper does not misuse their return values or leak resources—on error it both frees the stateid and clears the flag bits.  
- No unsafe memory accesses, unchecked pointers, or arithmetic on user data are visible here. Concurrency issues (e.g., racing flag bits) would need to be addressed at a higher locking level, which is outside the scope of this snippet.

3. Decision

No, this code contains no evident vulnerabilities—it cleanly tests a stateid, frees it on failure, and updates flags accordingly.

original_information.Summary: The __nfs4_get_acl_uncached function in fs/nfs/nfs4proc.c in the NFSv4 implementation in the Linux kernel before 3.3.2 uses an incorrect length variable during a copy operation, which allows remote NFS servers to cause a denial of service (OOPS) by sending an excessive number of bitmap words in an FATTR4_ACL reply.  NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2011-4131.

- Call __archive_read_ahead(a, 1, &bytes) to fetch at least 1 byte of raw archive data into the buffer b; bytes receives the number of bytes actually available or a negative error code.  
- If bytes < 0, propagate the error code. If bytes == 0, report “Truncated archive file” and return ARCHIVE_FATAL.  
- If the available bytes exceed the caller’s remaining byte quota, reduce bytes to that quota.  
- Store the (possibly clamped) byte count in *used.  
- Call decompress(a, buff, size, b, used), which consumes up to *used input bytes from b, allocates or points *buff at the decompressed data, sets *size to the output length, and may adjust *used to the actual number of input bytes consumed.

1. Functional Analysis  
   
   The function fcrypt_setkey initializes a DES-like cipher key schedule from an 8-byte key input. It does so differently on 64-bit vs. 32-bit platforms, but the overall steps are:  
   • Read eight input bytes, drop each byte’s least significant bit (the DES parity bit), and pack the remaining 56 bits into either a single 64-bit word (u64 k) or two words (hi:upper 24 bits, lo:lower 32 bits).  
   • Generate 16 round subkeys by taking the current 56-bit state, extracting its low 32 bits in big-endian order into ctx->sched[i], then rotating the full 56-bit state left by 11 positions before the next round.  
   • Return success (0).  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  

   • Buffer Overread / Out-of-Bounds Access  
     – The code reads exactly eight bytes from the pointer key without checking keylen. If the caller passes a key pointer shorter than 8 bytes (or an invalid pointer), this could overrun memory. However, in a well-formed crypto API, keylen is expected to be 8 and the caller enforces it. As written, the function itself does not guard against a too-small key buffer.  
   • Integer Overflows / Undefined Behavior  
     – All shifts and bit-masks are on u64 or u32/24+32 parts and are bounded; no undefined shift counts occur. The custom rotate macros (ror56_64/ror56) handle rotation on a 56-bit value and do not overflow beyond their container.  
   • Endianness / Portability  
     – The code explicitly stores each subkey in big-endian form (cpu_to_be32). That is intentional for the DES rounds and not a vulnerability.  
   • Side-Channel (Timing)  
     – There are no secret-dependent branches or table lookups here—just fixed shifts, rotates, and stores—so timing side-channels in key schedule generation are minimal.  
   • Other  
     – No dynamic allocation, no use of unsafe string or memory functions.  

3. Decision  
No, the code does not inherently contain memory or logic vulnerabilities assuming the caller supplies a valid 8-byte key. The only minor gap is that keylen is ignored, so misuse (keylen < 8) could lead to an overread.

net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

This prevents numerous uninitialized memory leaks we had in the
recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

Optimize for the case recvfrom is called with NULL as address. We don't
need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Also document these changes in include/linux/net.h as suggested by David
Miller.

Changes since RFC:

Set msg->msg_name = NULL if user specified a NULL in msg_name but had a
non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "
if (!uaddr || msg_sys->msg_namelen == 0)
	msg->msg_name = NULL
".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

Also remove two unnecessary curly brackets in ___sys_recvmsg and change
comments to netdev style.

  - For flush or FUA bios, attach the bio to the request, insert the flush, and jump to `run_queue`.

  - Retrieve the current task’s plug.

  - No arithmetic on bio lengths or queue depths that could overflow.  
  - Splitting ensures no bio exceeds hardware limits.  

- Authorization or Privilege Checks  
  - Not applicable at this layer; proper higher‑level checks are assumed.  

- Resource Leaks  
  - The mapping context and request objects are cleaned up on error or normal completion.  

Overall, this code follows standard block‑layer patterns for I/O merging, splitting, flushing, and queue insertion without exposing memory corruption, race conditions, or unchecked arithmetic.

No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities.

- It calls `put_NXAST_CLONE(out)`, which appends a placeholder "clone" action header into the buffer and returns a pointer (`eah`) to that header.

- It adds the size of the header (`sizeof *eah`) to `len` to compute the total length of the clone action (header + nested actions).
- It retrieves the header pointer again at the original offset via `ofpbuf_at(out, ofs, sizeof *eah)`.

  → No raw pointers or unchecked writes outside the `ofpbuf` API are used, so standard buffer-overflow risks are mitigated.

  - `len` is computed as the sum of two size_t values: the nested-actions length and the header size. If that sum were to overflow, the stored length could be wrong.

  - All memory writes go through `ofpbuf`-managed functions; no raw malloc/free or manual pointer arithmetic is used outside these safe wrappers.

original_information.commit_message:
tunnels: Don't apply GRO to multiple layers of encapsulation.

When drivers express support for TSO of encapsulated packets, they
only mean that they can do it for one layer of encapsulation.
Supporting additional levels would mean updating, at a minimum,
more IP length fields and they are unaware of this.

No encapsulation device expresses support for handling offloaded
encapsulated packets, so we won't generate these types of frames
in the transmit path. However, GRO doesn't have a check for
multiple levels of encapsulation and will attempt to build them.

UDP tunnel GRO actually does prevent this situation but it only
handles multiple UDP tunnels stacked on top of each other. This
generalizes that solution to prevent any kind of tunnel stacking
that would cause problems.

original_information.commit_message:
crypto: aesni - fix memory usage in GCM decryption

The kernel crypto API logic requires the caller to provide the
length of (ciphertext || authentication tag) as cryptlen for the
AEAD decryption operation. Thus, the cipher implementation must
calculate the size of the plaintext output itself and cannot simply use
cryptlen.

The RFC4106 GCM decryption operation tries to overwrite cryptlen memory
in req->dst. As the destination buffer for decryption only needs to hold
the plaintext memory but cryptlen references the input buffer holding
(ciphertext || authentication tag), the assumption of the destination
buffer length in RFC4106 GCM operation leads to a too large size. This
patch simply uses the already calculated plaintext size.

In addition, this patch fixes the offset calculation of the AAD buffer
pointer: as mentioned before, cryptlen already includes the size of the
tag. Thus, the tag does not need to be added. With the addition, the AAD
will be written beyond the already allocated buffer.

Note, this fixes a kernel crash that can be triggered from user space
via AF_ALG(aead) -- simply use the libkcapi test application
from [1] and update it to use rfc4106-gcm-aes.

Using [1], the changes were tested using CAVS vectors to demonstrate
that the crypto operation still delivers the right results.

[1] http://www.chronox.de/libkcapi.html

Ignore updatePipBounds before initial bounds is set

When PIP enter/exit transition happens, window state change and
initial bounds change are committed in the same commit. However,
as state change is applied first in OnPreWidgetCommit and the
bounds is update later, if updatePipBounds is called between the
gap, it ends up returning a wrong bounds based on the previous
bounds.

Currently, there are two callstacks that end up triggering
updatePipBounds between the gap: (i) The state change causes
OnWindowAddedToLayout and updatePipBounds is called in OnWMEvent,
(ii) updatePipBounds is called in UpdatePipState to prevent it
from being placed under some system ui.

As it doesn't make sense to call updatePipBounds before the first
bounds is not set, this CL adds a boolean to defer updatePipBounds.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - Allocate a temporary `cfg` struct to hold port settings (packet length, baud rate, etc.).  
   - Call `klsi_105_chg_port_settings(port, cfg)` to send an initial configuration to the device.  
   - Acquire the driver’s spinlock and copy the line-discipline (termios) settings from the `tty` into the driver’s private data, and mirror the `cfg` values into `priv->cfg`.  
   - Release the spinlock.  
   - Invoke `usb_serial_generic_open()` to set up the USB serial pipes and URBs.  
   - Send a vendor-specific control message (READ_ON) to enable inbound data.  
   - Query the device’s modem line state via `klsi_105_get_line_state()` and store it under lock in `priv->line_state`.  
   - On any failure along the way, undo what has been done (disable READ, close generics, free `cfg`) and return the error.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - No user-supplied data is copied into fixed-size buffers, so there is no obvious buffer overflow.  
   - The use of spinlocks around accesses to shared state prevents race conditions on `priv->termios`, `priv->cfg`, and `priv->line_state`.  
   - Control messages use fixed-size transfers (zero-length payloads or well-defined sizes), so there is no risk of a length-mismatch exploit there.  
   - One minor issue: on the success path `cfg` is never freed, leading to a memory (resource) leak, but not a security boundary violation.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a security vulnerability. It functions correctly aside from leaking the temporary `cfg` allocation on success.

original_information.Summary: The klsi_105_get_line_state function in drivers/usb/serial/kl5kusb105.c in the Linux kernel before 4.9.5 places uninitialized heap-memory contents into a log entry upon a failure to read the line status, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information by reading the log.
original_information.commit_message:
USB: serial: kl5kusb105: fix line-state error handling

The current implementation failed to detect short transfers when
attempting to read the line state, and also, to make things worse,
logged the content of the uninitialised heap transfer buffer.

Fixes: abf492e7b3ae ("USB: kl5kusb105: fix DMA buffers on stack")
Fixes: 1da177e4c3f4 ("Linux-2.6.12-rc2")

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `bgp_route_refresh_print` is a packet‐printing routine, intended to be called when a BGP Route Refresh message has been captured.  
   - It takes three parameters:  
     • `ndo` – a pointer to printing/context options (`netdissect_options`).  
     • `pptr` – a pointer to the raw packet bytes.  
     • `len`  – the number of bytes remaining in the packet buffer.  
   - It first checks (via `ND_TCHECK2`) that at least `BGP_ROUTE_REFRESH_SIZE` bytes are available at `pptr`.  
   - If `len` is less than the minimum header size (`BGP_ROUTE_REFRESH_SIZE`), it returns immediately (no output).  
   - It then casts `pptr` to a `struct bgp_route_refresh *` to access the AFI (Address Family Identifier) and SAFI (Subsequent Address Family Identifier) fields.  
   - It prints the AFI and SAFI values (both as numeric values and human‐readable names obtained via `tok2str`).  
   - If the verbosity flag `ndo->ndo_vflag` is greater than 1, it again bounds‐checks the full `len` bytes and dumps any remaining data in hex.  
   - On any truncation error, control flows to the `trunc:` label and prints a generic “[|BGP]” truncation indicator.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer over‐reads/writes: The code uses `ND_TCHECK2` macros before accessing packet data and also compares `len` against the minimum header size. This prevents out‐of‐bounds reads.  
   - Integer overflows: There are no pointer arithmetic or length calculations that could overflow. The two‐byte AFI field is extracted in a fixed, safe manner.  
   - Format‐string issues: All `ND_PRINT` calls use constant format strings; no user‐controlled input is used as a format specifier.  
   - Other issues: The redundant `ND_TCHECK2(*pptr, len)` in the verbosity branch is consistent with the style in tcpdump’s dissection code and ensures the entire payload is captured before calling `print_unknown_data`. There is no evidence it leads to misuse or a security hole.  

   Conclusion: all data accesses are pre‐validated for length, and there is no unbounded memory operation or format‐string exposure.  

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly performs bounds checks before data access, uses safe format strings, and handles truncation gracefully.

original_information.Summary: The BGP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-bgp.c:decode_rt_routing_info().
original_information.commit_message:
CVE-2017-13053/BGP: fix VPN route target bounds checks

decode_rt_routing_info() didn't check bounds before fetching 4 octets of
the origin AS field and could over-read the input buffer, put it right.

It also fetched the varying number of octets of the route target field
from 4 octets lower than the correct offset, put it right.

It also used the same temporary buffer explicitly through as_printf()
and implicitly through bgp_vpn_rd_print() so the end result of snprintf()
was not what was originally intended.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,
SecT/TU Berlin.

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

original_information.commit_message:
perf/core: Fix concurrent sys_perf_event_open() vs. 'move_group' race

Di Shen reported a race between two concurrent sys_perf_event_open()
calls where both try and move the same pre-existing software group
into a hardware context.

The problem is exactly that described in commit:

  f63a8daa5812 ("perf: Fix event->ctx locking")

... where, while we wait for a ctx->mutex acquisition, the event->ctx
relation can have changed under us.

That very same commit failed to recognise sys_perf_event_context() as an
external access vector to the events and thereby didn't apply the
established locking rules correctly.

So while one sys_perf_event_open() call is stuck waiting on
mutex_lock_double(), the other (which owns said locks) moves the group
about. So by the time the former sys_perf_event_open() acquires the
locks, the context we've acquired is stale (and possibly dead).

Apply the established locking rules as per perf_event_ctx_lock_nested()
to the mutex_lock_double() for the 'move_group' case. This obviously means
we need to validate state after we acquire the locks.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `ehci_frame_timer(void *opaque)` is a timer callback invoked periodically to advance the EHCI (USB 2.0 host controller) frame and microframe scheduler in QEMU.  
- It reads the current virtual time (`t_now`) and computes how many microframes have elapsed since the last run (`ns_elapsed / UFRAME_TIMER_NS`).  
- If the periodic schedule is active or the port state is not inactive, it:  
  • Marks that it will need to re-arm the timer (`need_timer++`).  
  • Caps the number of microframes processed per invocation to prevent overly long loops (“skips” extra microframes).  
  • Iterates up to that capped count of microframes:  
    – Commits an interrupt if the guest has requested one (IOC)  
    – Updates the frame index (`ehci_update_frindex`)  
    – Advances the internal periodic schedule every 8 microframes  
    – Advances the recorded last-run timestamp by one microframe each iteration  
- If the periodic schedule is inactive, it simply advances the frame index and last-run timestamp by the total elapsed microframes, and clears the periodic active counter.  
- Next, it updates an “async stepdown” counter based on whether periodic scheduling remains active; this controls how quickly asynchronous transfers are revisited.  
- It then services asynchronous transfers once per timer tick if enabled or pending (`ehci_advance_async_state`).  
- Any pending USB status changes or frame list rollover requests bump `need_timer` so that the timer is re-armed.  
- Finally, it chooses the next expiration time:  
  • If an interrupt was just raised by asynchronous processing, it schedules a fast follow-up  
  • Otherwise it uses a delay proportional to the current async stepdown count  
- The timer is re-armed via `timer_mod()` if `need_timer` is nonzero.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety: the code makes no unbounded allocations or pointer arithmetic, and it does not read or write past defined arrays or buffers.  
- Integer overflow:  
  • The computation of `ns_elapsed = t_now - ehci->last_run_ns` is performed in uint64_t; in normal operation `t_now ≥ last_run_ns`. If QEMU is suspended for a very long time, `ns_elapsed` may become very large, but the code immediately caps the per-invocation microframe count to `maxframes * 8`.  
  • The subtraction `skipped_uframes = uframes - cap` can be large only if `uframes` is slightly above the cap; in fact the code ensures afterwards `uframes = cap`. The update to `last_run_ns += UFRAME_TIMER_NS * skipped_uframes` multiplies two 32‑bit quantities and adds to a 64‑bit timestamp; in an extreme VM‑pause scenario, this could wrap the timestamp. In practice this only affects timing behavior, not memory safety or control flow, and is bounded by the cap.  
- Denial‑of‑service: a very long VM pause (or injected large timestamp gap) could cause the code to “skip” a large number of microframes in one shot. This may make the EHCI state advance abruptly, but it does not lead to unbounded loops (the loop is capped) or crashes.  
- Interrupt handling: the code properly checks and clears flags on each frame, so no interrupt starvation or “silent” hangs should occur.  
- Overall, there is no buffer overflow, code‑injection, use‑after‑free, or other typical memory‑corruption vulnerability. The worst‐case behavior under extreme time gaps is a transient scheduling hiccup, not a security compromise.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities. It safely bounds its per‑tick work, does not perform unsafe memory access, and handles its timer accounting in a controlled manner.

vfs: Carefully propogate mounts across user namespaces

As a matter of policy MNT_READONLY should not be changable if the
original mounter had more privileges than creator of the mount
namespace.

Add the flag CL_UNPRIVILEGED to note when we are copying a mount from
a mount namespace that requires more privileges to a mount namespace
that requires fewer privileges.

if any of the mnt flags that should never be changed are set.

This protects both mount propagation and the initial creation of a less
privileged mount namespace.

original_information.commit_message:
ext4: fix undefined behavior in ext4_fill_flex_info()

Commit 503358ae01b70ce6909d19dd01287093f6b6271c ("ext4: avoid divide by
zero when trying to mount a corrupted file system") fixes CVE-2009-4307
by performing a sanity check on s_log_groups_per_flex, since it can be
set to a bogus value by an attacker.

	sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex = sbi->s_es->s_log_groups_per_flex;
	groups_per_flex = 1 << sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex;

	if (groups_per_flex < 2) { ... }

This patch fixes two potential issues in the previous commit.

1) The sanity check might only work on architectures like PowerPC.
On x86, 5 bits are used for the shifting amount.  That means, given a
large s_log_groups_per_flex value like 36, groups_per_flex = 1 << 36
is essentially 1 << 4 = 16, rather than 0.  This will bypass the check,
leaving s_log_groups_per_flex and groups_per_flex inconsistent.

2) The sanity check relies on undefined behavior, i.e., oversized shift.
A standard-confirming C compiler could rewrite the check in unexpected
ways.  Consider the following equivalent form, assuming groups_per_flex
is unsigned for simplicity.

	groups_per_flex = 1 << sbi->s_log_groups_per_flex;
	if (groups_per_flex == 0 || groups_per_flex == 1) {

We compile the code snippet using Clang 3.0 and GCC 4.6.  Clang will
completely optimize away the check groups_per_flex == 0, leaving the
patched code as vulnerable as the original.  GCC keeps the check, but
there is no guarantee that future versions will do the same.

- Parameter setup  
  The function takes a connection record (`conn`), an optional directory configuration (`dir_config`), a lookup type (`type`), and an optional flag pointer (`str_is_ip`). If the caller does not supply `str_is_ip`, the function uses a local `ignored_str_is_ip` and initializes it to zero.

  If `dir_config` is present, the code pulls the `hostname_lookups` setting from the core module config. If that setting is unset, it defaults to `HOSTNAME_LOOKUP_OFF`. Without `dir_config`, it also defaults to off.

- First reverse lookup pass  
  If the caller has requested a lookup (anything other than `REMOTE_NOLOOKUP`), the connection’s `remote_host` has not yet been set, and either  
    • the caller explicitly asked for a double reverse lookup (`REMOTE_DOUBLE_REV`), or  
    • hostname lookups are enabled in the config,  
  then the code invokes `apr_getnameinfo()` on the client address. On success, it lower‐cases the returned hostname.  
  If the configuration demanded a “double” reversal, it calls `do_double_reverse()`. If that check does not yield a match (i.e., the forward lookup of the PTR record does not match the original IP), it discards the hostname.  
  On failure of any lookup, it sets `conn->remote_host` to the empty string to mark “lookup attempted but no name.”

- Second pass for strict double reverse  
  If the caller explicitly requested only `REMOTE_DOUBLE_REV`, the function again calls `do_double_reverse()`. If that fails with `-1`, it returns `NULL` immediately.

- Return decision  
  Finally, if `conn->remote_host` is non‐empty, it returns that string. Otherwise, if the request was for a hostname (`REMOTE_HOST` or `REMOTE_DOUBLE_REV`), it returns `NULL`; for any other request type, it sets `*str_is_ip = 1` and returns the client’s IP string.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory safety  
  All string operations (`apr_getnameinfo`, `ap_str_tolower`, and the empty‐string assignment) operate on APR‐managed or pool‐allocated buffers. There is no manual buffer slicing or unchecked `strcpy`-style use. This code path does not introduce stack or heap overflow risks.

- Input validation / injection  
  The function never uses the hostname in a context that would introduce injection (e.g., shell or SQL) without further sanitization. It simply returns a pointer to an APR-allocated string.

- Denial of Service (performance)  
  Reverse DNS lookups over the network can block or slow request processing, potentially opening a path to resource exhaustion if abused. However, the code respects configuration flags (`HOSTNAME_LOOKUP_OFF` by default) and only performs lookups when explicitly enabled or requested, mitigating accidental DoS.

- DNS spoofing or poisoning  
  The “double reverse” check attempts to mitigate simple DNS spoofing by verifying that the forward lookup of the PTR record matches the original IP. Beyond that, it relies on the underlying DNS infrastructure and APR routines.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a direct vulnerability. It safely handles memory, respects configuration, and includes a “double reverse” guard against basic DNS spoofing.

respond_before:
1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function returns the number of bytes per pixel that WebGL is “externally” allocating (i.e. color, depth, stencil, and any multisample buffers) for a given rendering context.  
   - It first checks if the context is lost; if so, it reports 0.  
   - It assumes a base color buffer size of 4 bytes per pixel and accounts for both front and back buffers (hence `bytes_per_pixel * 2`).  
   - It queries the drawing buffer’s sample count (for multisampling) and retrieves the current context attributes (antialias, depth, stencil).  
   - If antialiasing is enabled, there are samples > 0, and the drawing buffer uses explicit multisample resolve:  
       • If depth or stencil are also enabled, it adds `samples * bytes_per_pixel` to cover the multisampled depth/stencil buffer.  
       • It always adds `samples * bytes_per_pixel` for the multisampled color buffer.  
   - Otherwise, if just depth or stencil is enabled (but no explicit multisample resolve), it adds a single `bytes_per_pixel` for a regular depth/stencil buffer.  
   - Finally it returns the computed total.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - There is no use of user‐provided strings, no pointer arithmetic, no external memory writes, and no dynamic allocations driven by this value—so classic buffer overflows, injection flaws, or use‐after‐free bugs are not present.  
   - The only internal numeric inputs are the sample count and fixed byte‐per‐pixel constants. In pathological cases a very large sample count could wrap the 32‑bit integer, but in practice sample counts are small (commonly 0, 2, 4, 8). Even if overflow occurred, it would only yield a nonsensical size metric, not a security breach.  

3. Decision  
   No, this code does not contain a security vulnerability. It performs a straightforward, bounded arithmetic computation to report resource usage.

original_information.Summary: Heap buffer overflow in WebGL in Google Chrome prior to 61.0.3163.79 for Windows allowed a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code inside a sandbox via a crafted HTML page.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function kvm_vm_ioctl is the entry point for VM-level ioctls on a KVM file descriptor.  
- It first checks that the calling process’s mm_struct matches the VM’s owner (kvm->mm vs. current->mm), returning -EIO otherwise.  
- It then switches on the ioctl number and, for each supported command, performs these general steps:  
  • Copies an input structure from userspace to kernel space via copy_from_user (if the ioctl takes a struct argument).  
  • Invokes an internal helper (e.g. kvm_vm_ioctl_create_vcpu, kvm_vm_ioctl_set_memory_region, kvm_irqfd, etc.) to perform the requested operation.  
  • If the ioctl returns data, copies results back to userspace via copy_to_user.  
  • Sets or returns an appropriate error code in r.  
- For commands that allocate temporary kernel memory (e.g. GSI routing entries), it allocates with vmalloc, checks for allocation failure, and always frees the memory before returning.  
- Unrecognized ioctls are forwarded first to kvm_arch_vm_ioctl and, if still -ENOTTY, to kvm_vm_ioctl_assigned_device.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- User-to-kernel copies  
  All user-supplied structs are copied in via copy_from_user with an immediate check for failure returning -EFAULT.  Any data returned to the caller is copied out via copy_to_user.  There are no raw user pointers dereferenced without validation.  
- Bounds checks  
  - KVM_SET_GSI_ROUTING verifies routing.nr < KVM_MAX_IRQ_ROUTES and that flags == 0 before allocating.  
  - Other numeric arguments (e.g. memory-region slot numbers, irq numbers) are passed to lower-level routines which perform their own validation.  
- Resource management  
  - vmalloc’ed memory is freed on all failure paths.  
  - No memory leaks or use-after-free scenarios in this snippet.  
- Special-case paths  
  - KVM_SET_BOOT_CPU_ID stores the raw arg into kvm->bsp_vcpu_id but only if no vCPUs are online.  That ID is normally validated later when vCPUs are created.  
- No obvious integer overflows, buffer overruns, or missing privilege checks in this code fragment.  All user data is marshalled through well-defined structs, and error returns are handled immediately.

3. Decision

No, the code as shown does not contain any direct vulnerabilities. It properly marshals user data, bounds-checks counts, frees resources on error, and applies the necessary permission check.

original_information.Summary: Array index error in the kvm_vm_ioctl_create_vcpu function in virt/kvm/kvm_main.c in the KVM subsystem in the Linux kernel through 3.12.5 allows local users to gain privileges via a large id value.
original_information.commit_message:
KVM: Improve create VCPU parameter (CVE-2013-4587)

In multiple functions the vcpu_id is used as an offset into a bitfield.  Ag
malicious user could specify a vcpu_id greater than 255 in order to set or
clear bits in kernel memory.  This could be used to elevate priveges in the
kernel.  This patch verifies that the vcpu_id provided is less than 255.
The api documentation already specifies that the vcpu_id must be less than
max_vcpus, but this is currently not checked.

  Verifies (in debug builds) that the caller holds the queue’s spinlock. This is a self-check to ensure proper locking discipline before manipulating the queue state.

- WARN_ON_ONCE(q->mq_ops);  
  Emits a one-time warning if the queue has multi-queue operations enabled. It flags an unexpected code path but does not alter control flow.

- queue_flag_clear(QUEUE_FLAG_STOPPED, q);  
  Clears the “stopped” flag on the request queue. This marks the queue as runnable again.

- __blk_run_queue(q);  
  Internally invokes the block layer’s request dispatch logic to begin or resume processing I/O requests on the queue.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory Safety:  
  No pointer arithmetic or buffer operations are performed on user-supplied data. The only pointer dereferences (q->queue_lock, q->mq_ops) are on a kernel structure that is presumed valid when the lock is held.

- Concurrency/Races:  
  The function requires the queue lock held (enforced by lockdep_assert_held) before clearing the flag or running the queue. This prevents concurrent modification of the flag or queue state.

- Control-Flow Integrity:  
  The WARN_ON_ONCE is purely diagnostic. It does not skip critical code or introduce unsafe behavior.

- Input Validation:  
  There is no user input here; all operations act on internal kernel structures. No untrusted data influences the control flow in a way that could be exploited.

- Privilege/Access Control:  
  This function is internal to the block layer and only callable with the appropriate spinlock held. There is no public interface exposed to unprivileged code.

Conclusion: There is no indication of buffer overflows, use-after-free, integer overflows, race conditions (lock enforced), or other typical vulnerabilities in software. The WARN_ON_ONCE serves as a safety check but not a security issue.

No, this code does not contain vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
bpf: fix branch pruning logic

when the verifier detects that register contains a runtime constant
and it's compared with another constant it will prune exploration
of the branch that is guaranteed not to be taken at runtime.
This is all correct, but malicious program may be constructed
in such a way that it always has a constant comparison and
the other branch is never taken under any conditions.
In this case such path through the program will not be explored
by the verifier. It won't be taken at run-time either, but since
all instructions are JITed the malicious program may cause JITs
to complain about using reserved fields, etc.
To fix the issue we have to track the instructions explored by
the verifier and sanitize instructions that are dead at run time
with NOPs. We cannot reject such dead code, since llvm generates
it for valid C code, since it doesn't do as much data flow
analysis as the verifier does.

original_information.commit_message:
sctp: fix ASCONF list handling

->auto_asconf_splist is per namespace and mangled by functions like
sctp_setsockopt_auto_asconf() which doesn't guarantee any serialization.

Also, the call to inet_sk_copy_descendant() was backuping
->auto_asconf_list through the copy but was not honoring
->do_auto_asconf, which could lead to list corruption if it was
different between both sockets.

This commit thus fixes the list handling by using ->addr_wq_lock
spinlock to protect the list. A special handling is done upon socket
creation and destruction for that. Error handlig on sctp_init_sock()
will never return an error after having initialized asconf, so
sctp_destroy_sock() can be called without addrq_wq_lock. The lock now
will be take on sctp_close_sock(), before locking the socket, so we
don't do it in inverse order compared to sctp_addr_wq_timeout_handler().

Instead of taking the lock on sctp_sock_migrate() for copying and
restoring the list values, it's preferred to avoid rewritting it by
implementing sctp_copy_descendant().

Issue was found with a test application that kept flipping sysctl
default_auto_asconf on and off, but one could trigger it by issuing
simultaneous setsockopt() calls on multiple sockets or by
creating/destroying sockets fast enough. This is only triggerable
locally.

original_information.Summary: Use-after-free vulnerability in the shmem_remount_fs function in mm/shmem.c in the Linux kernel before 3.7.10 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (system crash) by remounting a tmpfs filesystem without specifying a required mpol (aka mempolicy) mount option.
original_information.commit_message:
tmpfs: fix use-after-free of mempolicy object

The tmpfs remount logic preserves filesystem mempolicy if the mpol=M
option is not specified in the remount request.  A new policy can be
specified if mpol=M is given.

Before this patch remounting an mpol bound tmpfs without specifying
mpol= mount option in the remount request would set the filesystem's
mempolicy object to a freed mempolicy object.

To reproduce the problem boot a DEBUG_PAGEALLOC kernel and run:
    # mkdir /tmp/x

    # mount -t tmpfs -o size=100M,mpol=interleave nodev /tmp/x

    # grep /tmp/x /proc/mounts
    nodev /tmp/x tmpfs rw,relatime,size=102400k,mpol=interleave:0-3 0 0

    # mount -o remount,size=200M nodev /tmp/x

    # grep /tmp/x /proc/mounts
    nodev /tmp/x tmpfs rw,relatime,size=204800k,mpol=??? 0 0
        # note ? garbage in mpol=... output above

    # dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/x/f count=1
        # panic here

Panic:
    BUG: unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at           (null)
    IP: [<          (null)>]           (null)
    [...]
    Oops: 0010 [#1] SMP DEBUG_PAGEALLOC
    Call Trace:
      mpol_shared_policy_init+0xa5/0x160
      shmem_get_inode+0x209/0x270
      shmem_mknod+0x3e/0xf0
      shmem_create+0x18/0x20
      vfs_create+0xb5/0x130
      do_last+0x9a1/0xea0
      path_openat+0xb3/0x4d0
      do_filp_open+0x42/0xa0
      do_sys_open+0xfe/0x1e0
      compat_sys_open+0x1b/0x20
      cstar_dispatch+0x7/0x1f

Non-debug kernels will not crash immediately because referencing the
dangling mpol will not cause a fault.  Instead the filesystem will
reference a freed mempolicy object, which will cause unpredictable
behavior.

The problem boils down to a dropped mpol reference below if
shmem_parse_options() does not allocate a new mpol:

    config = *sbinfo
    shmem_parse_options(data, &config, true)
    mpol_put(sbinfo->mpol)
    sbinfo->mpol = config.mpol  /* BUG: saves unreferenced mpol */

This patch avoids the crash by not releasing the mempolicy if
shmem_parse_options() doesn't create a new mpol.

How far back does this issue go? I see it in both 2.6.36 and 3.3.  I did
not look back further.

Previously StyleDifference was an enum that proximately bigger values
imply smaller values (e.g. StyleDifferenceLayout implies

- diff == StyleDifferenceEqual (&& !context) => diff.hasNoChange()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaintObjectOnly()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff == StyleDifferenceRepaint || diff == StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaint => diff.needsRepaint() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff >= StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsRepaintLayer() || diff.needsLayout()
- diff > StyleDifferenceRepaintLayer => diff.needsLayout()
- diff == StyleDifferencePositionedMovementLayoutOnly => diff.needsPositionedMovementLayoutOnly()

dccp: fix freeing skb too early for IPV6_RECVPKTINFO

In the current DCCP implementation an skb for a DCCP_PKT_REQUEST packet
is forcibly freed via __kfree_skb in dccp_rcv_state_process if
dccp_v6_conn_request successfully returns.

in dccp_rcv_state_process.

Fix by calling consume_skb instead of doing goto discard and therefore
calling __kfree_skb.
